docs.title: meta_cells_per_group
docs.text:
meta_cells_per_group(
    sc: SingleCells,
    group_col: str,
    *,
    method: MetacellMethod = "bootstrapped",
    mc_params: Mapping[str, object] | None = None,
    pipeline: Pipeline | None = None,
    groups: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    feature_space: str = "intersect",
    verbose: Verbose = True,
) -> MetaCells

Source-pure meta cells: one generator run per group, merged.

Meta cells never mix two groups (patients, samples), yet end up in one object. The generators need an embedding and usually a kNN, so pipeline will normally be step_hvg() >> step_pca(30) >> step_neighbours().

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sc SingleCells

The experiment.

required group_col str

obs column to split on.

required method MetacellMethod

"bootstrapped", "seacells" or "supercells".

'bootstrapped' mc_params Mapping[str, object] | None

Keyword arguments for the generator; SEACells needs seacell_params.

None pipeline Pipeline | None

Run on each subset before its meta cells are generated. Must hand back the subset.

None groups Sequence[str] | None

The levels to use; None for every level among the kept cells, in order of appearance.

None feature_space str

Passed to merge_meta_cells.

'intersect' verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

Returns:

Type Description MetaCells

The merged meta cells, a source_id column in obs.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If pipeline cannot run on, or does not return, a SingleCellsSubset, or mc_params do not bind to the generator.

ValueError

On a missing column, or a group without meta cells.

Examples:

>>> pipeline = bv.pipeline.step_hvg(hvg_no=500) >> bv.pipeline.step_pca(20)
>>> pipeline = pipeline >> bv.pipeline.step_neighbours()
>>> mc = bv.metacells.meta_cells_per_group(sc, "batch_index", pipeline=pipeline)

docs.title: merge_meta_cells
docs.text:
merge_meta_cells(
    inputs: Sequence[MetaCells] | dict[str, MetaCells],
    *,
    source_ids: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    feature_space: str = "intersect",
    prefix_ids: bool = True,
    verbose: Verbose = True,
) -> MetaCells

Row-bind several MetaCells into one.

The typical case is sample-pure meta cells, generated per patient and merged so that downstream methods run across the full set. The normalised counts carry over: they are normalised per meta cell, so row-binding leaves them valid. Caches and HVGs are per source and dropped.

original_cell_idx stays in each source's index space, which is why the diffusion and manifold metrics refuse a merged object.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inputs Sequence[MetaCells] | dict[str, MetaCells]

The meta cells; a dict names them by source.

required source_ids Sequence[str] | None

Source ids, unique, one per input. None takes the dict keys, else source_01, source_02, ...

None feature_space str

"intersect" or "union" of the gene spaces; with "union" a gene an input lacks is a structural zero for its meta cells.

'intersect' prefix_ids bool

Prefix the meta cell ids with "<source_id>__". Without it, ids repeated across inputs are an error.

True verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

Returns:

Type Description MetaCells

The merged meta cells, is_merged set, a source_id obs column and

MetaCells

the source ids in other_data["sources"].

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

docs.title: Multi-modal
docs.text:
Multi-modal single cell: ADT counts, their PCA and the WNN graph.

Adds a protein modality to a SingleCellsMultiModal, normalises it (CLR or DSB), runs a PCA over it and fuses it with the RNA through a weighted nearest neighbour (WNN) graph. The RNA side is a plain SingleCells, so every RNA function takes the object as it is.

Start with add_adt_counts, then calculate_pca_adt. Run the RNA PCA the usual way (bv.pp.find_hvg, bv.pp.calculate_pca) and call generate_wnn_graph. From there bv.graph.find_clusters and bv.embed take modality="wnn"; modality="adt" does the same for the protein side alone.

What lands where. add_adt_counts cuts the counts to the kept cells, normalises them and stores them in mm.adt; it also writes the var_adt table to the DuckDB and adt_nnz and adt_lib_size to obs. The counts stay in memory, not in the count store, and bv.io.save keeps them. calculate_pca_adt writes scores, loadings and singular values to mm.adt_cache. generate_wnn_graph puts the fused kNN, its graph and the per-cell modality weights in mm.wnn. new_adt_counts_clr, new_adt_counts_dsb and the get_* functions return their result and leave the experiment alone.

# adt_counts: dense cells x proteins array; barcodes and proteins: their labels
mm = bv.SingleCellsMultiModal(sc.dir)
bv.mm.add_adt_counts(mm, adt_counts, barcodes, proteins, method="clr")
bv.pp.find_hvg(mm, hvg_no=500)
bv.pp.calculate_pca(mm, no_pcs=20)
bv.mm.calculate_pca_adt(mm, no_pcs=10)
bv.mm.generate_wnn_graph(mm)
bv.graph.find_clusters(mm, modality="wnn")
weights = bv.mm.get_wnn_weights(mm)

Gotchas. Every kept cell needs a row in the ADT barcodes, or add_adt_counts raises. The matrix is cut to the kept cells when you add it: dropping cells afterwards is fine, putting dropped cells back is not (calculate_pca_adt then raises). DSB wants the isotype controls by default (DsbParams.use_isotype_controls), so pass isotype_names, or switch the option off. Leave the isotypes out of the ADT PCA with features=. generate_wnn_graph needs the PCA of both modalities, rebuilds the per-modality kNN graphs itself at knn_range neighbours rather than reusing the cached ones, and replaces any earlier WNN result with its embeddings.

Worked through in Multi-modal single cell analysis with bixverse.

generate_wnn_graph(
    mm: SingleCellsMultiModal,
    *,

docs.title: NMF
docs.text:
Non-negative matrix factorisation of the counts into gene programmes.

HALS NMF, factorising genes by cells into gene loadings (w, genes by k) and cell usages (h, k by cells). One run, random restarts, consensus NMF in the cNMF style, and a sweep over k.

Start with nmf_k_sweep to pick k: it runs the consensus step for every k in the range and returns stability and reconstruction error per k. High stability while the error is still falling is the sweet spot. Then fit consensus_nmf at that k. nmf is one run, stabilised_nmf keeps all the random restarts and get_best_run pulls out the lowest-loss one.

What lands where. Nothing is written to the experiment. Every function returns a result object, and get_w gives the gene loadings as a frame. get_data turns the cell usages of an NmfResult or ConsensusNmfResult into an obs frame, one comp_XX column per component, for sc.add_obs. All functions take a SingleCells, a SingleCellsSubset or a MetaCells. Genes default to the HVGs, so run bv.pp.find_hvg first or pass gene_ids; cells default to the kept ones.

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=500)
sweep = bv.nmf.nmf_k_sweep(sc, k_range=range(3, 8), n_runs=10)
sweep.frame
res = bv.nmf.consensus_nmf(sc, k=5, n_runs=10)
sc.add_obs(bv.nmf.get_data(res))
loadings = bv.nmf.get_w(res)

Gotchas. The factorisation uses the normalised counts; pass use_second_layer=False for the raw ones. The consensus step needs k and n_runs of at least 2 and raises when the restarts do not agree, with a message on what to change (a higher density_threshold in NmfConsensusParams, more runs, another k). In nmf_k_sweep a failing k gets a null stability and a warning instead. consensus_target="w" clusters in cell space and gets expensive past 20,000 cells. Indices are 0-based, the comp_XX and component_id names count from 1.

Worked through in Gene set analysis and GRN inference on PBMCs.

True nmf_hals_params NmfHalsParams | None

The solver.

None nmf_consensus_params NmfConsensusParams | None

The consensus step. None uses the defaults.

None n_runs int

Number of restarts, at least 2.

30 seed int

Base seed of the restarts and the consensus k-means.

42 verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

docs.title: nn
docs.text:
Neural network models trained straight off a bixverse store.

scVI (Lopez et al., 2018) for batch correction, on torch, MLX or JAX. Counts stream from the store through the Rust loader; nothing goes through AnnData. Importing this module needs no framework; training on one needs its extra, bixverse[torch], bixverse[mlx] or bixverse[jax].

>>> import bixverse.nn as bvnn
>>> fit = bvnn.train_scvi("counts_cells.bin", cells, hvg, batch)
>>> latent = bvnn.scvi_latent(fit, "counts_cells.bin", cells, batch)

Wrapper function for parameters for neighbour identification in single cell

Attributes:

Name Type Description knn_sym Literal['snn', 'umap', 'knn']

How to symmetrise the kNN into a graph. Clustering resolutions do not carry over between the methods: the "umap" and "knn" graphs only hold kNN pairs, the sNN graph also links cells that share neighbours and prunes weak edges. The same resolution can give more or fewer communities depending on the data, so retune it when switching.

snn_similarity Literal['jaccard', 'rank']

"snn" only. "jaccard" weighs an edge by the Jaccard index of the two (self-inclusive) neighbour sets. "rank" takes the shared neighbour with the lowest combined rank, so closer shared neighbours give heavier edges. Both are scaled to [0, 1].

pruning float

"snn" only. Edges below this weight are dropped. For the Jaccard weight a threshold p keeps pairs that share at least a fraction 2p / (1 + p) of their (self-inclusive) neighbourhoods, rounded up to whole cells, so the same value means the same thing at any k. The default asks for about 12%, i.e. 2 of 16 shared cells at k = 15, in line with Seurat's 1/15. Avoid a threshold that equals one of the discrete weights exactly, or float rounding decides whether the edge survives.

rescue bool

"snn" only. Reconnect the small components that pruning cuts off via their strongest sNN edge, so they do not turn up as tiny clusters.

local_connectivity float

"umap" only. Number of nearest neighbours assumed to be fully connected, as in umap-learn.

mix_ratio float

"umap" only. 1 is the fuzzy union of the directed kNN memberships, 0 the fuzzy intersection (umap-learn's set_op_mix_ratio).

binary bool

"knn" only. If True, every edge weighs 1. Otherwise mutual neighbours weigh 2 and one-sided ones 1.

k int

Number of neighbours.

knn_method Literal['kmknn', 'hnsw', 'annoy', 'nndescent', 'ivf', 'exhaustive']

Which method to use for the approximate nearest neighbour search. "nndescent" hands back the graph the NN-Descent built, with no index and no query pass. Rows the descent left short are re-queried exactly.

diversify_prob float

ef_budget int | None

NNDescent param: optional query budget. Only used where a query runs against an NN-Descent index, not for the graph of a self kNN.

docs.title: FastClusterParams dataclass
docs.text:
FastClusterParams(
    *,
    n_centroids: int | None = None,
    km_type: Literal["standard", "minibatch"] = "standard",
    k_means_iter: int = 100,
    batch_size: int = 4096,
    drift_threshold: float = 0.0001,
    lr_alpha: float = 1.0,
    dist: Literal["euclidean", "cosine"] = "euclidean",
    cell_mediated: bool = False,
    n_anchors: int = 5,
    centroid_k: int = 15,
    knn_sym: Literal["snn", "umap", "knn"] = "snn",
    snn_similarity: Literal["jaccard", "rank"] = "jaccard",
    pruning: float = 0.0625,
    rescue: bool = True,
    local_connectivity: float = 1.0,
    mix_ratio: float = 1.0,
    binary: bool = False,
    algorithm: Literal["louvain", "leiden"] = "louvain",
    n_iterations: int | None = None,
    beta: float = 0.01,
    min_gain: float = 0.0,
    local_moving: Literal["queue", "coloured"] = "queue",
    multi_level: bool = True,
    max_evals: int = 10,
)

Fast single cell clustering parameters

Fast clustering coarsens the cells with k-means, builds a graph over the centroids and runs Louvain or Leiden on it. The community of each centroid is handed back to its cells.

Attributes:

Name Type Description n_centroids int | None

Number of k-means centroids. If None, defaults to floor(4 * sqrt(n_cells)).

km_type Literal['standard', 'minibatch']

Which k-means to run for the coarsening.

k_means_iter int

Number of k-means iterations.

batch_size int

km_type = "minibatch" only. Batch size.

drift_threshold float

km_type = "minibatch" only. The mini batch k-means stops once the centroid drift falls below this.

lr_alpha float

km_type = "minibatch" only. Learning rate alpha.

dist Literal['euclidean', 'cosine']

Distance for the k-means and the centroid graph.

cell_mediated bool

Shall the cell-mediated centroid graph from Secuer be built instead of the kNN graph on the centroids. Centroids are then linked by the cells that sit near both, so two centroids that are close in space but have no cells between them stay apart. If True, centroid_k and centroid_graph are ignored.

n_anchors int

Number of nearest centroids each cell links to in the cell- mediated graph. Only used if cell_mediated = True.

centroid_k int

Neighbours per centroid in the exact centroid kNN. Only used if cell_mediated = False.

knn_sym Literal['snn', 'umap', 'knn']

How to symmetrise the kNN into a graph. Clustering resolutions do not carry over between the methods: the "umap" and "knn" graphs only hold kNN pairs, the sNN graph also links cells that share neighbours and prunes weak edges. The same resolution can give more or fewer communities depending on the data, so retune it when switching.

snn_similarity Literal['jaccard', 'rank']

"snn" only. "jaccard" weighs an edge by the Jaccard index of the two (self-inclusive) neighbour sets. "rank" takes the shared neighbour with the lowest combined rank, so closer shared neighbours give heavier edges. Both are scaled to [0, 1].

pruning float

"snn" only. Edges below this weight are dropped. For the Jaccard weight a threshold p keeps pairs that share at least a fraction 2p / (1 + p) of their (self-inclusive) neighbourhoods, rounded up to whole cells, so the same value means the same thing at any k. The default asks for about 12%, i.e. 2 of 16 shared cells at k = 15, in line with Seurat's 1/15. Avoid a threshold that equals one of the discrete weights exactly, or float rounding decides whether the edge survives.

rescue bool

"snn" only. Reconnect the small components that pruning cuts off via their strongest sNN edge, so they do not turn up as tiny clusters.

local_connectivity float

"umap" only. Number of nearest neighbours assumed to be fully connected, as in umap-learn.

mix_ratio float

"umap" only. 1 is the fuzzy union of the directed kNN memberships, 0 the fuzzy intersection (umap-learn's set_op_mix_ratio).

binary bool

"knn" only. If True, every edge weighs 1. Otherwise mutual neighbours weigh 2 and one-sided ones 1.

algorithm Literal['louvain', 'leiden']

Community detection on the centroid graph.

n_iterations int | None

Number of iterations of the community detection. A negative value iterates until stable. If None, 2 for Louvain and 5 for Leiden, which gave the best modularity across synthetic graphs.

beta float

Leiden only. Randomness of the refinement step.

min_gain float

With a negative n_iterations, also stop once an iteration gains no more than this in modularity.

local_moving Literal['queue', 'coloured']

"queue" is Traag's sequential queue. "coloured" moves the nodes of one colour class in parallel, which only kicks in on larger levels of the graph.

multi_level bool

Shall the communities be aggregated and refined in levels.

max_evals int

Cap on the node evaluations per local moving phase, in units of the number of nodes.

CellsweepParams(
    *,
    freeze_empties: bool = True,
    freeze_ambient_profile: bool = True,
    init_alpha: float = 0.9,
    init_beta: float = 0.1,
    alpha_cap: float = 0.9,
    repulsion_strength: float = 0.0001,
    max_frac_gene_repulsion: float = 0.2,
    celltype_lambda: float = 50.0,
    ambient_lambda: float = 50.0,
    bulk_lambda: float = 10.0,
    eps: float = 1e-12,
    log_eps: float = 9.999999999999994e-301,
    max_iter: int = 2000,
    del0_ll_tol: float = 0.001,
    min_ll_tol: float = 1e-06,
    tol_p: float = 0.0001,
    tol_f: float = 0.0001,
    norm_from_rounded: bool = False,
    seed: int = 42,
)

Default parameters for CellSweep denoising

Mirrors the CellSweep reference implementation's defaults. The pseudocounts (celltype_lambda, ambient_lambda, bulk_lambda) are given on the scale you see here and divided by the gene count internally. Two of these are worth knowing about before you touch anything else. freeze_ambient_profile = True keeps the ambient profile at its empty-droplet estimate, which is the recommended path and the only one where alpha_cap, the repulsion terms and cell-type reassignment are live. And freeze_empties only accepts True: the reference gives empty droplets a cell-type component they have no label for, which indexes past the end of the profile matrix and wraps onto the last cell type.

Attributes:

Name Type Description freeze_empties bool

Keep the contamination fraction of empty droplets pinned at 1. Only True is supported, see the description.

freeze_ambient_profile bool

Keep the ambient profile at its empty-droplet estimate rather than re-estimating it as a mixture over the cell-type profiles.

init_alpha float

Starting ambient fraction for every real barcode. With freeze_ambient_profile = True the final result barely depends on it, so it sits at alpha_cap.

init_beta float

Starting bulk contamination fraction. Set below init_alpha on purpose: bulk and ambient are not fully separable, so this biases unassignable contamination towards ambient.

alpha_cap float

Ceiling on the per-cell ambient fraction before the log- likelihood converges. Barcodes wanting to exceed it are excluded from the cell-type profile update and allowed to switch cell type.

repulsion_strength float

Strength of the repulsion pushing cell-type profiles away from the ambient profile. Scales with cluster mass, so it is inert on small data and only bites at realistic cell counts.

max_frac_gene_repulsion float

Ceiling on the fraction of any single profile entry that repulsion may remove.

celltype_lambda float

Pseudocount smoothing the cell-type profile update. Higher values give smoother profiles.

ambient_lambda float

Pseudocount smoothing the ambient profile estimate.

bulk_lambda float

Pseudocount smoothing the bulk profile estimate.

eps float

Floor on denominators.

log_eps float

Floor on the argument of log.

max_iter int

Hard cap on EM iterations.

del0_ll_tol float

Log-likelihood change, as a fraction of the first EM step's change, below which stage one ends and parameter convergence starts being checked.

min_ll_tol float

Floor on the adaptive tolerance, relative to the current log- likelihood. Stops del0_ll_tol chasing floating point noise.

tol_p float

Convergence threshold on the maximum row-wise L1 change in the cell- type profiles.

tol_f float

Convergence threshold on the change in the total contamination fraction.

norm_from_rounded bool

Derive the normalised layer from the integerised counts rather than the denoised floats. Consistent across the two layers at the cost of the sub-integer signal, which is where CellSweep is most informative.

seed int

Seed for the stochastic rounding of the denoised counts.

EmptyDropletsParams(
    *,
    method: Literal[
        "supplied", "umi_cutoff", "expected_cells", "knee"
    ] = "supplied",
    is_empty_column: str | None = "is_empty",
    umi_cutoff: int | None = None,
    expected_cells: int | None = None,
)

Parameters for identifying empty droplets

CellSweep trains its ambient profile on the empty droplets, so it needs them called before it runs. Four ways to do that, in descending order of how much you should trust them. "supplied" takes an existing logical column from the obs table. This is the common case: if you have CellRanger's filtered barcode list you already know which barcodes are empty, and nothing here will beat that. "umi_cutoff" calls everything below an absolute library size empty. "expected_cells" turns a cell count into that cutoff via the sorted library sizes. "knee" finds the cutoff from the curvature of the rank / log-count curve; it is experimental in the reference too, and smoothing puts the curvature minimum a few ranks ahead of the actual cliff, so it sweeps up the real barcodes nearest the transition.

Attributes:

Name Type Description method Literal['supplied', 'umi_cutoff', 'expected_cells', 'knee']

How the empty droplets are called, see the description.

is_empty_column str | None

Name of the logical obs column holding the mask, True for an empty droplet. Used by method = "supplied", ignored otherwise.

umi_cutoff int | None

Barcodes with a library size strictly below this are empty. Required for method = "umi_cutoff", ignored otherwise.

expected_cells int | None

Number of real cells expected in the run. Required for method = "expected_cells", ignored otherwise.

    ] = "TMM",

    min_mean: float = 0.0,
    robust: bool = False,
    legacy: bool = False,
)

Wrapper function for parameters for the edgeR quasi-likelihood workflow

Parameters for the edgeR quasi-likelihood chain, implemented in Rust via the edge-rs crate and gated against edgeR 4.8.2. Defaults are edgeR's own. The legacy switch picks between two genuinely different pipelines. The current route estimates its own dispersion from the most abundant genes and skips estimateDisp(), which is where most of the runtime went and is edgeR 4's own recommendation. The legacy route shrinks the raw residual deviance, needs a dispersion handed to it, and is the only one where the Poisson bound bites.

Run filterByExpr() before fitting. Turn this off for anything that is not gene expression, e.g. Milo neighbourhood counts, where the heuristic means nothing.

min_mean float

Drop features whose mean count across samples is below this. Applied on top of filter.

robust bool

Robust empirical Bayes squeezing, giving outlier features their own smaller prior degrees of freedom.

legacy bool

Take edgeR's pre-4.0 quasi-likelihood pipeline.

docs.title: NebulaParams dataclass
docs.text:
NebulaParams(
    *,
    nebula_method: Literal["ln", "hl"] = "ln",
    min_sigma: float = 0.0001,
    min_phi: float = 0.0001,
    max_sigma: float = 10.0,
    max_phi: float = 1000.0,
    cutoff_cell: float = 20.0,
    kappa: float = 800.0,
    cpc: float = 0.005,
    mincp: int = 5,
    min_subjects: int = 0,
    reml: bool = False,
    eps: float = 1e-06,
    gene_batch_size: int = 1000,
    shrink_dispersion: bool = True,
)

Wrapper function for parameters for NEBULA

Parameters for the NEBULA negative binomial gamma mixed model, implemented in Rust via the edge-rs crate and ported from the nebula package's own C++. Defaults follow the nebula package. NEBULA splits the variance into a subject- level random effect and a cell-level overdispersion. Run it on meta cells and the cell-level term becomes the spread between aggregates within a subject rather than between cells, so it is smaller and absorbs whatever the aggregation smoothed away. The subject-level term keeps its meaning either way.

Attributes:

Name Type Description nebula_method Literal['ln', 'hl']

Which variant to run. NEBULA downgrades "ln" to "hl" below 30 cells per subject.

min_sigma float

Lower bound on the subject-level overdispersion.

min_phi float

Lower bound on the cell-level overdispersion.

max_sigma float

Upper bound on the subject-level overdispersion.

max_phi float

Upper bound on the cell-level overdispersion.

cutoff_cell float

Refit both overdispersions when the product of the cells per subject and the estimated phi falls below this.

kappa float

Threshold on NEBULA's kappa_obs above which the subject-level overdispersion from stage one is trusted as is.

cpc float

Drop a gene whose mean count per cell is at most this.

mincp int

Drop a gene expressed in fewer than this many cells.

min_subjects int

Drop a gene that fewer than this many subjects express, a subject expressing it when its own mean count per cell is above cpc. cpc and mincp pool every cell, so one subject can carry a gene through on its own. 0 switches the check off, as in the nebula package.

reml bool

Estimate the overdispersions by restricted maximum likelihood. This arm has not been validated against a reference. Leave it off unless you know why you want it.

eps float

Absolute stopping tolerance for the optimiser.

gene_batch_size int

Genes read and fitted per batch. Bounds how much of the store is resident at once and changes nothing about the answer, since NEBULA is gene-independent.

shrink_dispersion bool

Shrink the cell-level overdispersions towards an empirical Bayes prior once the sweep is done.

The defaults are the reference ones.

docs.title: GeneTrendsParams dataclass
docs.text:
GeneTrendsParams(
    *,
    resolution: int = 500,
    weighting: Literal[
        "hard_mask", "fate_probability"
    ] = "hard_mask",
    length_scale: float = 1.0,
    sigma: float = 1.0,
    jitter: float = 1e-06,
    max_jitter_retries: int = 3,
    chunk_size: int = 2048,
)

Wrapper function for gene trend parameters

Parameters controlling the landmark Gaussian process that run_gene_trends() fits per branch. The kernel is a Matern-5/2 one and the prediction grid doubles as the landmark set. The defaults come from the reference and are prior- dominated. Palantir's pseudotime is min-max scaled to [0, 1], so a length_scale of 1.0 spans the entire domain and a sigma of 1.0 sits at roughly the signal scale of log-normalised expression. The posterior will flatten genuine transient structure and resolve almost any gene into a smooth monotone or single-peaked curve. That is a presentation choice, not inference. Shorten length_scale before believing a bump.

Attributes:

Name Type Description resolution int

Grid points per branch. Kept at the default even when a branch holds fewer cells, as the reference does.

weighting Literal['hard_mask', 'fate_probability']

With "hard_mask" every selected cell enters its branch's fit with equal weight, which is what the reference does. With "fate_probability" every cell enters every fit weighted by its fate probability, which is more defensible: a cell at 0.6 is not a member.

length_scale float

Matern-5/2 length scale.

sigma float

Noise standard deviation.

jitter float

Added to the landmark covariance diagonal before the Cholesky.

max_jitter_retries int

Times the jitter is raised and the Cholesky retried before giving up.

chunk_size int

Training points held at once when accumulating the cross- covariance.

docs.text:
BonsaiParams(
    *,
    variance_rule: Literal[
        "marginalise",
        "posterior_mean",
        "max_posterior",
        "fixed",
    ] = "marginalise",
    fixed_variance: float | None = None,
    variance_bins: int = 161,
    variance_min: float = 0.001,
    variance_max: float = 50.0,
    min_signal_to_noise: float = 1.0,
    start: Literal["linkage", "greedy_merge"] = "linkage",
    spr_search: Literal[
        "approximate", "exact"
    ] = "approximate",
    nni_search: Literal[
        "approximate", "exact"
    ] = "approximate",
    seed: int = 42,
    reroot: bool = True,
    layout: Literal[
        "equal_angle", "equal_daylight", "dendrogram"
    ] = "equal_angle",
    hyperbolic: bool = False,
)

Wrapper function for Bonsai parameters

Parameters for bonsai(). Sanity turns the raw counts into posterior log fold changes with error bars, Bonsai builds a tree over the cells from those, and the tree is laid out in 2D for plotting. The Sanity defaults come from sanity-sc-rs, the search defaults from bonsai-rs.

Attributes:

Name Type Description variance_rule Literal['marginalise', 'posterior_mean', 'max_posterior', 'fixed']

How Sanity treats each gene's variance in log fold change. "marginalise" integrates over the variance grid, "posterior_mean" and "max_posterior" collapse it to one value first (cheaper, less accurate error bars), and "fixed" uses fixed_variance for every gene.

fixed_variance float | None

The variance for variance_rule = "fixed". Ignored otherwise.

variance_bins int

Bins in the log-spaced variance grid.

variance_min float

Smallest variance on the grid.

variance_max float

Largest variance on the grid.

min_signal_to_noise float

Genes whose signal-to-noise ratio falls below this are left out of the tree.

start Literal['linkage', 'greedy_merge']

Initial topology. "linkage" is a Ward linkage over a neighbour graph: faster and a better tree on real data. "greedy_merge" is the paper's star merge, kept for comparisons with the published method.

spr_search Literal['approximate', 'exact']

Subtree pruning and regrafting. "approximate" stays within a few nats of "exact" on bonsai-rs's benchmarks at up to twice the speed.

nni_search Literal['approximate', 'exact']

Nearest-neighbour interchange. "approximate" found the same tree as "exact" on every bonsai-rs benchmark, and faster.

seed int

Seed for the linkage, SPR and NNI searches.

reroot bool

Reroot the finished tree for display. Changes the drawing, not the likelihood.

layout Literal['equal_angle', 'equal_daylight', 'dendrogram']

2D layout. "equal_daylight" refines equal angle but falls back to it above 2,048 nodes, so it only matters for small trees. Can be changed later with relayout_bonsai().

hyperbolic bool

Project the layout onto the hyperbolic disk.

docs.title: AucellParams dataclass
docs.text:
AucellParams(
    *,
    auc_type: Literal[
        "recovery", "wilcox", "ap"
    ] = "recovery",
    max_rank: float | None = None,
    standardise: bool = False,
)

Wrapper function for parameters for AUCell

The three statistics consume the same within-cell ranking, but weight it very differently. "wilcox" is a pure function of the gene set's rank sum, so a gene at rank 2 and one at rank 200 count for almost the same thing. "recovery" and "ap" are top-heavy. For SCENIC use "recovery", the default. "wilcox" is a bixverse addition and its flatter score does not separate into on/off populations, so it binarises badly. Ranking ties are averaged (midranks) rather than broken at random the way AUCell does it, which is why there is no need for SCENIC's trick of setting the cutoff to the 1st percentile of genes detected per cell. Undetected genes all collapse onto one rank well outside any sensible max_rank. Note the recovery AUC is normalised by max_rank * length(gene_set), matching pySCENIC and AUCell's normAUC = False. Modern AUCell divides by the attainable maximum instead, so absolute values differ by a per-gene-set constant. Cell ordering within a regulon is unaffected.

Attributes:

Name Type Description auc_type Literal['recovery', 'wilcox', 'ap']

Which statistic to calculate. "wilcox" is the AUC derived from the Mann-Whitney U statistic over the full ranking, with the null at 0.5 for any gene set size. "recovery" is the recovery-curve AUC under a rank cutoff, i.e. the actual AUCell statistic of Aibar, et al. "ap" is average precision, the most top-heavy of the three, but its null tracks the gene set prevalence so raw values are not comparable across gene sets of different size unless standardise is on.

max_rank float | None

Rank cutoff for "recovery", counted from the top of the within- cell ranking. If None, resolves to the top 5% of the gene universe, following Aibar, et al. Ignored by the other two statistics.

standardise bool

Shall each gene set's scores be z-scored across the cells. This is what makes "ap" comparable across gene sets of different size.

docs.text:
CistargetParams(
    *,
    auc_threshold: float = 0.05,
    nes_threshold: float = 3.0,
    max_rank: int = 5000,
    n_mean: int = 100,
    rcc_method: Literal["approx", "icistarget"] = "approx",
    high_conf_cats: tuple[str, ...] = (
        "directAnnotation",
        "inferredBy_Orthology",
    ),
    low_conf_cats: tuple[str, ...] = (
        "inferredBy_MotifSimilarity",
        "inferredBy_MotifSimilarity_n_Orthology",
    ),
)

Wrapper function to CisTarget parameters

auc_threshold and max_rank are two different cutoffs and are easy to confuse. The first truncates the recovery curve used to score motif enrichment, the second sets how deep into the ranking the background curve (mean + 2 SD across all motifs) is built, and therefore where the leading edge cuts. RcisTarget uses maxRank = 5000 and nMean = 100; the defaults here follow it. auc_threshold follows pySCENIC at 5%, RcisTarget itself uses 3%.

Attributes:

Name Type Description auc_threshold float

Numeric between 0 and 1. Proportion of genes to use for AUC threshold calculation. Default is 0.05 (5% of genes).

nes_threshold float

Normalised Enrichment Score threshold for significant motifs. Default is 3.0.

max_rank int

Depth of the recovery curves used to derive the background and the leading edge. Clamped to the number of genes in the ranking database. Default is 5000, the RcisTarget value.

n_mean int

Window for the rolling mean smoothing the background recovery curve. Only read when rcc_method = "approx". Default is 100, the RcisTarget value.

rcc_method Literal['approx', 'icistarget']

Method for recovery curve calculation. Either "approx" (approximate, faster) or "icistarget" (exact, slower).

high_conf_cats tuple[str, ...]

Annotation categories considered high confidence. Default includes direct annotations and orthology-based inferences.

low_conf_cats tuple[str, ...]

Annotation categories considered lower confidence. Default includes motif similarity-based inferences.

docs.title: ScenicBinariseParams dataclass
docs.text:
ScenicBinariseParams(
    *,
    bw_adjust: float = 1.0,
    n_grid: int = 512,
    n_bins: int = 512,
)

Wrapper function for parameters for the SCENIC binarisation

Each regulon gets its own threshold. A two-component Gaussian mixture is fitted and compared against a single Gaussian by BIC; if the mixture wins, the threshold is the kernel density minimum between the two component means, otherwise it falls back to mean + 2 * sd. This follows pySCENIC. AUCell fits six candidates and then lets the density trough override all of them whenever one exists, so the two land in much the same place. Turn bw_adjust up if shallow wobbles in the density are being picked up as troughs. AUCell effectively runs at 2.

Attributes:

Name Type Description bw_adjust float

Multiplier on the Silverman bandwidth of the kernel density estimate. Higher values smooth more.

n_grid int

Number of points at which the density is evaluated between the two component means.

n_bins int

Number of histogram bins used to approximate the density.

docs.title: KnnGraphDefaults dataclass
docs.text:
KnnGraphDefaults(
    *,
    knn_sym: Literal["snn", "umap", "knn"] = "snn",
    snn_similarity: Literal["jaccard", "rank"] = "jaccard",
    pruning: float = 0.0625,
    rescue: bool = True,
    local_connectivity: float = 1.0,
    mix_ratio: float = 1.0,
    binary: bool = False,
)

Helper function to generate the kNN graph defaults

Controls how a kNN is turned into the undirected, weighted graph that the clustering runs on. "snn" is the shared nearest neighbour graph of bluster/Seurat, "umap" the fuzzy simplicial set ScanPy builds (its obsp/connectivities) and "knn" the plain kNN union. Each method only reads its own parameters.

Attributes:

Name Type Description knn_sym Literal['snn', 'umap', 'knn']

How to symmetrise the kNN into a graph. Clustering resolutions do not carry over between the methods: the "umap" and "knn" graphs only hold kNN pairs, the sNN graph also links cells that share neighbours and prunes weak edges. The same resolution can give more or fewer communities depending on the data, so retune it when switching.

snn_similarity Literal['jaccard', 'rank']

"snn" only. "jaccard" weighs an edge by the Jaccard index of the two (self-inclusive) neighbour sets. "rank" takes the shared neighbour with the lowest combined rank, so closer shared neighbours give heavier edges. Both are scaled to [0, 1].

pruning float

"snn" only. Edges below this weight are dropped. For the Jaccard weight a threshold p keeps pairs that share at least a fraction 2p / (1 + p) of their (self-inclusive) neighbourhoods, rounded up to whole cells, so the same value means the same thing at any k. The default asks for about 12%, i.e. 2 of 16 shared cells at k = 15, in line with Seurat's 1/15. Avoid a threshold that equals one of the discrete weights exactly, or float rounding decides whether the edge survives.

rescue bool

"snn" only. Reconnect the small components that pruning cuts off via their strongest sNN edge, so they do not turn up as tiny clusters.

local_connectivity float

"umap" only. Number of nearest neighbours assumed to be fully connected, as in umap-learn.

mix_ratio float

"umap" only. 1 is the fuzzy union of the directed kNN memberships, 0 the fuzzy intersection (umap-learn's set_op_mix_ratio).

binary bool

"knn" only. If True, every edge weighs 1. Otherwise mutual neighbours weigh 2 and one-sided ones 1.

docs.title: Gene sets and regulons
docs.text:
Gene set scores, HotSpot gene modules and SCENIC regulons.

Three jobs. Score every cell against gene sets (module scores, AUCell, VISION, ULM / MLM), find gene modules that vary smoothly over the kNN graph (HotSpot), and infer TF regulons and score those (SCENIC).

Start with aucell for gene sets; vision takes signed signatures, lm_activity a weighted TF-target network. For modules call hotspot_autocor, then hotspot_gene_cor on the genes that score, then generate_hotspot_membership. For regulons run scenic_grn, identify_tf_to_genes, tf_to_genes_correlations, optionally tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment, then build_regulons and score them with aucell. Each SCENIC step takes the ScenicGrn of the last and returns an updated copy; the input is never modified.

What lands where. Nothing here writes to obs, var, sc.map or sc.cache. Scores come back as an ScMatrixRes (cells by gene sets) and get_data turns one into an obs frame for sc.add_obs. The HotSpot, VISION autocorrelation and SCENIC functions return their own result objects and data frames. All of them take a SingleCells, a SingleCellsSubset or a MetaCells (the meta cells compute on their in-memory counts), except module_scores, which takes no meta cells.

genes = sc.gene_ids().tolist()
gene_sets = {"set_a": genes[:20], "set_b": genes[20:50]}
res = bv.pathways.aucell(sc, gene_sets)
sc.add_obs(bv.pathways.get_data(res))

HotSpot reads the PCA and, by default, the cached kNN graph:

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=500)
bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=20)
bv.graph.find_neighbours(sc)
autocor = bv.pathways.hotspot_autocor(sc)
top = autocor.sort("z_score", descending=True)["gene_id"].head(100).to_list()
hs = bv.pathways.hotspot_gene_cor(sc, genes_to_take=top)
hs = bv.pathways.generate_hotspot_membership(hs, min_size=5)
modules = bv.pathways.get_hotspot_membership(hs)

The SCENIC chain, without the motif step:

tf_ids = genes[:30]  # your TF list, as gene ids
grn = bv.pathways.scenic_grn(sc, tf_ids)
grn = bv.pathways.identify_tf_to_genes(grn, n_sd=1.5)
grn = bv.pathways.tf_to_genes_correlations(grn, sc)
regulons = bv.pathways.build_regulons(grn, use_leading_edge=False, min_genes=5)
auc = bv.pathways.aucell(sc, regulons)
on_off = bv.pathways.binarise_regulon_activity(auc)

Gotchas. Gene sets, TFs and networks use the gene ids of var, not symbols. Unknown ids drop; for the TFs in scenic_grn you only hear about it with verbose on. hotspot_autocor and hotspot_gene_cor raise if the embedding or the cached kNN is stale after a change of the cell filter, and the gene by gene output of hotspot_gene_cor grows with the square of genes_to_take, so cut it down by autocorrelation first. cells_to_take drops the cached kNN and searches again. The motif ranking database and the motif-to-TF annotation are yours to supply: run_cistarget and tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment take the ranks as a genes by motifs integer matrix and the annotation as a frame with motif, TF and annotationSource, and build_regulons keeps only links with motif support unless you pass use_leading_edge=False. build_regulons and lm_activity return None with a warning when nothing survives their size filters.

Worked through in Gene set analysis and GRN inference on PBMCs.

docs.title: TF activity from a network
docs.text:
Gene set scores, HotSpot gene modules and SCENIC regulons.

Three jobs. Score every cell against gene sets (module scores, AUCell, VISION, ULM / MLM), find gene modules that vary smoothly over the kNN graph (HotSpot), and infer TF regulons and score those (SCENIC).

Start with aucell for gene sets; vision takes signed signatures, lm_activity a weighted TF-target network. For modules call hotspot_autocor, then hotspot_gene_cor on the genes that score, then generate_hotspot_membership. For regulons run scenic_grn, identify_tf_to_genes, tf_to_genes_correlations, optionally tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment, then build_regulons and score them with aucell. Each SCENIC step takes the ScenicGrn of the last and returns an updated copy; the input is never modified.

What lands where. Nothing here writes to obs, var, sc.map or sc.cache. Scores come back as an ScMatrixRes (cells by gene sets) and get_data turns one into an obs frame for sc.add_obs. The HotSpot, VISION autocorrelation and SCENIC functions return their own result objects and data frames. All of them take a SingleCells, a SingleCellsSubset or a MetaCells (the meta cells compute on their in-memory counts), except module_scores, which takes no meta cells.

genes = sc.gene_ids().tolist()
gene_sets = {"set_a": genes[:20], "set_b": genes[20:50]}
res = bv.pathways.aucell(sc, gene_sets)
sc.add_obs(bv.pathways.get_data(res))

HotSpot reads the PCA and, by default, the cached kNN graph:

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=500)
bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=20)
bv.graph.find_neighbours(sc)
autocor = bv.pathways.hotspot_autocor(sc)
top = autocor.sort("z_score", descending=True)["gene_id"].head(100).to_list()
hs = bv.pathways.hotspot_gene_cor(sc, genes_to_take=top)
hs = bv.pathways.generate_hotspot_membership(hs, min_size=5)
modules = bv.pathways.get_hotspot_membership(hs)

The SCENIC chain, without the motif step:

tf_ids = genes[:30]  # your TF list, as gene ids
grn = bv.pathways.scenic_grn(sc, tf_ids)
grn = bv.pathways.identify_tf_to_genes(grn, n_sd=1.5)
grn = bv.pathways.tf_to_genes_correlations(grn, sc)
regulons = bv.pathways.build_regulons(grn, use_leading_edge=False, min_genes=5)
auc = bv.pathways.aucell(sc, regulons)
on_off = bv.pathways.binarise_regulon_activity(auc)

Gotchas. Gene sets, TFs and networks use the gene ids of var, not symbols. Unknown ids drop; for the TFs in scenic_grn you only hear about it with verbose on. hotspot_autocor and hotspot_gene_cor raise if the embedding or the cached kNN is stale after a change of the cell filter, and the gene by gene output of hotspot_gene_cor grows with the square of genes_to_take, so cut it down by autocorrelation first. cells_to_take drops the cached kNN and searches again. The motif ranking database and the motif-to-TF annotation are yours to supply: run_cistarget and tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment take the ranks as a genes by motifs integer matrix and the annotation as a frame with motif, TF and annotationSource, and build_regulons keeps only links with motif support unless you pass use_leading_edge=False. build_regulons and lm_activity return None with a warning when nothing survives their size filters.

docs.title: Motif enrichment
docs.text:
Gene set scores, HotSpot gene modules and SCENIC regulons.

Three jobs. Score every cell against gene sets (module scores, AUCell, VISION, ULM / MLM), find gene modules that vary smoothly over the kNN graph (HotSpot), and infer TF regulons and score those (SCENIC).

Start with aucell for gene sets; vision takes signed signatures, lm_activity a weighted TF-target network. For modules call hotspot_autocor, then hotspot_gene_cor on the genes that score, then generate_hotspot_membership. For regulons run scenic_grn, identify_tf_to_genes, tf_to_genes_correlations, optionally tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment, then build_regulons and score them with aucell. Each SCENIC step takes the ScenicGrn of the last and returns an updated copy; the input is never modified.

What lands where. Nothing here writes to obs, var, sc.map or sc.cache. Scores come back as an ScMatrixRes (cells by gene sets) and get_data turns one into an obs frame for sc.add_obs. The HotSpot, VISION autocorrelation and SCENIC functions return their own result objects and data frames. All of them take a SingleCells, a SingleCellsSubset or a MetaCells (the meta cells compute on their in-memory counts), except module_scores, which takes no meta cells.

genes = sc.gene_ids().tolist()
gene_sets = {"set_a": genes[:20], "set_b": genes[20:50]}
res = bv.pathways.aucell(sc, gene_sets)
sc.add_obs(bv.pathways.get_data(res))

HotSpot reads the PCA and, by default, the cached kNN graph:

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=500)
bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=20)
bv.graph.find_neighbours(sc)
autocor = bv.pathways.hotspot_autocor(sc)
top = autocor.sort("z_score", descending=True)["gene_id"].head(100).to_list()
hs = bv.pathways.hotspot_gene_cor(sc, genes_to_take=top)
hs = bv.pathways.generate_hotspot_membership(hs, min_size=5)
modules = bv.pathways.get_hotspot_membership(hs)

The SCENIC chain, without the motif step:

tf_ids = genes[:30]  # your TF list, as gene ids
grn = bv.pathways.scenic_grn(sc, tf_ids)
grn = bv.pathways.identify_tf_to_genes(grn, n_sd=1.5)
grn = bv.pathways.tf_to_genes_correlations(grn, sc)
regulons = bv.pathways.build_regulons(grn, use_leading_edge=False, min_genes=5)
auc = bv.pathways.aucell(sc, regulons)
on_off = bv.pathways.binarise_regulon_activity(auc)

Gotchas. Gene sets, TFs and networks use the gene ids of var, not symbols. Unknown ids drop; for the TFs in scenic_grn you only hear about it with verbose on. hotspot_autocor and hotspot_gene_cor raise if the embedding or the cached kNN is stale after a change of the cell filter, and the gene by gene output of hotspot_gene_cor grows with the square of genes_to_take, so cut it down by autocorrelation first. cells_to_take drops the cached kNN and searches again. The motif ranking database and the motif-to-TF annotation are yours to supply: run_cistarget and tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment take the ranks as a genes by motifs integer matrix and the annotation as a frame with motif, TF and annotationSource, and build_regulons keeps only links with motif support unless you pass use_leading_edge=False. build_regulons and lm_activity return None with a warning when nothing survives their size filters.

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
Pipelines: the preprocessing calls you repeat on every subset, written once.

Chain steps with >> into a Pipeline and apply it. A step_* function wraps one module function (step_hvg is bv.pp.find_hvg, step_pca is bv.pp.calculate_pca, and so on) with its arguments bound; Step wraps any other function that takes the object first. Nothing runs until apply_pipeline. It checks the chain against the class of the object, then calls each step in order. Start with apply_pipeline_per_group when the point is sub-clustering or per-donor processing.

What lands where. A pipeline is inert, so building one touches nothing. apply_pipeline runs the steps on the object you pass and the results land where each wrapped function puts them: the HVGs and PCA in sc.map and sc.cache, the clusters in obs. apply_pipeline_per_group cuts one SingleCellsSubset per obs level over the kept cells, runs the pipeline on each and returns a dict keyed by group; the parent is left alone. step_metacells is the one step that changes the class: it takes a SingleCells or SingleCellsSubset and hands a MetaCells to the steps after it, so a pipeline ending on it gives you meta cells that never mix two groups. meta_cells_per_group does that in one call and merges them with merge_meta_cells.

pipe = (
    bv.pipeline.step_hvg(hvg_no=500)
    >> bv.pipeline.step_pca(20)
    >> bv.pipeline.step_neighbours()
    >> bv.pipeline.step_clusters(res=0.5, name="sub_leiden")
)
per_sample = bv.pipeline.apply_pipeline_per_group(pipe, sc, "sample_id")

# End on meta cells: one set per sample, never mixed
params = bv.params.BtMetacellsParams(target_no_metacells=50)
mc_pipe = pipe >> bv.pipeline.step_metacells("bootstrapped", params=params)
per_sample_mc = bv.pipeline.apply_pipeline_per_group(mc_pipe, sc, "sample_id")

Step also takes the bixverse_gpu twins:

import bixverse_gpu as bvg

gpu_pca = bv.pipeline.Step("gpu_pca", bvg.pp.calculate_pca, {"no_pcs": 20})
bv.pipeline.apply_pipeline(bv.pipeline.step_hvg(hvg_no=500) >> gpu_pca, sc)

Gotchas. Arguments are bound when the step is built, so a misspelt keyword fails there, and the class check runs before the first step does, so a bad chain fails before the expensive part. Order is on you otherwise: clusters and meta cells need step_neighbours first, which needs the PCA. The integration steps (step_harmony, step_harmony_v1, step_bbknn, step_fast_mnn) take a SingleCells or a subset, not MetaCells, so they go before step_metacells. step_fast_mnn wants the batch-aware HVGs from bv.pp.find_hvg_batch_aware. After step_harmony, point step_neighbours at it with embd_to_use="harmony". Applied to a SingleCells, a pipeline writes into that object.

Worked through in Sub-clustering and per-group pipelines.

docs.title: Preprocessing steps
docs.text:
Pipelines: the preprocessing calls you repeat on every subset, written once.

Chain steps with >> into a Pipeline and apply it. A step_* function wraps one module function (step_hvg is bv.pp.find_hvg, step_pca is bv.pp.calculate_pca, and so on) with its arguments bound; Step wraps any other function that takes the object first. Nothing runs until apply_pipeline. It checks the chain against the class of the object, then calls each step in order. Start with apply_pipeline_per_group when the point is sub-clustering or per-donor processing.

What lands where. A pipeline is inert, so building one touches nothing. apply_pipeline runs the steps on the object you pass and the results land where each wrapped function puts them: the HVGs and PCA in sc.map and sc.cache, the clusters in obs. apply_pipeline_per_group cuts one SingleCellsSubset per obs level over the kept cells, runs the pipeline on each and returns a dict keyed by group; the parent is left alone. step_metacells is the one step that changes the class: it takes a SingleCells or SingleCellsSubset and hands a MetaCells to the steps after it, so a pipeline ending on it gives you meta cells that never mix two groups. meta_cells_per_group does that in one call and merges them with merge_meta_cells.

pipe = (
    bv.pipeline.step_hvg(hvg_no=500)
    >> bv.pipeline.step_pca(20)
    >> bv.pipeline.step_neighbours()
    >> bv.pipeline.step_clusters(res=0.5, name="sub_leiden")
)
per_sample = bv.pipeline.apply_pipeline_per_group(pipe, sc, "sample_id")

# End on meta cells: one set per sample, never mixed
params = bv.params.BtMetacellsParams(target_no_metacells=50)
mc_pipe = pipe >> bv.pipeline.step_metacells("bootstrapped", params=params)
per_sample_mc = bv.pipeline.apply_pipeline_per_group(mc_pipe, sc, "sample_id")

Step also takes the bixverse_gpu twins:

import bixverse_gpu as bvg

bv.pipeline.apply_pipeline(bv.pipeline.step_hvg(hvg_no=500) >> gpu_pca, sc)

Gotchas. Arguments are bound when the step is built, so a misspelt keyword fails there, and the class check runs before the first step does, so a bad chain fails before the expensive part. Order is on you otherwise: clusters and meta cells need step_neighbours first, which needs the PCA. docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
Plot data extractors and matplotlib plots for single cell results.

Two layers. The extract_* functions pull what one plot needs out of an experiment into a polars frame and need nothing beyond the core package. The plots draw from the same data, take the object or the frame its extractor returns, and need matplotlib, the plots extra (pip install bixverse[plots]). matplotlib is imported on first use of a plot, not with this module. Hand a plot the frame when you want to restyle it, or draw the same data with another library.

Where to start. embedding_plot for an obs column on an embedding, feature_plot for genes on an embedding, dot_plot, stacked_violin_plot and heatmap_plot for markers across groups, feature_scatter_plot for two genes against each other. The QC plots (violin_plot, density_plot, joint_plot) take the CellQc from bv.qc.run_cell_qc or a frame. paga_plot and milo_nhood_plot take the result of bv.traj.run_paga and the tested MiloR from bv.de.

What lands where. Nothing here writes to the experiment. Every plot reads the kept cells of a SingleCells, SingleCellsSubset, MetaCells or SingleCellsMultiModal and returns a matplotlib object: the single panel plots take an optional ax and return it, the multi-panel ones return the Figure. The extractors return one row per kept cell (per meta cell for MetaCells), long over genes where the plot needs it. Gene arguments are var ids.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

genes = sc.gene_ids()[:4].tolist()
bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "umap", "cell_grp", label_by="cell_grp")
bv.pl.feature_plot(sc, genes, "umap", ncol=2)
bv.pl.dot_plot(sc, genes, "cell_grp")

frame = bv.pl.extract_embedding_data(sc, "umap", obs_cols=["cell_grp"])
plt.show()

Gotchas. The embedding has to exist (bv.embed.umap and friends; "pca" works after bv.pp.calculate_pca). Numeric obs columns get a colour bar, and label_by refuses them: cluster ids stored as numbers need discrete=True. Point and label sizes are in mm and point_size=None picks a size from the cell count; above 100,000 cells the points are rasterised. density_plot needs a CellQc run with groups. violin_plot and density_plot take a plain frame too, with grouping_column and variable; the outliers are then recomputed by MAD per group.

Worked through in A guide to single-cell plotting functions.

Plot data extractors and matplotlib plots for single cell results.

Two layers. The extract_* functions pull what one plot needs out of an experiment into a polars frame and need nothing beyond the core package. The plots draw from the same data, take the object or the frame its extractor returns, and need matplotlib, the plots extra (pip install bixverse[plots]). matplotlib is imported on first use of a plot, not with this module. Hand a plot the frame when you want to restyle it, or draw the same data with another library.

Where to start. embedding_plot for an obs column on an embedding, feature_plot for genes on an embedding, dot_plot, stacked_violin_plot and heatmap_plot for markers across groups, feature_scatter_plot for two genes against each other. The QC plots (violin_plot, density_plot, joint_plot) take the CellQc from bv.qc.run_cell_qc or a frame. paga_plot and milo_nhood_plot take the result of bv.traj.run_paga and the tested MiloR from bv.de.

What lands where. Nothing here writes to the experiment. Every plot reads the kept cells of a SingleCells, SingleCellsSubset, MetaCells or SingleCellsMultiModal and returns a matplotlib object: the single panel plots take an optional ax and return it, the multi-panel ones return the Figure. bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "umap", "cell_grp", label_by="cell_grp")

docs.title: Graphs over an embedding
docs.text:
Plot data extractors and matplotlib plots for single cell results.

Two layers. The extract_* functions pull what one plot needs out of an experiment into a polars frame and need nothing beyond the core package. The plots draw from the same data, take the object or the frame its extractor returns, and need matplotlib, the plots extra (pip install bixverse[plots]). matplotlib is imported on first use of a plot, not with this module. Hand a plot the frame when you want to restyle it, or draw the same data with another library.

Where to start. embedding_plot for an obs column on an embedding, feature_plot for genes on an embedding, dot_plot, stacked_violin_plot and heatmap_plot for markers across groups, feature_scatter_plot for two genes against each other. The QC plots (violin_plot, density_plot, joint_plot) take the CellQc from bv.qc.run_cell_qc or a frame. paga_plot and milo_nhood_plot take the result of bv.traj.run_paga and the tested MiloR from bv.de.

What lands where. Nothing here writes to the experiment. Every plot reads the kept cells of a SingleCells, SingleCellsSubset, MetaCells or SingleCellsMultiModal and returns a matplotlib object: the single panel plots take an optional ax and return it, the multi-panel ones return the Figure. The extractors return one row per kept cell (per meta cell for MetaCells), long over genes where the plot needs it. Gene arguments are var ids.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

genes = sc.gene_ids()[:4].tolist()
bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "umap", "cell_grp", label_by="cell_grp")
bv.pl.feature_plot(sc, genes, "umap", ncol=2)
bv.pl.dot_plot(sc, genes, "cell_grp")

frame = bv.pl.extract_embedding_data(sc, "umap", obs_cols=["cell_grp"])
plt.show()

Gotchas. The embedding has to exist (bv.embed.umap and friends; "pca" works after bv.pp.calculate_pca). Numeric obs columns get a colour bar, and label_by refuses them: cluster ids stored as numbers need discrete=True. Point and label sizes are in mm and point_size=None picks a size from the cell count; above 100,000 cells the points are rasterised. density_plot needs a CellQc run with groups. violin_plot and density_plot take a plain frame too, with grouping_column and variable; the outliers are then recomputed by MAD per group.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
Highly variable genes, PCA, residual models and MAGIC.

Everything here reads the count stores in Rust and works on the cells you kept. Start with find_hvg, then calculate_pca: the PCA uses the HVG set that find_hvg stored. The kNN graph, clustering and embeddings live in bv.graph and bv.embed.

What lands where. find_hvg writes the per-gene statistics to var and the selected genes to sc.map.hvg. calculate_pca writes scores, loadings and singular values to sc.cache. fit_residuals writes the fitted model to sc.cache.residual_fit, which find_hvg (with method="residual"), calculate_pca(residuals=True) and sct_corrected_counts then read. run_magic writes the imputed genes to sc.cache.magic. Every cached result is stamped, so sc prints what has gone stale after the cell filter moves. get_hvg_data, find_hvg_batch_aware and sct_corrected_counts leave the experiment alone and return their result.

Object types. SingleCells works everywhere. A SingleCellsSubset is accepted by all functions except get_hvg_data; on a subset find_hvg stores the selection but leaves var alone. MetaCells is accepted by find_hvg, get_hvg_data, calculate_pca and fit_residuals, and computes on its in-memory counts.

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=2000)
bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=30)

The residual route fits a model once and reuses it for the HVGs and the PCA:

bv.pp.fit_residuals(sc, method="analytic_pearson")
bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_params=bv.params.HvgParams(method="residual"))
bv.pp.calculate_pca(
    sc, 30, pca_params=bv.params.PcaParams(normalise_variance=False), residuals=True
)

Gotchas. calculate_pca without HVGs warns and returns, so run find_hvg first or pass hvg=. A residual model is bound to the current cell set: change the filter and find_hvg or calculate_pca refuse it until you refit. With method="residual", hvg_no counts per group and the union is kept. For several batches use find_hvg_batch_aware and hand its hvg_gene_idx to calculate_pca. run_magic needs a kNN graph over the kept cells from bv.graph.find_neighbours; do not feed its output to correlation-based methods, the smoothing inflates gene-gene correlation.

Worked through in Analysing PBMCs with bixverse and Pearson residuals and scTransform.

docs.title: find_hvg
docs.text:
find_hvg(
    sc: ScOrMc,
    *,
    hvg_no: int = 2000,
    hvg_params: HvgParams | None = None,
    streaming: bool | None = None,
    verbose: Verbose = True,
) -> None

Select highly variable genes over the kept cells.

The per-gene statistics go to var (mean, var, var_exp, var_std for "vst"; mean, dispersion, dispersion_scaled, bin for "meanvarbin" / "dispersion"; scran_mean, scran_var, scran_fitted, scran_residual for "scran"), the top hvg_no genes on the ranking statistic to sc.map.hvg. On a SingleCellsSubset only the selection is stored.

method = "residual" ranks on the residual variance of the model from fit_residuals, writes residual_variance instead, and treats hvg_no as a per-group count whose union is kept.

On MetaCells the statistics come from the in-memory counts (raw for "vst", normalised otherwise) and go to its var, the selection to mc.hvg; the residual method writes no statistics there. streaming is ignored.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sc ScOrMc

The experiment.

required hvg_no int

Number of HVGs (per group for "residual").

2000 hvg_params HvgParams | None

The HVG parameters. None uses the defaults.

None streaming bool | None

Read the genes in batches. None streams above N_CELLS_STREAMING_THRESHOLD kept cells.

None verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If hvg_no exceeds the gene count, or the residual model is missing or stale.

Examples:

>>> bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=2000)
>>> bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_params=bv.params.HvgParams(method="meanvarbin"))

docs.title: PCA
docs.text:
Highly variable genes, PCA, residual models and MAGIC.

Everything here reads the count stores in Rust and works on the cells you kept. Start with find_hvg, then calculate_pca: the PCA uses the HVG set that find_hvg stored. The kNN graph, clustering and embeddings live in bv.graph and bv.embed.

What lands where. find_hvg writes the per-gene statistics to var and the selected genes to sc.map.hvg. calculate_pca writes scores, loadings and singular values to sc.cache. fit_residuals writes the fitted model to sc.cache.residual_fit, which find_hvg (with method="residual"), calculate_pca(residuals=True) and sct_corrected_counts then read. run_magic writes the imputed genes to sc.cache.magic. Every cached result is stamped, so sc prints what has gone stale after the cell filter moves. get_hvg_data, find_hvg_batch_aware and sct_corrected_counts leave the experiment alone and return their result.

Object types. SingleCells works everywhere. A SingleCellsSubset is accepted by all functions except get_hvg_data; on a subset find_hvg stores the selection but leaves var alone. MetaCells is accepted by find_hvg, get_hvg_data, calculate_pca and fit_residuals, and computes on its in-memory counts.

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=2000)
bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=30)

The residual route fits a model once and reuses it for the HVGs and the PCA:

bv.pp.fit_residuals(sc, method="analytic_pearson")
bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_params=bv.params.HvgParams(method="residual"))
bv.pp.calculate_pca(
    sc, 30, pca_params=bv.params.PcaParams(normalise_variance=False), residuals=True
)

Gotchas. calculate_pca without HVGs warns and returns, so run find_hvg first or pass hvg=. A residual model is bound to the current cell set: change the filter and find_hvg or calculate_pca refuse it until you refit. With method="residual", hvg_no counts per group and the union is kept. For several batches use find_hvg_batch_aware and hand its hvg_gene_idx to calculate_pca. run_magic needs a kNN graph over the kept cells from bv.graph.find_neighbours; do not feed its output to correlation-based methods, the smoothing inflates gene-gene correlation.

required method ResidualMethod

docs.title: Quality control
docs.text:
Cell QC: per-cell metrics, then MAD or fixed-threshold outlier calls.

Two steps. gene_set_proportions and top_genes_perc read the cell store in Rust and write their metrics to obs. The outlier calls (run_cell_qc, run_cell_qc_fixed) work on plain vectors you pull out of obs and return a CellQc record. get_data turns that into an obs frame, and you decide which cells to keep with sc.set_cells_to_keep. Nothing is deleted. rescue_cells and flag_cells adjust a CellQc afterwards. The metric passes take a SingleCells; the outlier calls know nothing about experiments.

What lands where. gene_set_proportions writes one obs column per gene set, named by its key, as a fraction in [0, 1]. top_genes_perc writes top_<N>_genes_percentage. lib_size and nnz are already in obs from the loaders. The outlier calls write nothing: sc.add_obs(get_data(qc)) stores the calls, and sc.set_cells_to_keep applies the filter.

mito_genes = sc.gene_ids()[:13].tolist()  # on real data: the MT- genes
bv.qc.gene_set_proportions(sc, {"mito": mito_genes})
bv.qc.top_genes_perc(sc)

obs = sc.obs(filtered=True)
metrics = {"lib_size": obs["lib_size"], "nnz": obs["nnz"], "mito": obs["mito"]}
directions = {"lib_size": "below", "nnz": "below", "mito": "above"}
qc = bv.qc.run_cell_qc(metrics, obs["cell_idx"].to_numpy(), directions=directions)

sc.add_obs(bv.qc.get_data(qc))
sc.set_cells_to_keep(qc.cell_idx[~qc.combined])

Gotchas. Pass the metrics for the kept cells (sc.obs(filtered=True)) with their cell_idx, so the two line up. get_data writes the metrics back to obs under their own names, so a transformed metric such as log10_lib_size needs its own key or it overwrites the original column. directions, if given, must name every metric. With groups (donor, sample) MAD runs per group, hard thresholds do not. rescue_cells only clears MAD flags, never hard ones. The metric passes stream the cells in batches above N_CELLS_STREAMING_THRESHOLD kept cells, and streaming= overrides that.

Worked through in Analysing PBMCs with bixverse.

docs.title: Adjusting the calls
docs.text:
Cell QC: per-cell metrics, then MAD or fixed-threshold outlier calls.

Two steps. gene_set_proportions and top_genes_perc read the cell store in Rust and write their metrics to obs. The outlier calls (run_cell_qc, run_cell_qc_fixed) work on plain vectors you pull out of obs and return a CellQc record. get_data turns that into an obs frame, and you decide which cells to keep with sc.set_cells_to_keep. Nothing is deleted. rescue_cells and flag_cells adjust a CellQc afterwards. The metric passes take a SingleCells; the outlier calls know nothing about experiments.

What lands where. gene_set_proportions writes one obs column per gene set, named by its key, as a fraction in [0, 1]. top_genes_perc writes top_<N>_genes_percentage. lib_size and nnz are already in obs from the loaders. The outlier calls write nothing: sc.add_obs(get_data(qc)) stores the calls, and sc.set_cells_to_keep applies the filter.

mito_genes = sc.gene_ids()[:13].tolist()  # on real data: the MT- genes
bv.qc.gene_set_proportions(sc, {"mito": mito_genes})
bv.qc.top_genes_perc(sc)

obs = sc.obs(filtered=True)
metrics = {"lib_size": obs["lib_size"], "nnz": obs["nnz"], "mito": obs["mito"]}
directions = {"lib_size": "below", "nnz": "below", "mito": "above"}
qc = bv.qc.run_cell_qc(metrics, obs["cell_idx"].to_numpy(), directions=directions)

sc.add_obs(bv.qc.get_data(qc))
sc.set_cells_to_keep(qc.cell_idx[~qc.combined])

Gotchas. Pass the metrics for the kept cells (sc.obs(filtered=True)) with their cell_idx, so the two line up. get_data writes the metrics back to obs under their own names, so a transformed metric such as log10_lib_size needs its own key or it overwrites the original column. directions, if given, must name every metric. With groups (donor, sample) MAD runs per group, hard thresholds do not. rescue_cells only clears MAD flags, never hard ones. The metric passes stream the cells in batches above N_CELLS_STREAMING_THRESHOLD kept cells, and streaming= overrides that.

docs.title: bixverse
docs.text:
Single-cell streaming for Python, in Rust.

Opens a bixverse binary sparse store and yields minibatches fast enough to keep a GPU training loop fed. The decode never leaves Rust: a feeder thread decompresses and materialises batches ahead of the consumer, releasing the GIL while it works.

>>> import bixverse as bv
>>> reader = bv.CellReader("counts.bin")
>>> loader = bv.CellLoader(reader, batch_size=256, layer="norm")
>>> for batch in loader:
...     x = batch.scipy_csr()

Batches are sparse CSR by default. Pass sparse=False for a dense (batch_size, n_genes) array, and expect it to cost a zero-fill and a scatter over every gene whether or not it holds a count.

docs.title: Trajectories
docs.text:
Palantir pseudotime, PAGA graph abstraction and gene trends.

Palantir orders cells along differentiation and gives each cell a fate probability per terminal state, PAGA abstracts the kNN graph into a cluster graph, and run_gene_trends fits a curve per gene along each Palantir branch. Start with run_paga to see the topology, then run_palantir with a start cell (and terminal states, if you know them), then run_gene_trends on its result. Trees over every cell live in bv.trees.

What lands where. Nothing. All three take a SingleCells, SingleCellsSubset or MetaCells, read the cached kNN graph (and obs, for the PAGA clusters) and return a frozen result keyed by cell id. To colour by pseudotime, join res.pseudotime onto obs on cell_id with sc.add_obs.

import polars as pl

bv.graph.find_clusters(sc, res=0.5, name="leiden_clusters")
paga = bv.traj.run_paga(sc, "leiden_clusters")

early_cell = sc.obs()["cell_id"][0]
res = bv.traj.run_palantir(sc, early_cell)
trends = bv.traj.run_gene_trends(sc, res, features=["gene_0001", "gene_0002"])

obs = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "cell_id"], filtered=True)
sc.add_obs(
    obs.join(res.pseudotime, on="cell_id", how="left").select(
        "cell_idx", pl.col("pseudotime").alias("palantir_pseudotime")
    )
)

Gotchas. Run bv.pp.find_hvg, bv.pp.calculate_pca and bv.graph.find_neighbours first. A stale kNN raises; a missing one warns and run_palantir and run_paga return None. Palantir's start and terminal cells must be ids the kNN was built over. Without terminal states it detects them, and res.terminal_states names them by cell id. A disconnected kNN graph is patched with repair edges, counted in res.run_info. The kNN metric should be Euclidean or cosine, or Palantir warns. run_gene_trends needs features, or use_magic=True after bv.pp.run_magic on a SingleCells or subset (not on MetaCells). The Gaussian process defaults are prior-dominated, so shorten length_scale before believing a bump. The PAGA graphs are dense arrays, one row and column per cluster.

Worked through in Trajectory inference with Palantir and PAGA.

docs.title: run_palantir
docs.text:
run_palantir(
    sc: ScOrMc,
    early_cell: str,
    *,
    terminal_states: Sequence[str]
    | dict[str, str]
    | None = None,
    modality: Modality = "rna",
    palantir_params: PalantirParams | None = None,
    seed: int = 42,
    verbose: Verbose = True,
) -> PalantirRes | None

Palantir trajectory inference over the cached kNN graph.

Models differentiation as a Markov chain over a diffusion map of the cells: a pseudotime per cell, the probability of each cell reaching each terminal state, and the differentiation entropy of those probabilities. The kNN graph feeds the diffusion kernel; the geodesics are measured over a second kNN graph built on the multiscale space, sized by palantir_params.knn.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sc ScOrMc

The experiment, a subset or meta cells, with the kNN.

required early_cell str

Id of the start cell, one the kNN was built over.

required terminal_states Sequence[str] | dict[str, str] | None

Terminal state cell ids, or label to cell id, the labels then naming the branch_probs columns. None detects them from the waypoint Markov chain.

None modality Modality

The kNN graph: "rna", or "adt" / "wnn" on a SingleCellsMultiModal.

'rna' palantir_params PalantirParams | None

The parameters. None uses the defaults.

None seed int

Seed for the eigensolver, the waypoints and the multiscale kNN.

42 verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

Returns:

Type Description PalantirRes | None

The PalantirRes, or None with a warning if there is no kNN.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

On a stale kNN, a non-RNA modality without a multi-modal object, or a cell not in the kNN graph.

References

Setty, et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2019.

Examples:

>>> early_cell = "cell_0001"
>>> res = bv.traj.run_palantir(sc, early_cell)
>>> params = bv.params.PalantirParams(n_eigs=10, knn=30)
>>> res = bv.traj.run_palantir(sc, early_cell, palantir_params=params)
>>> ends = {"branch_a": "cell_0100", "branch_b": "cell_0200"}
>>> res = bv.traj.run_palantir(sc, early_cell, terminal_states=ends)

run_gene_trends(
    sc: ScOrMc,
    palantir_res: PalantirRes,
    *,
    features: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    use_magic: bool = False,
    branch_params: BranchSelectionParams | None = None,

Gene trends over the Palantir pseudotime.

Assigns cells to branches from their fate probabilities, then fits a landmark Gaussian process with a Matern-5/2 kernel per branch, the Mellon-based estimator of the reference. One smooth curve per gene and branch on a common grid.

The defaults are prior-dominated: the pseudotime spans [0, 1], so a length_scale of 1 covers the whole domain. Shorten it before believing a bump.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sc ScOrMc

The experiment, a subset or meta cells, the one Palantir ran on.

required palantir_res PalantirRes

The run_palantir result over the same cells.

required features Sequence[str] | None

Gene ids to fit. None takes every gene of the imputed layer, so needs use_magic. Unknown ids warn and drop.

None use_magic bool

Fit the MAGIC imputed layer instead of the normalised counts; SingleCells and SingleCellsSubset only.

False branch_params BranchSelectionParams | None

Branch cell selection. None uses the defaults.

None gene_trend_params GeneTrendsParams | None

The Gaussian process. None uses the defaults.

None verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

Returns:

Type Description GeneTrendsRes

The GeneTrendsRes.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If features is missing without MAGIC, the Palantir result does not cover the cells, or the imputed layer is unusable.

References

Setty, et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2019.

Examples:

>>> genes = ["gene_0001", "gene_0002"]
>>> res = bv.traj.run_palantir(sc, "cell_0001")
>>> trends = bv.traj.run_gene_trends(sc, res, features=genes)
>>> bv.pp.run_magic(sc, genes)
>>> trends = bv.traj.run_gene_trends(sc, res, use_magic=True)

docs.title: Cell trees
docs.text:
Bonsai trees over cells or meta cells.

Bonsai builds a tree with every cell a leaf and inferred ancestors inside, from the raw counts after Sanity, and lays it out in 2D. Use it where a hierarchy over all cells says more than a process with a start (that is bv.traj). Call bonsai first, change the drawing with relayout_bonsai, and put the leaf coordinates in sc.cache.embeddings with set_bonsai_embedding to plot them like a UMAP.

What lands where. bonsai and relayout_bonsai return a BonsaiTree and leave the experiment alone. set_bonsai_embedding is the only writer: it stores the (n_leaves, 2) leaf positions in sc.cache.embeddings[name] (default "bonsai") and stamps it. bonsai takes a SingleCells or a MetaCells, not a SingleCellsSubset.

tree = bv.trees.bonsai(sc)
tree = bv.trees.relayout_bonsai(tree, layout="dendrogram")
bv.trees.set_bonsai_embedding(sc, tree)

On meta cells every meta cell is a leaf, with n_cells counting the cells behind it. That is the way to large data. The generators want the kNN from bv.graph.find_neighbours on sc first:

mc = bv.metacells.generate_supercells(sc)
tree_mc = bv.trees.bonsai(mc)

Gotchas. No HVGs, PCA or kNN are needed; the signal-to-noise filter picks the genes, or pass hvg= to restrict the candidates. tree.nodes is 0-based with a null parent for the root, leaves first in the object's cell order. relayout_bonsai renumbers the inferred ancestors, the leaves keep their numbers. set_bonsai_embedding refuses a tree built over other cells than the object now keeps, so rerun bonsai after changing the cell filter.

Worked through in Cell trees with Bonsai.

docs.title: BonsaiTree dataclass
docs.text:
BonsaiTree(
    nodes: DataFrame,
    loglik: float,
    steps: DataFrame,
    timings: DataFrame,
    genes_used: tuple[str, ...],
    genes_dropped: tuple[str, ...],
    cell_idx: ndarray,
    layout: str,
    hyperbolic: bool,
    params: BonsaiParams,
)

A Bonsai tree with its layout.

Attributes:

Name Type Description nodes DataFrame

node (0-based), parent (0-based, null for the root), branch, is_leaf, cell_id (null for the inferred ancestors), n_cells (cells behind a leaf: 1 for a cell, the originating cells for a meta cell; null for the ancestors), x and y. The leaves come first, in the object's cell or meta cell order.

loglik float

Loglikelihood of the final tree.

steps DataFrame

step, loglik after it and its wall time in seconds.

timings DataFrame

Wall time in seconds per stage: sanity, ingest, bonsai, layout and total, the whole call.

genes_used tuple[str, ...]

Ids of the genes the tree was built on.

genes_dropped tuple[str, ...]

The candidate genes left out: no counts, ill conditioned Sanity posteriors, or a signal-to-noise below min_signal_to_noise.

cell_idx ndarray

The 0-based cells (store indices) or meta cells the tree was built over, in leaf order.

layout str

The current layout.

hyperbolic bool

Whether the layout is on the hyperbolic disk.

params BonsaiParams

The parameters of the run.

docs.title: bonsai
docs.text:
bonsai(
    sc: SingleCells | MetaCells,
    *,
    hvg: ndarray | Sequence[int] | None = None,
    bonsai_params: BonsaiParams | None = None,
    verbose: Verbose = True,
) -> BonsaiTree

A Bonsai tree over the cells.

Every cell is a leaf and the internal nodes are inferred ancestral states, with branch lengths that carry the amount of change between them. The raw counts go through Sanity first for posterior log fold changes with error bars, and only genes with enough signal over their own noise (min_signal_to_noise) are kept for the tree; no HVG selection needed.

On MetaCells every meta cell is a leaf. Their summed raw counts are Poisson like a cell's, so Sanity treats them alike, and a bigger meta cell gets tighter error bars. That is the way to large data; what goes is any structure inside a meta cell.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sc SingleCells | MetaCells

The experiment or meta cells.

required hvg ndarray | Sequence[int] | None

0-based candidate genes, e.g. sc.map.hvg. None takes every gene.

None bonsai_params BonsaiParams | None

The parameters. None uses the defaults.

None verbose Verbose

0 (False) silent, 1 (True) progress, 2 extra detail where the method has it.

True

Returns:

Type Description BonsaiTree

The BonsaiTree, leaves in the kept cell or meta cell order.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

On a gene index out of range, or if no gene survives the signal-to-noise filter.

References

de Groot, et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2026; Breda, et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2021.

Examples:

>>> tree = bv.trees.bonsai(sc)
>>> bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=500)
>>> tree = bv.trees.bonsai(sc, hvg=sc.map.hvg)
