docs.title: bixverse_gpu
docs.text:
GPU twins of the bixverse single cell methods, on wgpu.

Each module mirrors its bixverse namesake (bixverse_gpu.pp for bixverse.pp, and so on) and its functions take the same experiment objects, write the same cache slots (bar Harmony and fastMNN, which write harmony_gpu and mnn_gpu) and obs columns and return the same result types as the CPU functions, so a pipeline swaps one import for the other:

>>> from bixverse import pp
>>> from bixverse_gpu import pp as pp_gpu
>>> pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=2000)
>>> pp_gpu.calculate_pca(sc, 30)

The GPU-specific knobs live in bixverse_gpu.params; everything else takes the bixverse.params bundles. Probe the device with gpu_available(); the twins raise bixverse.BixverseError without one.

docs.text:
GPU UMAP, densMAP, t-SNE and PHATE.

The work runs in the manifolds_rs GPU estimators (UMAPGpu, DensMAPGpu, TSNEGpu, PHATEGpu); inputs, slots and stamps are handled exactly as in bixverse.embed, which runs the same code with the CPU estimators. >>> bixverse_gpu.graph.find_neighbours(sc)
>>> umap(sc)

docs.text:
NebulaGpuParams(
    *,
    nebula_method: Literal["ln", "hl"] = "ln",
    min_sigma: float = 0.0001,
    min_phi: float = 0.0001,
    max_sigma: float = 10.0,
    max_phi: float = 1000.0,
    cutoff_cell: float = 20.0,
    kappa: float = 800.0,
    cpc: float = 0.005,
    mincp: int = 5,
    min_subjects: int = 0,
    eps: float = 1e-06,
    gene_batch_size: int = 1000,
    shrink_dispersion: bool = True,
)

Wrapper function for parameters for GPU NEBULA

GPU counterpart to NebulaParams. Same knobs and defaults, minus reml: the device fit does not implement it. Stage two of NEBULA, the per-gene penalised fits, runs in f32 on the device and is finished on the host in f64, so the estimates sit close to the CPU ones rather than on them.

Attributes:

Name Type Description nebula_method Literal['ln', 'hl']

Which variant to run. NEBULA downgrades "ln" to "hl" below 30 cells per subject.

min_sigma float

Lower bound on the subject-level overdispersion.

min_phi float

Lower bound on the cell-level overdispersion.

max_sigma float

Upper bound on the subject-level overdispersion.

max_phi float

Upper bound on the cell-level overdispersion.

cutoff_cell float

Refit both overdispersions when the product of the cells per subject and the estimated phi falls below this.

kappa float

Threshold on NEBULA's kappa_obs above which the subject-level overdispersion from stage one is trusted as is.

cpc float

Drop a gene whose mean count per cell is at most this.

mincp int

Drop a gene expressed in fewer than this many cells.

min_subjects int

Drop a gene that fewer than this many subjects express, a subject expressing it when its own mean count per cell is above cpc. cpc and mincp pool every cell, so one subject can carry a gene through on its own. 0 switches the check off, as in the nebula package.

eps float

Absolute stopping tolerance for the optimiser.

gene_batch_size int

Genes read and fitted per batch. Bounds how much of the store is resident at once and changes nothing about the answer, since NEBULA is gene-independent.

shrink_dispersion bool

Shrink the cell-level overdispersions towards an empirical Bayes prior once the sweep is done.

Maximum number of k-means iterations.

k_means_init str | None

Initialisation method. One of "random", "parallel" or "plusplus". If None, picked on the Rust side based on the number of centroids.

fixed bool

Shall k-means run for a fixed number of iterations, without checking for convergence. wgpu only; MLX always runs every iteration.

quantise bool

Shall the data buffer be held at fp16 on the GPU. Halves the buffer and helps when the assignment kernels are memory bound. wgpu only.

dist Literal['euclidean', 'cosine']

Distance for the k-means and the centroid graph.

cell_mediated bool

Shall the cell-mediated centroid graph from Secuer be built instead of the kNN graph on the centroids. Centroids are then linked by the cells that sit near both, so two centroids that are close in space but have no cells between them stay apart. If True, centroid_k and centroid_graph are ignored.

n_anchors int

Number of nearest centroids each cell links to in the cell- mediated graph. Only used if cell_mediated = True.

centroid_k int

Neighbours per centroid in the exact centroid kNN. Only used if cell_mediated = False.

knn_sym Literal['snn', 'umap', 'knn']

How to symmetrise the kNN into a graph. Clustering resolutions do not carry over between the methods: the "umap" and "knn" graphs only hold kNN pairs, the sNN graph also links cells that share neighbours and prunes weak edges. The same resolution can give more or fewer communities depending on the data, so retune it when switching.

snn_similarity Literal['jaccard', 'rank']

"snn" only. "jaccard" weighs an edge by the Jaccard index of the two (self-inclusive) neighbour sets. "rank" takes the shared neighbour with the lowest combined rank, so closer shared neighbours give heavier edges. Both are scaled to [0, 1].

pruning float

"snn" only. Edges below this weight are dropped. For the Jaccard weight a threshold p keeps pairs that share at least a fraction 2p / (1 + p) of their (self-inclusive) neighbourhoods, rounded up to whole cells, so the same value means the same thing at any k. The default asks for about 12%, i.e. 2 of 16 shared cells at k = 15, in line with Seurat's 1/15. Avoid a threshold that equals one of the discrete weights exactly, or float rounding decides whether the edge survives.

rescue bool

"snn" only. Reconnect the small components that pruning cuts off via their strongest sNN edge, so they do not turn up as tiny clusters.

local_connectivity float

"umap" only. Number of nearest neighbours assumed to be fully connected, as in umap-learn.

mix_ratio float

"umap" only. 1 is the fuzzy union of the directed kNN memberships, 0 the fuzzy intersection (umap-learn's set_op_mix_ratio).

binary bool

"knn" only. If True, every edge weighs 1. Otherwise mutual neighbours weigh 2 and one-sided ones 1.

algorithm Literal['louvain', 'leiden']

Community detection on the centroid graph.

n_iterations int | None

Number of iterations of the community detection. A negative value iterates until stable. If None, the bixverse default for the chosen algorithm.

beta float

Leiden only. Randomness of the refinement step.

min_gain float

With a negative n_iterations, also stop once an iteration gains no more than this in modularity.

local_moving Literal['queue', 'coloured']

"queue" is Traag's sequential queue. "coloured" moves the nodes of one colour class in parallel, which only kicks in on larger levels of the graph.

multi_level bool

Shall the communities be aggregated and refined in levels.

max_evals int

Cap on the node evaluations per local moving phase, in units of the number of nodes.

def plot_scores_on_umap(scores, label, scale=False, ncol=2):
    """Facet the columns of an `ScMatrixRes` on the UMAP."""
    df = scores.frame().join(umap_df, on="cell_id")
    n = len(scores.columns)
    nrow = int(np.ceil(n / ncol))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrow, ncol, figsize=(4.5 * ncol, 4 * nrow), squeeze=False)
    for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, scores.columns, strict=False):
        v = df[col].to_numpy()
        if scale:
            v = (v - v.min()) / (v.max() - v.min())
        pts = ax.scatter(df["umap_1"], df["umap_2"], c=v, s=1, cmap="viridis")
        ax.set_title(col)
        ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_yticks([])
        fig.colorbar(pts, ax=ax, label=label)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.set_visible(False)
    fig.tight_layout()

method="mlm" fits all TFs in one model, so TFs sharing many targets compete for the signal instead of both lighting up. It errors on collinear TFs, i.e., two regulons with identical or proportional target sets. Unlike decoupler, genes that are zero in every cell stay in the model; on real data that shifts the scores a little. p_values=True adds p-values and an FDR per cell, but with thousands of correlated genes in each fit treat them as descriptive.

With the threshold in hand we grab the T cell IDs and recompute HVGs within this subset. This matters: HVGs computed across all PBMCs are dominated by inter-cell-type variation (T vs B vs monocyte). HVGs within T cells expose the genes that actually vary across T cell states, which is what we want NMF to factorise.

get_hvg_data() is a non-mutating variant of find_hvg(): it returns a polars frame with the HVG metrics and an is_hvg flag, without overwriting the HVGs stored on the object. Convenient when you want HVGs for a specific downstream analysis without disturbing the global state.

Error falls monotonically with k, so it would happily push you to the largest rank you can afford. Stability is the counterweight: take the last k before it falls away, while the error curve is still coming down. Here stability plateaus from 5 to 9 (with a dip at 7) and drops at 10, so that is 9, not the 10 we picked by eye for the runs above. Worth knowing before writing up ten programmes when the data supports nine. (Identifying two components is always trivial and unlikely to be the true signal.)

density_threshold=2 turns the outlier filter off, since cosine distance cannot exceed 2. Left on, components whose neighbours sit too far away get dropped, and if fewer than k survive the fit errors instead of returning something degenerate. Sensible on real data with enough restarts; with only a handful of them it fires more often than it should. get_stability() gives you the local_density values to pick a real threshold from.

docs.title: Gene set analysis and GRN inference on PBMCs¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Gene set analysis and GRN inference on PBMCs. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
This vignette demonstrates the gene set scoring, spatial autocorrelation and gene regulatory network (GRN) inference methods available in bixverse. It picks up where the PBMC vignette left off: QC, normalisation, PCA, nearest neighbours, clustering and UMAP are all assumed to be done already. If you have not read the design choices and the introductory vignette, please do so first.

The methods fall into three broad categories:

  • The first, module scores, AUCell and VISION, takes pre-defined gene sets and scores them per cell. ULM and MLM do the same for signed networks and show up after SCENIC, scoring its TF-to-gene links.
  • The second, Hotspot and SCENIC, discovers gene programmes and regulatory relationships from the data itself.
  • The third, NMF, also discovers gene programmes, via matrix factorisation, which is a different angle from SCENIC and Hotspot.

The LDA topic models over the binarised regulons are not ported to Python yet, so that part of the story is missing here.

We use the PBMC3k dataset throughout. At 2,700 cells this is likely too small for the GRN methods to produce biologically meaningful results, but it is large enough to show the API and the workflow end to end. On real datasets with tens of thousands of cells the same code applies unchanged.

docs.title: Rebuilding the processed object¶
docs.text: We reconstruct the processed SingleCells object from the PBMC vignette: it downloads the data, runs QC, HVG selection, PCA, neighbour computation, Leiden clustering and UMAP.

docs.title: Module scores¶
docs.text: The simplest approach to gene set activity is the module score from Tirosh et al. (2016): for each cell, compute the mean expression of the gene set and subtract the mean expression of a size-matched control set drawn from the same expression bins. We will just use some lineage-specific genes to have pretty visualisations.

docs.title: AUCell¶
docs.text:
AUCell ranks genes within each cell by expression and summarises where the gene set lands in that ranking. More robust to outliers than a simple mean. bixverse gives you three statistics via AucellParams, all reading the same ranking but weighting it differently:

  • "recovery", the default, is the recovery-curve AUC under a rank cutoff, i.e. what Aibar et al. published. Top-heavy: only genes inside the top max_rank contribute, so it is the sharper instrument for marker sets and the one to use for SCENIC.
  • "wilcox" is the AUC from the Mann-Whitney U statistic over the full ranking. Its null sits at 0.5 whatever the gene set size, which makes it a safe pick for pathway activity, but the flatter score splits less cleanly into on/off populations than "recovery" (the four lineage scores below still binarise as bimodal).
  • "ap" is average precision. Most top-heavy of the three, but its null tracks gene set prevalence, so don't compare raw values across sets of different size unless you switch standardise on.

We use the "wilcox" here.

docs.title: VISION with spatial autocorrelation¶
docs.text:
Scoring gene sets is useful, but a natural follow-up question is: are these scores spatially structured on the cell neighbourhood graph, or just noise? VISION provides a permutation-based test of spatial autocorrelation (Geary's C) on the kNN graph. Gene sets with significant autocorrelation are those whose activity varies smoothly across cell neighbourhoods, a strong indication that the signal is biologically meaningful rather than random.

VISION expects gene sets in a signed format with pos and (optionally) neg components. In the case of our cell lineage genes, we could use the other cell type's markers as negatives, but we will just leave it blank here.

docs.title: Hotspot¶
docs.text: Where the methods above test pre-defined gene sets, Hotspot (DeTomaso & Yosef, 2021) discovers gene programmes de novo by testing each gene for spatial autocorrelation on the kNN graph and then grouping the significant genes by their local correlation structure.

docs.title: Gene autocorrelation¶
docs.text: The first step computes Geary's C for every gene against the neighbour graph. Genes with significant autocorrelation are those whose expression varies smoothly across neighbouring cells, i.e., genes that mark spatially coherent programmes.

docs.title: Gene-gene local correlations and modules¶
docs.text: Taking the significant genes forward, we compute pairwise local correlations and cluster them into modules. Each module represents a group of genes that are not only individually autocorrelated but also co-vary locally, a much stronger signal than global correlation alone.

docs.title: SCENIC¶
docs.text:
SCENIC infers gene regulatory networks by asking: for each gene, which transcription factors (TFs) best predict its expression? The original implementation uses either random forests or GRNBoost2 (gradient boosted trees) to regress each target gene on all TFs, then extracts feature importances as a proxy for regulatory strength.

The bixverse implementation re-implements this in Rust with several optimisations that make the RF and ExtraTrees paths substantially faster than the single-target-at-a-time approach used by GRNBoost2:

  • Quantisation: TF expression values are discretised into 256 bins (u8), so histogram construction during tree building operates on single bytes and fits comfortably in L1 cache.
  • Multi-output batching: up to 64 target genes share a single tree structure. The histogram construction cost is paid once per node per feature, but the split score aggregates variance reduction across all targets in the batch. This amortises the dominant cost of tree building across targets.
  • Correlated gene batching: rather than assigning genes to batches randomly, an optional SVD + k-means step groups co-expressed genes together so that the shared tree structure is more informative for each target in the batch.
  • GRNBoost2 with histogram subtraction: for the gradient boosted path (single-target), the code builds full-feature histograms at each node and derives the larger child via parent-minus-smaller subtraction, avoiding a redundant scan of the larger child's samples. OOB early stopping prevents overfitting and is the main source of speedup.

On the 2,700-cell PBMC3k dataset these optimisations are not that noticeable... The data is too small for any method to take long. On datasets with tens of thousands of cells and thousands of TFs, the RF/ET multi-output path comfortably outperforms GRNBoost2. You need to just decide if you are okay with the batching of genes. The big signals get recovered again and again (from empirical testing).

docs.title: Gene filtering¶
docs.text: SCENIC first filters genes by minimum total counts and minimum proportion of expressing cells to remove uninformative targets.

docs.title: Transcription factor list¶
docs.text: We need a list of known TFs. The Aerts lab provides a curated list for human (allTFs_hg38.txt from their cisTarget resources). The Python package does not ship a copy yet, so we fetch it from there and map it to Ensembl IDs.

docs.title: GRN inference¶
docs.text: With genes and TFs in hand, we run the GRN inference step. Here we use random forests with a batch size of 64 to illustrate the multi-output path.

docs.title: TF-to-gene refinement¶
docs.text: The raw importance matrix is large and noisy. The next steps winnow it down to a candidate regulatory network by keeping only the top TF-gene pairs and filtering by pairwise expression correlation. Per gene only the TFs with an importance score >= mean(importance_score) + n_sd * sd(importance_score) for that gene are kept. Note that n_sd should be adjusted depending on the learner: RF and ExtraTrees spread importance more evenly across TFs than GRNBoost2, so a lower threshold keeps more TFs per gene, whereas GRNBoost2 concentrates importance onto fewer TFs and tolerates n_sd=1.5 or even n_sd=2. Below we use the strict n_sd=2.0 on the random forest too, which keeps only the strongest TFs per gene.

docs.title: CisTarget motif enrichment¶
docs.text:
The final (and optional) step in the SCENIC pipeline validates the predicted TF-gene links against known motif binding sites. This requires the CisTarget motif ranking database and motif-to-TF annotation files from the Aerts lab resources, which together are roughly 400 MB. The Python package has no downloader or reader for them yet: tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment() takes the ranking as an integer matrix (genes x motifs) plus its gene and motif names, and the annotation as a polars frame with motif, TF and annotationSource. Load them however you like and the rest looks like this:

scenic_res = bv.pathways.tf_to_genes_motif_enrichment(
    scenic_res,
    rankings,
    rank_genes,
    rank_motifs,
    annotations,
    # we store everything as Ensembl... The SCENIC data has gene symbols,
    # hence the need to provide a conversion
    gene_id_to_symbol=ensembl_to_symbol,
    cis_target_params=CistargetParams(),
    only_high_conf_tf=False,
    verbose=True,
)

# CisTarget results per TF
bv.pathways.get_cistarget_res(scenic_res).sort("nes", descending=True).head()

# The TF-to-gene table now has an in_leading_edge column indicating which
# genes fall within the motif recovery curve
(
    bv.pathways.get_tf_to_gene(scenic_res)
    .filter(pl.col("in_leading_edge"))
    .sort("importance", descending=True)
    .head()
)

CisTarget is not a pass/fail filter on the module. Per enriched motif it builds a recovery curve, compares it against the mean + 2 SD curve across every motif in the database, and keeps only the genes above the point of maximum separation. So expect the regulons coming out of build_regulons() to be a good deal smaller than the modules going in.

build_regulons() applies that filter, adds the TF back to its own set and drops anything too small. Since we skipped CisTarget above, we pass use_leading_edge=False and it carries on without the motif filter. The regulons that come out are a lot bigger and noisier than a proper SCENIC run would give you, so read the biology below with that in mind. The API is identical either way.

docs.title: ULM and MLM on the TF-to-gene links¶
docs.text: AUCell only looks at whether the targets rank high in a cell. The TF-to-gene table carries more than that: tf_to_genes_correlations() gave every link a sign. lm_activity() uses it. It is the decoupler ULM/MLM: per cell, regress the normalised counts of all genes on the weights of a TF's targets and take the t-value as the activity. Activated targets up and repressed ones down gives a positive score. Normally you would use a curated network like CollecTRI here; the inferred links do for the demo and keep the vignette offline.

docs.title: NMF on single cells¶
docs.text:
The methods so far have all started from either a pre-defined gene set, a graph-based notion of locality, or a TF-centric regression framework. NMF (non-negative matrix factorisation) takes yet another angle: it factorises the expression matrix V ≈ W H into a small number of latent factors, where W carries non-negative gene loadings and H carries non-negative cell activations. The non-negativity constraint tends to push the factors into something interpretable as additive gene programmes rather than abstract directions of variance like PCA. bixverse implements HALS (Hierarchical Alternating Least Squares) in Rust, which converges fast and scales nicely.

A few practical notes before diving in:

  • NMF is non-convex: different random initialisations land in different local optima. The package therefore provides nmf() for a single run, stabilised_nmf() for multiple restarts, and consensus_nmf() which takes those restarts and returns the programmes they agree on. The last one is the right default for any serious analysis.
  • Picking k is the eternal question. Too small and programmes get smushed together; too large and they fragment into redundant copies. nmf_k_sweep() turns that into something you can actually look at: stability against reconstruction error across a range of k. It is not a free lunch, but it beats licking your finger and seeing from where the wind comes... (Joke)
  • NMF on a heterogeneous dataset often just rediscovers the obvious cell-type axis. The interesting use case is running it within a cell type to find finer-grained programmes (activation, exhaustion, cycling, etc.). We will do exactly that here.

We will focus on the T cells as an example. Think of your own use cases in your data set and analyses.

docs.title: Identifying T cells¶
docs.text: We will use the AUC scores from earlier to pull out the T cell population. The Python package has no Otsu threshold yet, so we borrow the binariser from the SCENIC section: a two-component Gaussian mixture on the AUC with the threshold at the trough between the two modes, which is just as data-driven for a bimodal distribution.

docs.title: Running a single NMF run¶
docs.text: nmf() runs one NMF on the chosen cells and genes. The default initialisation is NNDSVD, which is deterministic and gives a sensible starting point.

docs.title: Running multiple NMF runs¶
docs.text: For anything beyond exploratory work you want multiple restarts. stabilised_nmf() runs n_runs HALS NMFs with random initialisations (seeded by seed + i) and column-binds the resulting W matrices. Looking at this stabilised data allows you to identify components that constantly show up between random initialisations.

docs.title: Consensus NMF¶
docs.text:
Picking the lowest-loss restart is a reasonable default, but it dodges the question you actually care about: did the restarts agree? Consensus NMF (cNMF, Kotliar, et al.) answers it directly. Pool the components of every restart, drop the ones sitting on their own in the pool, k-means the survivors into k groups, and take the median of each group. What comes out is the programme structure the restarts agree on, and the mean silhouette of those clusters says how strongly they agreed.

Before fitting, though, you need a k. nmf_k_sweep() runs the consensus step across a range of ranks and reports stability against reconstruction error, keeping no factors, so a wide sweep stays affordable.

docs.title: Downstream analysis¶
docs.text:
What you do next depends entirely on what you are after. Some natural directions:

  • Inspect the components: rank genes by loading in W to read off what each component represents. Components that recover known programmes (cytotoxicity, exhaustion, ribosomal, IFN response, etc.) are a good sign; components that load on uninteresting genes you can ignore or merge.
  • Score cells: H gives you per-cell activations for each programme. Project them onto your UMAP, correlate against existing annotations, or use them as features for downstream clustering.
  • Add activations to the obs table: bv.nmf.get_data() on an NmfResult or a ConsensusNmfResult returns a polars frame of cell activations keyed on cell_idx that goes straight into add_obs(), the same way module scores did earlier.

We leave the choice of analysis here to you: the right downstream depends on the biology and your questions to the data, not the API.

Where did the time go? Every stage is timed, and total is the whole call as Python saw it, so a gap between total and the stages would be time spent somewhere nobody measured. Sanity fits every one of the 11k candidate genes, the search only sees the few hundred that survive but has to place 2,400 leaves, and on PBMC3k the search ends up taking the bigger share.

def plot_tree(tree, colour_by=None, point_size=2.0, size_by_cells=False, ax=None):
    ax = ax or plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))[1]
    nodes = tree.nodes
    xy = nodes.select("x", "y").to_numpy()
    edges = nodes.filter(pl.col("parent").is_not_null())
    child = xy[edges["node"].to_numpy()]
    parent = xy[edges["parent"].to_numpy()]
    if tree.layout == "dendrogram":
        # depth along x, leaves along y: across to the parent's depth, then up
        elbow = np.column_stack([parent[:, 0], child[:, 1]])
        segs = np.concatenate(
            [np.stack([child, elbow], 1), np.stack([elbow, parent], 1)]
        )
    else:
        segs = np.stack([child, parent], 1)
        ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(list(segs), colors="grey", linewidths=0.2))

    leaves = nodes.filter(pl.col("is_leaf"))
    sizes: float | np.ndarray = point_size
    if size_by_cells:
        n = leaves["n_cells"].to_numpy()
        sizes = point_size * (1 + 4 * (n - n.min()) / max(n.max() - n.min(), 1))
    if colour_by is None:
        ax.scatter(leaves["x"], leaves["y"], s=sizes, linewidths=0)
    else:
        colour_by = np.asarray(colour_by)
        groups = np.unique(colour_by)
        palette = bv.pl.bx_colors("main", n=len(groups))
        for i, grp in enumerate(groups):
            m = colour_by == grp
            s = sizes[m] if isinstance(sizes, np.ndarray) else sizes
            ax.scatter(
                leaves["x"].to_numpy()[m],
                leaves["y"].to_numpy()[m],
                s=s,
                color=palette[i],
                label=grp,
                linewidths=0,
            )
        legend = ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.5))
        for handle in legend.legend_handles:
            handle.set_sizes([20])  # ty: ignore[missing-union-attribute] # matplotlib stubs type legend handles as Artist
    ax.set_axis_off()
    return ax

Every cell type gets its own subtree, and none of that was told to Bonsai: the annotation only colours the leaves. The CD16+ monocytes form their own clump next to the CD14+ monocytes, and the NK cells branch off close to the T cells, which is what you would expect from their biology. Branch length is change, so the long isolated branches are cells that look like nothing else in the data.

The default is the equal-angle layout: every subtree gets a wedge proportional to its size. Two alternatives, recomputed from the stored tree with relayout_bonsai() without searching again. The dendrogram draws the branch lengths along x:

    colour_by=cell_type,
    point_size=1.0,
)
plt.show()
plot_tree( bv.trees.relayout_bonsai(tree, layout="dendrogram"), colour_by=cell_type, point_size=1.0, ) plt.show()

The hyperbolic projection maps the same layout onto the unit disk. How much it changes the picture depends on how far the tips sit from the root; on PBMC3k the branches are short and it barely does, on deeper trees it gives the crowded centre more room:

plt.show()

The subtrees of the cell-level tree survive the compression, and the monocytes come out sharper: CD14+ and CD16+ split into two branches of one monocyte subtree. A few T-cell metacells sit on the NK branch; T and NK cells share much of their cytotoxic programme, so that is where the tree is least sure of the labels. What the metacell tree cannot show is anything inside a metacell, so pick the compression to match the resolution you care about.

docs.title: Cell trees with Bonsai¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Cell trees with Bonsai. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
UMAP and t-SNE squash a kNN graph into two dimensions and lose most of the global structure on the way. Bonsai (de Groot, et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2026) takes a different route: it reconstructs a tree over the cells, every cell a leaf and every internal node an inferred ancestral state, with branch lengths that carry how much changed between them. The tree is the representation; a 2D layout is just a way to draw it.

What makes it work is that Bonsai uses the error bar on every measurement, not only the measurement. Those come from Sanity (Breda, et al., Nat. Biotechnol., 2021), which turns raw UMI counts into posterior log fold changes with error bars, gene by gene. bv.trees.bonsai() runs both: counts from disk, Sanity, Bonsai, layout. Both are Rust ports under the hood, sanity-sc-rs and bonsai-rs.

We use the PBMC3k data here. If you have not worked through the PBMC vignette, do that first; the preprocessing below is the same, just condensed.

docs.title: Preparing the data¶
docs.text: Loading, QC and the usual HVG, PCA, neighbours and clustering chain. Bonsai itself needs none of the last four, but the clusters and cell types make the tree readable, and the UMAP gives us something to compare against.

docs.title: Running Bonsai¶
docs.text: One call. No HVG selection needed: by default every gene is a candidate, and Sanity streams them through in chunks of 1,024, keeping only the genes with enough signal over their own noise (min_signal_to_noise in BonsaiParams, 1 by default). That is the gene selection of the Bonsai paper. Memory stays at one chunk of counts plus the survivors, whatever the number of candidates.

docs.title: Which genes made it?¶
docs.text: Most genes carry no usable signal over their Poisson noise and are dropped. The ones that stay overlap with, but are not, the HVGs.

docs.title: Plotting¶
docs.text: There is no tree plot in bv.pl yet, so here is a short matplotlib one: every branch as a segment from a node to its parent and a point per leaf. Radial layouts get straight branches at a fixed aspect ratio, the dendrogram right angles. colour_by takes one value per leaf, in the order of the object's kept cells.

docs.title: Bonsai next to UMAP¶
docs.text: The leaf coordinates can go into the object as an embedding, so everything that plots embeddings works on them.

docs.title: Bonsai on metacells¶
docs.text:
At 100k cells a tree over every cell is slow and hard to look at. Metacells compress first. Their raw counts are sums over their cells, and a sum of Poisson counts is Poisson, so Sanity treats a metacell exactly as it treats a cell, with its total counts as the library size. A metacell of 20 cells has about 20 times the counts, so its error bars are much tighter, and Bonsai weights by them. The same bonsai() call works on MetaCells; every metacell becomes a leaf.

Here SuperCells compresses the PBMCs into metacells, and each metacell gets the cell type most of its cells carry.

docs.title: Scaling¶
docs.text:
The search grows a little faster than linearly with the cell number. In bonsai-rs's own benchmarks on ten cores it took about 70 seconds at 10,000 cells and 210 seconds at 25,000. Sanity comes on top and grows with the number of candidate genes; CPU has been made fast, GPU is even faster. bixverse_gpu.trees.bonsai() takes the same arguments, returns the same BonsaiTree, and runs Sanity on the device.

On the 2,399 PBMCs of this vignette with every gene as a candidate (M1 Max, ten cores, mean of two runs):

Sanity Bonsai search total CPU 9.6 s 14.6 s 24.2 s GPU 1.0 s 14.6 s 15.6 s

Both kept the same 348 genes. With Sanity on the GPU the tree search is the clear cost, and that is where 100k cells will hurt. Metacells are the way around it: compress first and the tree has a few thousand leaves instead of 100k.

docs.title: Ambient RNA removal with CellSweep¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Ambient RNA removal with CellSweep. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
Cells lyse during dissociation and their transcripts end up in the buffer. Every droplet then gets loaded with a bit of that soup on top of whatever cell it caught, which is why you find monocyte genes in T cells, haemoglobin everywhere, and lineage markers that refuse to be clean. That background is the ambient RNA.

CellSweep attacks it as a mixture problem. Every observed count in a barcode comes from one of three places: the ambient profile of that emulsion, a global bulk profile, or the barcode's own cell type profile. An EM fit splits the counts three ways per barcode, and subtracting the first two components leaves the denoised matrix. The per-barcode ambient fraction, alpha, falls out of the same fit, which doubles as a quality metric: a barcode that is 60% soup is not a cell you want in your clustering.

Two things about where this sits in a workflow, because both are easy to get wrong.

It runs after annotation, not before. The model subtracts against cell type profiles, so it needs the labels on input. The chain is: ingest the raw barcodes, cluster and annotate as usual, then bv.doublets.cellsweep(), then redo the feature selection and reduction on the clean counts.

It needs the empty droplets. The ambient profile is estimated from their pooled counts, and they stay in the EM with their contamination fraction pinned at 1. So the object has to be ingested permissively. The load-time cutoffs in bixverse are irreversible, and the defaults delete exactly the barcodes the model trains on.

docs.title: The raw matrix¶
docs.text: We use the 10x Genomics 5' PBMC 1k run, the same data the CellSweep reference notebook works through. This is the unfiltered matrix, so every barcode the sequencer saw is in there.

docs.title: Calling the empty droplets¶
docs.text:
EmptyDropletsParams offers four ways to decide which barcode is empty, in descending order of how much you should trust them. "supplied" takes an existing boolean column from the obs table, and if you have Cell Ranger's filtered barcode list you already know the answer. The other three infer it from the library sizes alone.

The barcode rank curve is the thing they are all trying to read.

docs.title: Annotating the real cells¶
docs.text: CellSweep needs cell type labels, so the real barcodes have to go through a normal pipeline first. The raw object is not the place to do that, since 97k of its barcodes are soup. Load the same file a second time with QC that means something, and cluster there.

docs.title: Putting the labels back¶
docs.text: The labels live on the cell object and CellSweep reads them off the raw one, so they have to be joined across by barcode. Every barcode that is not a clustered cell keeps a null, which is exactly how cellsweep() finds the barcodes it should ignore.

docs.title: What came out¶
docs.text: The ambient profile is the first thing to look at, because it is the one part of the fit you can sanity check against what you know about the tissue.

docs.title: Does the subtraction do anything?¶
docs.text: The honest test is not whether alpha looks plausible but whether the counts change in the direction they should. Monocyte genes appearing in T cells are soup by construction, so track a couple of them across clusters, before and after.

docs.title: Reprocessing the clean counts¶
docs.text: Feature selection and reduction were computed on contaminated counts, so they have to be redone. Drop the barcodes CellSweep says are mostly soup while you are at it.

docs.title: Where this goes next¶
docs.text:
The obvious extension is multi-sample data, where the ambient profile is fitted per emulsion and sample_column starts earning its keep. A soup that differs between runs is a batch effect that no correction method will name for you, and having cellsweep_alpha and the per-sample profiles in hand is a much better starting point than pretending the contamination is uniform.

cellsweep_alpha is also worth keeping in the obs table after the fact. It is a QC metric in its own right, and a cluster with a suspiciously high median is usually debris rather than biology.

The point of this table: resolutions do not carry over between graphs. The "umap" and "knn" graphs only hold the kNN pairs, while the sNN graph also links cells that merely share neighbours and prunes weak edges. On this data the differences are a handful of communities at a given resolution, and not always in the same direction. On other data they can be larger. If you move a ScanPy pipeline over and switch to knn_sym="umap", keep its resolution; if you switch to sNN, retune it.

For the rest of the vignette we work on the sNN graph.

A few knobs on find_clusters():

  • n_iterations: defaults to 2 for Louvain and 5 for Leiden. A negative value iterates until the partition is stable.
  • min_gain: with a negative n_iterations, also stop once an iteration gains no more than this in modularity.
  • local_moving: "queue" is Traag's sequential queue, "coloured" moves the nodes of one colour class in parallel. The latter only kicks in on the larger levels of the graph, so on 6k cells don't expect much.

In [9]: Copied! 
def plot_overlap(a, b, name_a, name_b, title):
    df = (
        pl.DataFrame({"a": a, "b": b})
        .group_by("a", "b")
        .len()
        .with_columns(frac=pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum().over("a"))
    )
    a_levels = np.sort(df["a"].unique().to_numpy())
    b_levels = np.sort(df["b"].unique().to_numpy())
    mat = np.full((a_levels.size, b_levels.size), np.nan)
    ai = np.searchsorted(a_levels, df["a"].to_numpy())
    bi = np.searchsorted(b_levels, df["b"].to_numpy())
    mat[ai, bi] = df["frac"].to_numpy()

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5), layout="constrained")
    im = ax.imshow(mat, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1, origin="lower", aspect="auto")
    # light text on the dark end of viridis, dark text on the yellow end
    for i, j, f in zip(ai, bi, df["frac"].to_numpy(), strict=True):
        ax.text(
            float(j),
            float(i),
            f"{f:.2f}",
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            fontsize=6,
            color="white" if f < 0.5 else "black",
        )
    ax.set_xticks(range(b_levels.size), b_levels)
    ax.set_yticks(range(a_levels.size), a_levels)
    ax.set_xlabel(name_b)
    ax.set_ylabel(name_a)
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Fraction")
    return ax

docs.title: Clustering, cell type annotation and reference mapping¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Clustering, cell type annotation and reference mapping. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
Getting from a corrected embedding to cell type labels involves more choices than a single find_clusters() call suggests. Which graph do you cluster on? Leiden or Louvain, and how many iterations? Do you cluster every cell, or coarsen first because you have a million of them? Do you stamp one label per cluster, or score each cell? And once you have a well annotated data set, how do you avoid redoing all of it every time a new sample lands on your desk?

This vignette goes through these decisions in that order:

  1. Build a reference from two PBMC data sets (pbmc3k + pbmc4k), corrected with Harmony v2.
  2. Compare the three neighbour graphs bixverse can build (sNN, the UMAP fuzzy simplicial set and the plain kNN union) and what they do to the clustering.
  3. Leiden vs Louvain, and the fast clustering via k-means coarsening.
  4. Annotate with scType, per cluster and per cell.
  5. Compress the reference with Symphony (Kang, et al., 2021), map a third PBMC data set (pbmc8k) into it and transfer the labels.

If you have not read the batch correction vignette and the introductory vignette, please do so first; this vignette assumes familiarity with both.

docs.title: Loading the reference batches¶
docs.text: We use the same pbmc3k + pbmc4k pair as in the batch correction vignette. Two batches with the same broad cell type composition and a clear technical difference between them is exactly the situation Symphony is designed for: the reference learns the batch correction once, and that correction can then be applied to future queries without rerunning Harmony.

docs.title: Quality control¶
docs.text: Standard QC: mitochondrial gene proportions, library complexity, MAD-based outlier detection.

docs.title: HVGs, PCA, Harmony v2¶
docs.text: This block is the Harmony v2 path of the batch correction vignette: pick HVGs, run PCA, run Harmony v2, which is what bv.integrate.harmony() runs. Version 1 is still available via bv.integrate.harmony_v1() and HarmonyParams, but v2 is preferable in most settings (see the batch correction vignette for the reasoning).

docs.title: Which graph to cluster on¶
docs.text:
find_neighbours() does two things: it finds the kNN on the embedding and it symmetrises that kNN into the undirected, weighted graph the clustering runs on. The second step is controlled by knn_sym in NeighboursParams. Three options:

  • "snn" (default): the shared nearest neighbour graph of bluster/Seurat. Two cells are linked if their neighbourhoods overlap, weighted by Jaccard (or rank), and weak edges below pruning are dropped.
  • "umap": the fuzzy simplicial set from UMAP, i.e. what ScanPy stores in obsp/connectivities. Use this if you want your Leiden clusters to line up with a ScanPy pipeline.
  • "knn": the plain union of the kNN, every edge weighted 1.

Let's build all three on the Harmony embedding and cluster each across a few resolutions. Every call recomputes the kNN as well, which at ~6k cells costs nothing.

docs.title: Leiden vs Louvain¶
docs.text: Both run in Rust, and the labels depend on seed only, not on the global RNG or the number of threads. Leiden is the default; it guarantees connected communities, which Louvain does not (Traag, et al., 2019). Labels are 0-based with 0 being the largest cluster.

docs.title: Fast clustering¶
docs.text:
On a few thousand cells the full graph clustering is instant. On a million it isn't. fast_cluster() coarsens the cells with k-means first (floor(4 * sqrt(N)) centroids by default, the faiss default for IVF), builds a graph over the centroids and runs Louvain or Leiden on that. Each cell inherits the community of its centroid. Two options for the centroid graph:

  • the default, a symmetrised kNN between the centroids (centroid_k, knn_sym);
  • cell_mediated=True, the Secuer graph (Wei, et al., PLoS Comput Biol, 2022), where each cell links its n_anchors nearest centroids, so two centroids are connected if they share cells.

With n_seeds > 1 every resolution is run once per seed. The labels of the seed with the lowest mean conductance are kept, and the ARI and conductance across seeds come back as stability statistics.

docs.title: scType per cluster¶
docs.text: We annotate with scType (Ianevski, et al., Nat Comm, 2022) using a PBMC marker set.

docs.title: scType per cell¶
docs.text: The cluster level call stamps one label on every cell of a cluster. A small population that shares a Leiden community with a bigger one gets absorbed and nothing flags it. assign_sc_type() scores per cell instead: the score matrix is smoothed over the neighbour graph via label spreading (Zhou, et al., NIPS, 2004), then each cell takes its own argmax. Cells whose best score falls below score_floor come back as null. Pass cluster_col and you also get the per-cluster composition and a hybrid call: clusters at or above purity_threshold keep the cluster level label, mixed clusters fall back to the per-cell calls.

docs.title: Sanity checks¶
docs.text: Batches mixed, cell types separated:

docs.title: Reference mapping with Symphony¶
docs.text: Once you have a well annotated reference, you don't want to redo QC, HVG selection, PCA, batch correction, clustering and manual annotation for every new sample. Symphony compresses the reference into a small set of cached terms that map new query cells into the same coordinate system in a single shot, with no need to keep the reference cells around at query time.

docs.title: Compressing into a SymphonyReference¶
docs.text:
build_symphony_ref() re-runs PCA and Harmony internally using the supplied HVGs, then caches the loadings, centroids and compression terms (nr, c_cache) needed for query mapping. The Harmony version follows the type of harmony_params. Pass label_columns to snapshot one or more obs columns, here both scType annotations, into the reference for downstream label transfer.

A note on the apparent duplication: yes, PCA + Harmony are run again inside build_symphony_ref(), even though we just ran them on the same HVGs above. This is deliberate. The standard pipeline keeps its embeddings on the SingleCells object and streams from disk; the Symphony reference keeps a self-contained, in-memory copy of everything it needs to project queries without the reference cells. Sharing state across those two representations would tie them together in unhelpful ways. The cost is one extra PCA + Harmony run at build time.

docs.title: Loading the query¶
docs.text: We use pbmc8k as the query. Same tissue, same broad biology, but a different 10x run: exactly the kind of "another sample arrives" scenario Symphony is built for.

docs.title: Quality control on the query¶
docs.text: Same QC as the reference. We are not trying to match library sizes or anything fancy across data sets, just remove clearly bad cells.

docs.title: Projecting the query¶
docs.text:
map_symphony_query() does the actual projection: query cells are standardised against the reference's per-HVG means and SDs, projected through the reference PCA loadings, and assigned soft cluster weights against the reference centroids. Those weights then drive the cached MoE batch correction, putting query cells into the same z_corr coordinate system as the reference.

Genes are matched by id. Missing HVGs are treated as zero columns; with verbose=True the function reports how many were missing.

pbmc8k is a single batch, so we pass batch_column=None, which skips the query-side correction (the resulting symphony embedding then equals symphony_pca). With several query batches, pass the batch column and Symphony corrects them against the reference.

docs.title: Transferring labels¶
docs.text: transfer_labels_symphony() does a kNN majority vote on the reference's z_corr (the searchable index) using the query's "symphony" embedding. It reads labels from the reference's stored labels, the ones we populated via label_columns at build time. Distances on z_corr are Euclidean; the default KnnParams matches.

docs.title: Visualising the result¶
docs.text: Query UMAP coloured by transferred cell type:

docs.title: Slim references and post-hoc labels¶
docs.text:
The reference above stores z_corr, z_orig, the soft cluster assignments r and the labels. For large references that get checked into shared storage, z_orig and r are dead weight; passing slim=True at build time drops them. z_corr is always retained, since kNN label transfer searches against it.

If you want to add or update labels after the reference is built (say, you re-ran scType with a different marker set), use add_symphony_labels(). It reads obs columns from a SingleCells object in cells_to_keep order and snapshots them into a new reference (the input is left alone). The cells_to_keep state must match the reference; the function errors if the row count drifts.

slim_ref = bv.annotate.build_symphony_ref(
    sc_ref,
    "exp_id",
    hvg_indices,
    harmony_params=HarmonyV2Params(),
    no_pcs=30,
    slim=True,
)

slim_ref = bv.annotate.add_symphony_labels(slim_ref, sc_ref, ["sc_type"])

Multiple label columns can be attached at once, existing columns are protected unless you pass overwrite=True, and bv.annotate.get_symphony_labels(reference) returns the stored DataFrame (or None if there is none). save_symphony_ref() and load_symphony_ref() write the reference to a single .npz and back.

Got stores from an older version of the package? The idea is to use your disk space temporarily, stream data into the analysis methods in the right shape and when done, compress everything down. The store format is the same one the R package writes, so a directory written by one opens in the other.

Two things worth saying about how it is built. The stamps sit on the cache next to the payloads, and assigning a new payload to a slot drops its stamp, so a stamp cannot outlive the result it describes. And it tracks provenance, not parameters: a kNN over the first 5 PCs and one over all 15 of the same PCA look identical to it. Neither of those can produce an index mismatch, which is the only thing this is here to stop.

The response is graded rather than one blanket error. Moving the cell set with set_cells_to_keep() warns and names everything that just went stale, and so does reading a stale artefact through the getters, because plenty of call sites use those as presence probes on something they are about to overwrite anyway. Anything that hands cached indices to Rust or writes a derived result back raises outright. Clustering on the stale graph from above:

Cached `connectivities` is stale: its upstream `knn` is stale. Re-run the step that produces it, or drop it, before using it.

Nothing is ever silently recomputed or binned: a forty minute Harmony run is not the package's to throw away. Compare that with AnnData, where obsm and obsp are aligned to the object's rows and subsetting slices them along, so the rows always line up (though a PCA sliced down to a subset is still the PCA of the full set). Here the results and the cell set live apart, and the stamps are the price of that.

None of which means you get to stop thinking about on-disk state. It only means you find out before the biology is wrong rather than after. The worked example lives in the thinking about single cells vignette.

docs.title: Technical design choices for the single cell implementation¶
docs.text:
Python port of the R vignette Technical design choices for the single cell implementation. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

This is an opinionated piece, so take what is written here with a pinch of salt. The statements here reflect my personal opinions, not those of any of my past, current, or future employers.

docs.title: Why do we need yet another single cell framework ... ?¶
docs.text: Why the hell would you write a single cell framework from scratch and not use one of the established libraries? In Python we have scanpy on top of AnnData, and even GPU-accelerated RAPIDS-singlecell using CUDA and Nvidia GPUs. In R there is Seurat and the BioConductor single cell experiments. In Rust, we have SingleRust which is porting scanpy over... What the hell is the point, you might ask? Well, the design philosophy in this package is quite different from all of the above. Whether better or worse you shall discover, but it is different. Let's start with the problem though...

docs.title: Chapter 1: Single cell is just not (very) performant (on CPU)...¶
docs.text:
Some quotes from recent papers:

We benchmarked rapids-singlecell on 1 million cells from the 10x Genomics mouse brain dataset, running a standard workflow: preprocessing, normalization, HVG selection, dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP, t-SNE), neighborhood graph construction, and Leiden clustering (Methods). On a 32-core workstation, the pipeline took over 52 minutes (Methods) [...]

  • Dicks, et al., arXiv, 2026

For instance, a typical single-cell data analysis pipeline, encompassing data integration, clustering, visualisation, and differential expression analysis, requires about 16 h to process half a million cells on a standard desktop. When the cell number slightly increases to 600,000, the above pipeline can crash due to memory exceeding, even on a professional computing platform with 512 GB RAM

  • Li, et al., Nat Comm, 2025

Recommendations for executing the Scanpy analysis

To avoid computer crashes and program failures, we recommend you execute the Python code on a cloud computing platform. The instance you select on the cloud platform to run this analysis should consist of at least 8 threads and 160 GB of RAM.

  • Parse biosciences

Anyone who has worked with more than 500k cells can attest to it being painful. Actually VERY painful. The question is... why? Why can analytical engines like DuckDB and polars handle massive data sets without needing fat memory machines? You can easily analyse hundreds of millions of rows on a local laptop with those two. Why can we not do the same with single cell? Is the answer really "Bro, just throw more cores, memory, and GPUs at the problem"? Or is it time to rethink HOW we are doing this.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Do not keep data in memory...¶
docs.text:
Let's do some maths. Say we have a single cell experiment with 1M cells, with on average 1000 genes detected per cell, held the AnnData way: a scipy CSR matrix in X, float32 values, int32 indices.

# raw counts (X, or layers["counts"])
data    (values, float32):   1B x 4 bytes = 4 GB
                 (float64):  1B x 8 bytes = 8 GB
indices (column ids, int32): 1B x 4 bytes = 4 GB
indptr  (row pointers):      (1M+1) x 4   ~ 4 MB

Total: ~8 GB (float32) / ~12 GB (float64)

# normalised counts (X after normalise_total + log1p, raw kept in a layer)
Same sparsity, so another ~8 GB

# scaled counts with 2k HVG (dense; if 3k, just increase this by 50%)
2k HVGs:  1M x 2,000 x 4 bytes = 8 GB (float32), 16 GB (float64)

# embeddings (obsm)
PCA:              1M x 50 x 4 = 200 MB
Batch correction: 1M x 50 x 4 = 200 MB

Total: ~400 MB

# kNN graph (obsp, k = 20)
indices (int32):    20M x 4 = 80 MB
data (float32):     20M x 4 = 80 MB
indptr (int32):      1M x 4 =  4 MB

Total: ~164 MB, and you usually hold distances and connectivities

You are looking at 25 GB of occupied memory before anything clever has happened, and the moment something upcasts to float64 that climbs fast. Then you have obs as a pandas DataFrame with 1M rows; throw in a bunch of string columns and you are adding a few hundred MB more. Subset the AnnData, call .copy() on the view, and you hold all of it twice. You end up with bloated objects storing data you rarely actually need in memory. The question is: should we be doing any of this? Why do we keep raw and normalised counts in memory at all? AnnData's backed mode, BPCells or the Dask-based approaches are going in the right direction here, but can we do even better?

docs.title: Chapter 3: Python and R are slow...¶
docs.text:
There. It has been said. They are slow and let us stop pretending otherwise. There is a reason why "Rust rewrite by LLM" is becoming a meme. Yes, you can drop into NumPy, numba or Cython for the heavy lifting, but that argument rather proves the point! The real problem is not any single kernel; it is what happens between them.

A lot of algorithms in practice end up looking like this:

Python → low-level kernel → Python → low-level kernel → Python → ...

Each arrow is a context switch. Data gets passed across a language boundary, some "simple" bookkeeping happens in the interpreter (a filter here, a reshape there, maybe a quick normalisation) and then you hand it back down again. None of those individual steps looks expensive. Collectively, they are death by a thousand cuts: repeated allocations, temporary arrays you did not ask for, and the garbage collector doing God knows what in between. You also lose any hope of the compiler reasoning across those boundaries and optimising the full pipeline. Writing kernel fusions is maybe possible, but admittedly just easier in the low level part directly.

The solution is not to make the interpreted bits faster. It is to keep the data in low-level code for as long as possible and only surface results to Python when the user actually needs to look at something. Python then becomes a thin orchestration layer, not an active participant in the computation.

docs.title: What is your proposal then ... ?¶
docs.text: Okay, everything so far reads like a rant. What is the solution, mate?

docs.title: Let's not keep data in memory to start with ... ?¶
docs.text:
If we think this through, we can arrive at a solution. Ideally, we want an interface from an interpreted, dynamically typed language: going all-in on Rust is just too heavy. The average single cell enthusiast does not want to deal with the borrow checker, does not want to compile code, and wants to quickly analyse and iterate over data. The average bioinformatician lives in blissful ignorance and will not be able to comment on f32 vs f64 float representation in memory, when to use which and frankly should not have to. That means the interface should be a dynamically typed, interpreted language. This opens the package up to more people and makes plotting and the deep learning stack a lot easier to reach. From there we can make some design decisions.

  1. We do not keep data in memory if not needed! Most analyses using counts only need subsets of cells and genes. We can also avoid holding metadata in memory via DuckDB. Data will be streamed from disk when needed and Rust frees memory once it is no longer needed, sometimes enforced explicitly with drop(). Raw counts? Nope. Normalised counts? Nope. Scaled counts? Nope. We just removed the bulk of those 25 GB from memory (in our 1M cell example). Data can be loaded into memory in milliseconds if need be.

  2. We do not even load all data into memory to begin with. In 99.99% of cases, we know we do not want low quality cells with tiny library sizes and few unique features. We also almost always do the usual library-size-to-target-size normalisation with log transformation. (Anyone who has tried a fancy modelling approach with Pearson residual modelling on large data sets knows what I am talking about. But bixverse does also offer memory-frugal versions of scTransform v2 if you want them, see the residuals vignette.) That means when reading h5ad or mtx files, we can pre-scan them, take only what we want, and normalise in a single pass, avoiding the load-everything, then-filter, then-normalise pattern. The data also gets streamed into the binary files, which avoids sudden memory spikes and OOM errors.

  3. We accept that single cell is noisy and do not bother with f32 or even f64 precision for storage. Raw counts are integers and most of them are tiny, so on disk they get bit-packed to whatever width the block actually needs. A block of ones and twos costs a single bit per value, the rare gene with a count in the thousands only widens its own block, and nothing gets clipped. Normalised counts live at f16 precision: the ML field has shown you can get away with it, and they are pushing quantisation even further than that. We accept the precision loss and upcast to f64 where it matters, to avoid catastrophic cancellation issues at large N.

  4. We are not doing any heavy calculations in Python. Rust is superior for speed and optimisation: aggressive multi-threading, no interpreter in the hot loop, tight memory control, and SIMD acceleration for specific bottlenecks (distance calculations, averaging, summing, normalising). Python here is just an interface, telling the underlying Rust code what to do, and the GIL is released while Rust works.

But if the data is not in memory, will this not be slow? Well, no. We store data in structures like this. One for cells:

/// CsrCellChunk
///
/// This structure is designed to store the data of a single cell in a
/// CSR-like format optimised for rapid access on disk.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct CsrCellChunk {
    pub data_raw: RawCounts,
    pub data_norm: Vec<F16>,
    pub library_size: usize,
    pub indices: Vec<u32>,
    pub original_index: usize,
    pub to_keep: bool,
}

One for genes (if you are even vaguely familiar with compressed sparse formats, you have probably already clocked that this is essentially CSR and CSC storage with two data layers):

/// CscGeneChunk
///
/// This structure is designed to store the data of a single gene in a
/// CSC-like format optimised for rapid access on disk.
#[derive(Encode, Decode, Serialize, Deserialize, Debug)]
pub struct CscGeneChunk {
    pub data_raw: RawCounts,
    pub data_norm: Vec<F16>,
    pub avg_exp: F16,
    pub nnz: usize,
    pub indices: Vec<u32>,
    pub original_index: usize,
    pub to_keep: bool,
}

But you are duplicating the data! Yep, indeed. But this allows extremely efficient retrieval. Want to run DGE between two groups? Only those cells are loaded via CsrCellChunks. Want to iterate over genes to identify HVGs? That goes through CscGeneChunk. A further advantage is that for quite a few analyses, we can load subsets and stream over the data rather than reading everything at once, which massively reduces the memory footprint. The core philosophy is:

Disk space is cheap; memory ain't

The two-layer approach (heavily inspired by TileDB) means raw and normalised counts share one set of indices instead of each dragging their own. Every cell and every gene is its own independently compressed chunk, the file tail holds the offsets, and reads go through mmap. This assumes decent SSD speeds, but most modern hardware has that covered.

Here is what that looks like on disk for PBMC3k. One directory, two binary stores (cell-major and gene-major) and a DuckDB with obs and var:

docs.title: How does this compare to AnnData ... ?¶
docs.text:
If you come from scanpy, the mental model shifts quite a bit. An AnnData holds X (dense or scipy sparse), any layers, and obs and var as pandas DataFrames in memory; everything you compute lands in obsm, obsp, uns and friends on the same object. Backed mode (backed="r") leaves X in the h5ad file and reads it on access, but obs and var still sit in memory, and X stays in the one orientation it was written in.

bixverse flips that around. The counts stay on disk, twice, once per orientation, and only ever get streamed through Rust. obs and var live in the DuckDB; ask for them and you get a polars frame back, only the columns you asked for if you like. What sits in Python memory is the light stuff: the kept-cell indices, the HVG selection and the cache of results (PCA, kNN, embeddings). Counts only reach Python when you ask for them.

docs.title: The v4 file format¶
docs.text:
Cheap disk space is no excuse to waste it though. The first versions of the format were lazy: absolute u32 indices, u16 raw counts, the full f16 normalised layer, all thrown at lz4. lz4 is fast, but it cannot do much with a sorted list of absolute indices. Version 4 (the default for everything the package writes now) looks at what a chunk actually holds:

  • Indices are delta bit-packed in blocks of 128. Sorted gene (or cell) indices turn into small gaps, and each block is packed to the width of its largest gap.
  • Raw counts are bit-packed the same way, stored as count - 1 since a stored entry is never zero. That saves another bit per value, and in UMI data that bit matters.
  • The normalised layer is dropped. Library-size normalisation plus log1p is a pure function of the raw count, the library size and the target size, so we recompute it on read, bit for bit identical to what used to be stored. A chunk where the recompute does not reproduce the stored values keeps them verbatim, so nothing changes under your feet. Gene chunks need the library size of each cell for this, so the gene file carries a per-cell library-size table in its tail, plus a small lookup table for counts 1 to 4, which covers the common low counts without a single ln_1p call.
  • A fixed 32 byte header sits uncompressed in front of every chunk: nnz, library size (or average expression for genes), original index, flags and the codec. Things like library sizes can be read without decompressing anything.
  • The codec is per chunk: lz4 by default, zstd if you want smaller files and can live with slower decoding, or none. A chunk that does not shrink is stored raw whatever you asked for.

So in practice we store raw counts and only raw counts, wherever possible, and the normalised layer is computed on the fly. Reads also prefetch their byte range into the page cache, so cold reads do not crawl through one page fault at a time.

You can check the recompute yourself: log1p(count / library size x target size), rounded to f16, is exactly the norm layer the reader hands back.

docs.title: Let's not round trip into interpreted languages¶
docs.text:
Continuing from step 4, we avoid round trips to Python entirely. The core philosophy is to take a hard look at the algorithms and methods used and, where needed, implement a highly specialised version for single cell. Some examples:

  • Custom implementation of various kNN searches, all running in Rust: ann-search-rs. No on-disk index round trips, SIMD-accelerated distance calculations, optimised memory layouts, aggressive optimisations with single cell in mind. Since kNN graphs underlie a lot of downstream methods, speeding this up has a wide impact. The kNN vignette has the options.

  • PCA underlies a lot of algorithms, is a key dimensionality reduction step, and, perhaps embarrassingly, still beats fancy foundation models. A few tricks make it fast:

    • Lanczos on the sparse matrix. We only want the top 30 to 50 components, so there is no point in decomposing the whole thing. Lanczos runs on the n HVG x n HVG Gram matrix without ever building it: all it needs are sparse matrix-vector products, which is exactly what CSR and CSC storage is good at. It is thick-restarted, so the trailing components converge too, even on the flat spectrum single cell data likes to produce. And it is exact, not an approximation. This is the default now. Randomised SVD is still there if you want it, but it is approximate and the trailing components suffer the most. On the dense path, the default eigendecomposes the n HVG x n HVG cross-product instead.
    • Smart scaling without ever densifying the matrix. As shown in the numbers above, densifying with 2k HVGs means holding an 8 GB (float32) matrix in memory for a million cells, 40 GB for five million. Centring and scaling get folded into the matrix-vector products, so you never have to densify at all.

  • Of course there is also a library for everyone's favourite 2D embedding generation: manifolds-rs, behind the embed extra. Same philosophy: parallelise what can be parallelised, use CPU-friendly memory layouts, avoid round trips to the interpreter. Million-cell UMAP? Done in minutes on a laptop. Even good old tSNE, infamous for being slow, has two different FFT-accelerated versions (see Linderman, et al. for the OG variant). The "quick and dirty" Barnes-Hut approximation is provided too.

  • SCENIC infers gene regulatory networks by asking, for each target gene: which transcription factors best predict its expression? It does this by training a tree ensemble per gene, using the importance scores from those trees as a proxy for regulatory influence. The trees themselves are then thrown away. Only the importance scores matter. That means we can optimise purely for speed, without caring about prediction quality at all. A few tricks compound here:

    • Rather than training one ensemble per gene independently, we share the same tree structure across a batch of genes simultaneously: the splits are chosen to reduce prediction error across all targets in the batch at once, and each gene contributes its own importance scores as a side effect. This amortises most of the cost.
    • Transcription factor expression data is quantised down to 256 bins (one byte per cell), which makes histogram construction and split evaluation very fast and cache-friendly.
    • Single cell data is sparse, most genes are zero in most cells, so rather than densifying the target matrix (which would be enormous), we exploit that sparsity directly during tree building.

    The net result is GRN inference that runs in Rust end-to-end, with no data leaving low-level code until results are ready.

These are just some examples where purpose-built code can deliver massive gains in both memory usage and speed. This allows the package to run multi-million cell analyses (the GRNs will still be slow and take hours despite my best efforts, sorry) on a decent local laptop. I have churned through 3 million cell data sets on my loyal M1 Max MacBook Pro with 64 GB, doing the reading from h5ad, mt percentage detection, some cell filtering, HVG detection, PCA, kNN/sNN graph generation + clustering in <30 minutes. Something that would be completely impossible with several of the other data-held-in-memory libraries and approaches.

docs.title: There is no free lunch¶
docs.text:
While this all sounds great, one significant caveat is that using this package forces you to think differently about your data. Because data is NOT in memory, we need to carefully synchronise state between:

  • The binary files Rust writes to disk with specific indexing for cells and genes. At least Python and Rust agree on 0-indexing, which is one headache the R side has and you do not.

  • What is stored in DuckDB as metadata. This can get tricky once you start selecting subgroups of cells. In a standard workflow you might:

    1. Filter a first wave of cells/spots based on library size and number of features.
    2. Run doublet detection to remove doublets.
    3. Recheck library sizes, feature counts, transcriptional complexity, mitochondrial counts, and only then finalise your cell selection with sc.set_cells_to_keep().

    Any subsequent analysis (HVG detection, PCA, kNN construction, etc.) will operate on whatever is set here. This used to be THE footgun of the package. Move the cell set, forget to re-run the kNN, and you had a PCA over one set of cells sitting next to a kNN over another. Nothing complained. It either crashed deep in Rust or, much worse, quietly handed you mis-aligned biology.

  • The "ecosystem" (quotation marks because at the moment it is just the R package, this Python package and several Rust crates) is in its infancypuberty. Stuff will bug, break, breaking changes have been and will likely continue to be introduced. If you want to contribute at the methods level, you will need to go low-level and learn Rust (or ask your favourite LLM. But please no obvious AI slop.) The Rust code powering all of this is here.

This is a side/hobby project, mostly a labour of love. I do hope other people find it useful and at least rethink some of their assumptions.

docs.title: The cache checks¶
docs.text:
So the cell set footgun now complains. Every artefact that lands in the cache, the PCA, the embeddings, the kNN, the neighbour graph, the MAGIC layer, carries a provenance stamp: a hash of the cell set it was computed on, plus the ids of whatever it was derived from. The kNN records the PCA it was built on and the graph records the kNN, which is the bit that matters. Re-run the PCA on the same cells with fewer components and the kNN hanging off it is now stale, even though its own cell count never moved. A row-count check waves that straight through.

Here it is on PBMC3k. HVGs, a 30 component PCA and the neighbours, then cache_status():

docs.title: Future directions¶
docs.text:
A fair amount of the original roadmap has landed since this was first written. Trajectory inference is in (Palantir from Setty, et al., PAGA and gene trends along pseudotime), so is a decent spread of batch correction (Harmony, Harmony v2, fastMNN, BBKNN, Seurat CCA and rPCA, with kBET, ASW and LISI to score whether any of it worked), differential expression and abundance (Wilcoxon markers, pseudobulk into limma-voom and edgeR quasi-likelihood, NEBULA, Milo, MELD), the full SCENIC stack with cisTarget, meta cells via SEACells and SuperCell, DIALOGUE, Hotspot, VISION, NMF, multi-modal CITE-seq with WNN graphs, and Symphony reference mapping. The plots live in bv.pl, behind the plots extra.

What is still ahead:

  • More methods: the approach has always been to implement what I needed or found interesting, and that will not change. Slingshot never got done and is still on the list.

  • Spatial transcriptomics: Spatial data does not (yet) reach the scale of the largest single cell data sets most of the time. However, if you are analysing many Visium or similar data sets, it can become quite heavy, and a lot of current frameworks are built on top of single cell ones anyway. There are also some interesting methods that use the spatial grid information directly, which I find genuinely exciting. None of it exists yet though, and to be clear about what does: the graph autocorrelation in VISION and Hotspot runs over the kNN graph, not over tissue coordinates. There are some prototype branches the keen observer might have seen already. Watch the space.

  • GPU acceleration: GPUs are becoming increasingly accessible, and if you have the budget for data-centre-scale GPUs, please do use them. Nvidia knows what they are doing and cuBLAS is insanely fast, in ways that simply cannot be matched on CPUs. However, most people do not have several B200s lying around at home. So the GPU work goes through cubecl on the wgpu backend, which means Metal on macOS, Vulkan on Linux and DX12 on Windows off one set of kernels rather than a CUDA-only path. (A native CUDA backend is aspirational. I do not own an Nvidia GPU to test it on.) In Python it lives in the bixverse_gpu companion package, and there is a fair amount of it now: block Lanczos (or randomised SVD) for the PCA, Harmony v2 with the arrowhead inversion, kNN across exhaustive, IVF and NNDescent-into-CAGRA, k-means coarsened fast clustering, the UMAP Adam optimiser, SEACells (both Frank-Wolfe solves), Scrublet, the NMF HALS family, BBKNN and fastMNN with GPU-accelerated kNN searches, SCENIC's ExtraTrees and RandomForest learners, and Pearson/Spearman correlation.

  • Deep learning integration: this is the reason the Python package exists at all. It opens the same binary files and streams shuffled minibatches out of them through bv.CellLoader, raw, normalised or both, sparse by default. Decoding never leaves Rust and the GIL is released while it happens, so the loader keeps a GPU training loop fed without ever materialising the experiment in memory. The first consumer is a barebone scVI in bixverse.nn on torch, MLX or JAX, with the scvi-tools 1.5.1 defaults: load a trained scvi-tools module into it and you get the same loss back. On two PBMC batches (5k cells, M1 Max), the MLX version trains in about 30 seconds against just under three minutes for scvi-tools on MPS, at the same held-out ELBO. Toy-sized, sure, and the million-cell runs are still to come. Watch this space.

A programme is only interesting if it holds up across every pair, so the number to look at is the worst p in each programme, which is what the repr reports. The empirical p is a one-sided rank sum test of the observed fit against the n_permutations - 1 permuted ones, so it has a floor: about 0.045 at n_permutations=100, which mcp_00 hits in every pair. Do not read too much into the exact values; raise it for anything you intend to believe.

refit_fidelity says how well each cell type's score survived stage three, i.e. how much of the programme is really carried by the genes that passed the mixed model.

def collect_scores(res: bv.dialogue.DialogueResult) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """All cell types' scores in one long frame with the obs columns."""
    return pl.concat(
        [s.with_columns(pl.lit(ct).alias("cell_type")) for ct, s in res.scores.items()]
    ).join(obs_cols, on="cell_id")


def per_sample_test(scores: pl.DataFrame, mcp: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Donor means of one programme, Wilcoxon rank sum test per cell type."""
    per_sample = scores.group_by("sample", "cell_type", "pathology").agg(
        pl.col(mcp).mean()
    )
    rows = []
    for ct in cell_types:
        d = per_sample.filter(pl.col("cell_type") == ct)
        groups = d.partition_by("pathology", as_dict=True)
        x, y = (g[mcp].to_numpy() for g in groups.values())
        rows.append({"cell_type": ct, "p": mannwhitneyu(x, y).pvalue})
    return pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(pl.col("p").round_sig_figs(3))

def quality_cor(scores: pl.DataFrame, mcp: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Spearman correlation of one programme with the quality covariates per
    cell type."""
    return (
        scores.group_by("cell_type")
        .agg(
            pl.corr(mcp, cov, method="spearman").round(3).alias(f"rho_{cov}")
            for cov in ("lib_size", "cell_q")
        )
        .sort("cell_type")
    )

That is not a small correlation. mcp_00 is tracking library size at |rho| ~ 0.5 in every cell type (the sign of a programme is arbitrary), while cell_q barely moves with it. And library size itself differs between the UC and healthy donors on this subset. One oddity of this file: library size is the total of the rounded TPM/10 values, so it only varies by a few percent and is not sequencing depth in the usual sense. It is still a technical axis.
