docs.title: Batch correction with bixverse¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Batch correction with bixverse. Original authors: Grant Neilson, Gregor Lueg and Liesbeth François.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
Batch effects are systematic technical differences between experimental runs that can obscure genuine biological signal in single cell data. When datasets from multiple experiments, technologies, or laboratories are combined, cells tend to group by their source rather than by cell type. Batch correction methods aim to remove these technical artefacts whilst preserving biological variation.

bixverse provides four batch correction approaches, each with different trade-offs:

  • fastMNN (Haghverdi, et al., 2018) identifies mutual nearest neighbours across batches: pairs of cells from different batches that are each other's closest match. Correction vectors are computed from these pairs and applied to align the embeddings. It is particularly effective when cell type composition differs across batches.
  • Harmony (Korsunsky, et al., 2019) operates on PCA embeddings using iterative soft clustering with diversity penalties. It assigns cells to clusters, estimates batch effects per cluster via ridge regression, and corrects the embedding. It tends to be fast and works well across a range of scenarios. A version 2 has been released too, see Patikas, et al., 2026, with improvements that increase scalability to larger data sets and modifications to the objective functions to not overcorrect across batches when different cell types are there.
  • BBKNN (Polanski, et al., 2020) takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than correcting an embedding, it constructs a batch-balanced k-nearest neighbour graph by building separate neighbour indices per batch. The corrected graph can then be used directly for clustering and visualisation.
  • Seurat anchors (Stuart, et al., 2019) find pairs of cells that are mutual nearest neighbours in a space shared by two batches, score them by how much of their neighbourhood they share, and use them to pull one batch onto the other. Two flavours are available. CCA builds the shared space from canonical correlations and corrects hardest, which suits batches that don't share their cell types. rPCA projects each batch into the other's PCA basis instead: cheaper, gentler, and the better default when the batches broadly match. Both need batch-aware HVGs.

A correction has two jobs: mix the batches and keep the biology intact. Going too hard on the first ruins the second, so bixverse scores both, following the scIB benchmark (Luecken, et al., 2022).

Batch mixing:

  • kBET: tests whether neighbourhood batch proportions match the global ones.
  • Batch ASW: silhouette width on batch labels in the embedding.
  • iLISI: effective number of batches per neighbourhood. Works on any kNN graph.
  • PCR: how much of the embedding variance batch explains, before versus after correction.

Bio conservation, which needs cell type labels:

  • cLISI: effective number of cell types per neighbourhood. You want one.
  • Cell type ASW: silhouette width on cell type labels.
  • Graph connectivity: whether each cell type stays one connected piece of the kNN graph.

bv.integrate.calculate_integration_metrics() runs the lot and returns one row, every column rescaled so that higher is better.

docs.title: Loading the batches¶
docs.text: We use two PBMC datasets (pbmc3k and pbmc4k) as a standard benchmark for batch correction. These come from the same tissue but differ in sequencing depth and cell counts, introducing a clear batch effect.

docs.title: Quality control¶
docs.text: Before batch correction, we filter out low-quality cells using mitochondrial gene proportions and library complexity metrics. In a multi file import the additional var columns are dropped, so the gene symbols come from one of the h5ad files.

docs.title: Pre-processing¶
docs.text: Standard pre-processing: HVG selection, PCA, and neighbour computation.

docs.title: Cell type labels¶
docs.text:
The bio conservation metrics need cell types. We cluster the uncorrected data and annotate the clusters with scType (Ianevski, et al., 2022) on a handful of canonical PBMC markers, same as in the PBMC vignette. The labels are deliberately coarse: T cells stay lumped, since splitting CD4 from CD8 on uncorrected data is asking for trouble.

One caveat: the labels come from uncorrected data, so they carry whatever the batch effect did to the clusters. Good enough to spot a method that smears cell types together, not a ground truth.

docs.title: Comparing the different methods¶
docs.text: Let's check out the different methods and how they behave.

docs.title: Uncorrected data¶
docs.text: Before applying any correction, we can visualise the batch effect and compute baseline metrics. All t-SNEs here use the quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut optimiser.

docs.title: fastMNN¶
docs.text: fastMNN works on batch-aware HVGs and produces a corrected embedding. It identifies mutual nearest neighbours across batches to compute correction vectors. For it to work best, we need the batch-aware HVGs. We calculate these, provide them to fastMNN (which regenerates the PCA embedding based on the batch-aware HVGs) and then run the actual algorithm.

docs.title: Harmony¶
docs.text: Harmony operates on the PCA embedding directly. Leave k as None and the number of clusters is set to one per 30 cells, capped at 100. Both versions are supported and share one numerical core in Rust. They differ in the diversity penalty, the ridge regression and how the ridge penalty gets set. The intercept is never penalised in either. bv.integrate.harmony() runs v2; the original is bv.integrate.harmony_v1(). Let's start with the original:

docs.title: Version 2¶
docs.text:
Patikas, et al., 2026 changed four things compared to v1. The last three have knobs in bv.params.HarmonyV2Params:

  • Stabilised diversity penalty, which makes the objective scale-invariant.
  • Batch pruning in the ridge regression. A batch that puts less than batch_proportion_cutoff of its cells into a cluster is dropped from that cluster's regression. A cluster left with a single batch isn't corrected, so a cell type unique to one batch doesn't get pulled towards the others.
  • Dynamic lambda. With use_dynamic_lambda=True (the default) the ridge penalty is set per cluster as alpha times the expected counts and the fixed lambda_ is ignored.
  • Theta scaling by batch size via tau. Off by default (tau=0).

The paper's arrowhead matrix inversion for a single batch covariate is used by both versions here, so v1 gets that speed-up too. v2 also runs only 4 k-means iterations per Harmony round versus 20 in v1. Unless you need to reproduce an old v1 result, go with v2, which is why it is the default.

docs.title: Seurat CCA¶
docs.text:
Seurat's anchor methods take a different route. For each pair of batches they find cells that are mutual nearest neighbours in a shared space, treat those pairs as anchors, score them by how much of their neighbourhood they share, and then apply a kernel-weighted correction that pulls the query batch onto the reference. Batches get merged in the order of their pairwise anchor counts.

For CCA the shared space is a canonical correlation embedding computed per batch pair. Anchors also get filtered in gene space before scoring, which is CCA-only in Seurat.

A few things differ from Seurat's reference implementation:

  • The per-gene ScaleData step is skipped. We work directly from per-cell standardised log-normalised HVG expression.
  • M = X1^T @ X2 is never materialised. The canonical correlations come from a matrix-free randomised SVD, so memory stays at O((n1 + n2) * num_cc) rather than n1 x n2. On big batch pairs that is the difference between running and not running.
  • The correction is applied to the embedding (dims x cells), not to full log-expression.
  • The effective CC rank is max(num_cc, dims), not num_cc.

Anchor structure comes out close to identical. Like fastMNN, CCA wants batch-aware HVGs, so we reuse the ones computed above.

docs.title: Seurat rPCA¶
docs.text:
rPCA runs the same anchor pipeline on a cheaper shared space. Instead of computing canonical correlations, each batch keeps its own PCA basis and the other batch's expression is projected into it. Cross-batch neighbour queries then happen in these projected bases.

The trade-off is the usual one: rPCA is faster and corrects less aggressively, which makes it the safer choice when your batches share most of their cell types. CCA is the one to reach for when they don't. As in Seurat, no gene-space anchor filter runs here, that step is CCA-only.

docs.title: BBKNN¶
docs.text:
BBKNN doesn't touch the embedding. It builds a batch-balanced neighbour graph instead: neighbours_within_batch nearest neighbours from every batch, turned into UMAP-style connectivities. Here that's 10 per batch, so 20 neighbours per cell feed the connectivities. no_neighbours_to_keep only cuts the stored kNN, and the cut stays balanced: each batch keeps its nearest ceil(15 / 2) = 8, so a cell ends up with 8 from one batch and 7 from the other.

That makes BBKNN awkward to score. kBET and iLISI read the stored kNN, which is balanced by construction, so they come out near perfect whatever the data looks like. That's the method grading its own homework, not a sign of mixing. ASW and PCR need an embedding, and BBKNN doesn't have one, so we pass embd_to_use=None and those come back null. cLISI and graph connectivity are still fair, since they only look at cell types.

docs.title: Scaling to millions of cells with bixverse
Scaling to millions of cells with bixverse¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Scaling to millions of cells with bixverse. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
This vignette demonstrates how to run a single cell analysis on a data set containing nearly 1 million cells on a local machine... In this case, a MacBook Air with 24 GBs (if you think "IMPOSSIBLE!", you would not be wrong coming from other languages/frameworks). If you have not read the design choices and the introductory vignette, please do so first. The PBMC3k walkthrough covers every step in detail on a small data set; here we focus on what changes when the cell count moves from thousands to a million.

The data used here is the 1 million cell PBMC data set from Parse Biosciences, a commonly used reference for showing large single cell analyses, see the original article here. The important bit here is that this was run successfully on a MacBook Air with 24 GB (M3). And please contrast that with the following line for the analysis of this data:

To avoid computer crashes and program failures, we recommend you execute the Python code on a cloud computing platform. The instance you select on the cloud platform to run this analysis should consist of at least 8 threads and 160 GB of RAM. (Parse Biosciences)

Note: None of the code blocks below are executed. This vignette is a reference for how one would run such an analysis, not a live rendering: the data set is far too large for CI/CD runners and GitHub would not be happy. The timings quoted were measured through the R package on the MacBook Air. R and Python call the same Rust core for every step here, but the Python timings have not been measured.

If you want to reproduce this, download the data from Parse Biosciences (or any other fat data set you have) and go have fun.

wget "https://cdn.parsebiosciences.com/1M_PBMC_T1D_Parse.zip"

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

import bixverse as bv
import bixverse.embed
from bixverse.params import MtxIoParams, NeighboursParams

# GPU acceleration (experimental), the `gpu` extra
import bixverse_gpu as bvg
from bixverse_gpu.params import KnnGpuDefaults, ScrubletGpuParams

docs.title: Loading the data¶
docs.text:
Once you have unzipped the data, we can start streaming it into memory and writing the files to disk.

data_path = Path("~/Desktop/parse_pbmc_1m/").expanduser()

load_params = MtxIoParams(
    path_mtx=str(data_path / "DGE_1M_PBMC.mtx"),
    path_obs=str(data_path / "cell_metadata_1M_PBMC.csv"),
    path_var=str(data_path / "all_genes_1M_PBMC.csv"),
    cells_as_rows=True,
    has_hdr=True,
)

# We will write everything into a temporary directory
tempdir_big = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
exp_dir = Path(tempdir_big.name) / "parse_pbmc_1m"

# We cap the cell-to-gene conversion at 8 GB here. It will run for a bit
# longer, but ensures your memory never blows up
sc = bv.io.load_mtx(exp_dir, load_params, csc_mem_gb=8.0, verbose=True)

This step is one of the slowest... A lot of things are happening here.

  • The MTX (plain or gzipped) is parsed once. The entries spill into per-cell buckets on disk while the per-gene cell counts accumulate.
  • Genes expressed in fewer than min_cells cells are dropped, and the cell QC (minimum library size, minimum features) is corrected for the dropped genes afterwards.
  • The kept cells are written to the CSR-type file with the genes already re-indexed; the normalisation is done on the fly. The spill files are cleaned up at the end.
  • Lastly, the cell data are read back in chunks and transposed to the CSC style file for quick gene retrieval, with the buffers capped at csc_mem_gb.

This approach avoids loading the whole data into memory at any point. The DuckDB also gets populated with the obs (based on what has been filtered) and the var. Reading from an h5ad instead? bv.io.stream_h5ad() is the streaming twin of bv.io.load_h5ad() and takes the same csc_mem_gb.

Streaming the data in and processing it is what takes the most time. If you have already loaded the data and it exists on disk from a previous session, skip the streaming step entirely and reconnect. On a MacBook Air with 24 GB and an M3 chip, the load takes 90 seconds.

# the folder is hopefully not temp...
sc = bv.io.load_existing(exp_dir)

docs.title: Doublet detection¶
docs.text:
Before any QC on library sizes and gene set proportions, we run Scrublet to flag doublets. Doublets are called per sample via the group_by argument, which is what you want when sample-level differences in capture rates would otherwise distort a single global score. Results are merged back onto obs and the doublets are dropped from the set of cells to keep. The runs over the individual samples happen sequentially to not overwhelm memory, and each run is massively parallelised internally in Rust.

scrublet_res = bv.doublets.scrublet(sc, group_by="sample", verbose=True)

sc.add_obs(bv.doublets.get_data(scrublet_res))

cells_without_doublets = (
    sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "doublet"], filtered=True)
    .filter(~pl.col("doublet"))["cell_idx"]
    .to_numpy()
)

sc.set_cells_to_keep(cells_without_doublets)

Due to having run over 24 samples in this case, this will take ~6 minutes. Ideal moment for a podcast, video of your favourite YouTuber and/or coffee, whichever floats your boat. Once you have passed this, things get substantially faster.

docs.title: Scrublet on the GPU¶
docs.text:
Got a GPU? bixverse_gpu.doublets.scrublet() is a drop-in for bv.doublets.scrublet(). Three stages move to the device: the randomised sparse SVD, the projection of the simulated doublets into that PC space, and the kNN over the combined embedding. That embedding is (1 + sim_doublet_ratio) * n_cells rows tall, so the kNN is the stage that gets painful on the CPU as samples grow. HVG selection, the doublet simulation and the Otsu threshold stay on the CPU. group_by works the same way and the result is the same ScrubletRes, so everything downstream is unchanged.

scrublet_res = bvg.doublets.scrublet(
    sc,
    group_by="sample",
    # ivf squeezes more speed out on the GPU compared to exhaustive
    scrublet_params=ScrubletGpuParams(knn=KnnGpuDefaults(knn_method="ivf")),
    verbose=True,
)

sc.add_obs(bv.doublets.get_data(scrublet_res))

Pick one of the two. Scores correlate (~0.99 on the demuxlet PBMCs) but do not match bit for bit: the randomised SVD draws a different sketch and the GPU index breaks neighbour ties differently, so a handful of borderline calls can flip. On the MacBook Air this does not accelerate the method massively. More towards 5 minutes.

docs.title: Gene set proportions¶
docs.text:
The same gene set proportion logic from the PBMC3k vignette applies. The functions automatically recognise if you have more than 100k cells and use the streaming engine by default in this case. You have manual control via streaming=None. If you have a fat memory machine, you can set this to False despite a large data set.

var = sc.var()

gs_of_interest = {
    "MT": var.filter(pl.col("gene_name").str.contains("^MT-"))["gene_id"].to_list(),
    "Ribo": var.filter(pl.col("gene_name").str.contains("^RP[SL]"))[
        "gene_id"
    ].to_list(),
}

bv.qc.gene_set_proportions(sc, gs_of_interest, verbose=True)

This is where the streaming engine really comes into play. Done in under 10 seconds.

docs.title: MAD outlier detection¶
docs.text:
Outlier detection on library size, the number of detected genes and the mitochondrial proportion. We compute outliers per sample (groups=), which matters once batches have non-trivial differences in sequencing depth: a global threshold would otherwise penalise whole batches rather than individual cells within them.

qc_df = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "sample", "lib_size", "nnz", "MT"], filtered=True)

metrics = {
    "log10_lib_size": np.log10(qc_df["lib_size"].to_numpy()),
    "log10_nnz": np.log10(qc_df["nnz"].to_numpy()),
    "MT": qc_df["MT"].to_numpy(),
}

directions = {
    "log10_lib_size": "below",
    "log10_nnz": "below",
    "MT": "above",
}

qc = bv.qc.run_cell_qc(
    metrics,
    qc_df["cell_idx"].to_numpy(),
    directions=directions,
    threshold=3.0,
    groups=qc_df["sample"],
)

sc.add_obs(bv.qc.get_data(qc))

I cannot recommend trying to plot the metric distributions naively... matplotlib will not be happy at this cell count either.

docs.title: Filtering cells¶
docs.text: sc.set_cells_to_keep(qc.cell_idx[~qc.combined])

docs.title: Feature selection and PCA¶
docs.text:
HVG selection at this scale again streams (left as is, the auto-detection takes care of this and streams when more than 1e5 cells are detected; streaming=True forces it). There are two data passes to avoid materialising large data in memory: the first calculates means and standard deviations, and the second does the variance stabilisation. Again, the streaming keeps memory pressure low and the function runs in ~10 seconds on the mentioned MacBook Air.

bv.pp.find_hvg(sc, hvg_no=2000, verbose=True)

PCA is one of the points where GPU acceleration starts to noticeably matter (if you have some VRAM or unified memory to spare, it will make a difference). Both implementations share the same parameter interface, so swapping between them is a one-line change. The leading components should agree up to sign between the two, which is worth a quick visual check.

bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=32)

cpu_res = sc.cache.pca_factors.copy()
cpu_s = sc.cache.pca_singular_vals.copy()

This runs in ~8 seconds. Let's compare this against the GPU-accelerated version. Here the GEMMs of the randomised SVD, the ones before the thin SVD on the massively reduced matrix, run on the GPU. You pay for moving the data, but you should still see an acceleration compared to the CPU form.

bvg.pp.calculate_pca(sc, no_pcs=32, verbose=True)

gpu_res = sc.cache.pca_factors.copy()
gpu_s = sc.cache.pca_singular_vals.copy()

# sanity check on the leading component
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4))
ax.scatter(
    cpu_res[:, 0],
    gpu_res[:, 0],
    s=0.5,
    color=bv.pl.bx_colors("main", n=1)[0],
    rasterized=True,
)
ax.set_xlabel("PC1 (CPU)")
ax.set_ylabel("PC1 (GPU)")
plt.show()

On the test MacBook Air, this runs in 5 seconds. In practice you would pick one. The GPU path becomes the more attractive option as the cell count grows and the more powerful your GPU is; on this data set you can feel the difference (if VRAM permits). You might see some slight differences due to floating point differences between CPU and GPU.

docs.title: Nearest neighbours (GPU-accelerated)¶
docs.text:
The GPU wheel exposes GPU-accelerated nearest neighbour search via bixverse_gpu.graph.find_neighbours(), thanks to CubeCL and WGPU, as long as you can fit the data into VRAM. knn_method="nndescent" builds a CAGRA-style graph; "ivf" and "exhaustive" are also on offer. The GPU version takes ~10 seconds, the CPU version with NNDescent ~15 seconds.

bv.graph.find_neighbours(
    sc,
    embd_to_use="pca",
    neighbours_params=NeighboursParams(knn_method="nndescent"),
)

bvg.graph.find_neighbours(
    sc,
    embd_to_use="pca",
    knn_params=KnnGpuDefaults(knn_method="nndescent"),
    verbose=True,
)

docs.title: Batch effect quantification¶
docs.text:
A kBET score on the uncorrected neighbour graph gives a quantitative baseline to compare against once batch correction is applied...

kbet_prior = bv.integrate.calculate_kbet(sc, "sample")

print(
    f"kBET rejection rate: {kbet_prior.kbet_score:.3f} over "
    f"{kbet_prior.n_batches} batches"
)

docs.title: Plots¶
docs.text:
Or if you are a visual person, let's check UMAP and tSNE.

bv.embed.umap(sc, slot_name="umap_prior")

bv.embed.tsne(
    sc,
    slot_name="tsne_prior",
    # use FFT here! It will make a massive difference
    params=bv.embed.tsne_defaults().set_params(approx="fft", ann="nndescent"),
)

You might wonder why in the case of tSNE we regenerate the kNN graph. You do not have to (use_knn=True reuses the cached one), but the rule of thumb is k_neighbours = perplexity * 3.0. With the default perplexity of 10 we would need 30 neighbours, but we previously only returned 15. So, we just rerun this. Skip tSNE if you don't need it, but the (GPU-accelerated) FFT-accelerated version is substantially faster than you would expect from tSNE. Same for the GPU-accelerated Adam optimiser for UMAP. You can run them via:

bvg.embed.umap(sc, slot_name="umap_prior_gpu")

bvg.embed.tsne(sc, slot_name="tsne_prior_gpu")

ax = bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "umap_prior", "sample", discrete=True)
ax.set_title("No batch correction")
plt.show()

ax = bv.pl.embedding_plot(sc, "tsne_prior", "sample", discrete=True)
ax.set_title("No batch correction")
plt.show()

docs.title: Batch correction¶
docs.text:
Okay, there is clearly a big sample batch effect. Let's remove that one. Again you have two options here... Harmony (version 2, recommended) on the CPU or a GPU-accelerated version. The CPU version first (~4 seconds):

bv.integrate.harmony(sc, "sample")

If you have a GPU at hand, you can also just use the GPU version (also 4 seconds on the Air: the CPU path is already very optimised and the GPU is not particularly powerful). Again, you will observe some slight numerical differences... This is due to the GPU implementation, but the overall structure of the data is recovered in the same way. The result lands in the "harmony_gpu" embedding.

bvg.integrate.harmony(sc, "sample")

We overwrite the kNN graph with the now batch-corrected embedding:

bvg.graph.find_neighbours(
    sc,
    embd_to_use="harmony_gpu",  # or harmony if you just did the CPU version
    knn_params=KnnGpuDefaults(knn_method="nndescent"),
    verbose=True,
)

docs.title: Batch correction quantification¶
docs.text:
Requantify the kBET scores and see if we removed some of the batch effects...

kbet_post_gpu = bv.integrate.calculate_kbet(sc, "sample")

print(
    f"kBET rejection rate: {kbet_post_gpu.kbet_score:.3f} over "
    f"{kbet_post_gpu.n_batches} batches"
)

docs.title: Cell type annotations¶
docs.text:
This is a nice data set where the fast clustering makes a lot of sense... We use k-means to quantise the data to representative centroids, run the Louvain clustering on the centroids only and project the community membership back.

fast_cluster_res = bv.graph.fast_cluster(
    sc,
    embd_to_use="harmony_gpu",  # or harmony if you just did the CPU version
    return_kmeans=False,
    n_seeds=10,
    verbose=True,
)

sc.add_obs(fast_cluster_res.memberships)

sc.obs(filtered=True).head()

docs.title: Differential gene expression¶
docs.text:
meta_data = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "res_2"], filtered=True)

cells_grp_a = meta_data.filter(pl.col("res_2") == 1)["cell_idx"].to_numpy()
cells_grp_b = meta_data.filter(pl.col("res_2") == 2)["cell_idx"].to_numpy()

dge_results = bv.de.find_markers(sc, cells_grp_a, cells_grp_b)

dge_results.sort("fdr").head(25)

The data is again streamed from disk, which makes this very fast...

Training a model on the counts instead? bv.CellLoader streams shuffled minibatches straight out of the cell-major store, e.g. into torch, without ever holding the matrix in memory.

docs.title: Key differences from the small-data workflow¶
docs.text:
The API surface is intentionally identical to the PBMC3k walkthrough. The meaningful differences when working at the million-cell scale are:

  1. Streaming I/O. Use bv.io.load_mtx(..., csc_mem_gb=8.0) (or bv.io.stream_h5ad(), or the equivalent on whatever loader fits your input), and the streaming behaviour propagates through bv.qc.gene_set_proportions() and bv.pp.find_hvg(). This is what makes working with this data set on a laptop possible at all.
  2. On-disk persistence. bv.io.load_existing() lets you reconnect to a previously streamed data set without re-reading the source. (Works for any data.)
  3. Per-sample QC. With batches comes the need to compute outliers per sample rather than globally.
  4. Doublet detection per sample. Scrublet (or any other doublet detection) can be run with group_by, which matters once capture rates differ between batches.
  5. GPU-accelerated Scrublet, PCA, kNN and Harmony. bixverse_gpu provides GPU paths for Scrublet, PCA, nearest neighbour search and Harmony. The CPU versions remain highly optimised with SIMD and cache-aware memory layouts, but the GPU paths get faster as the data scales.

For context... The whole workflow here was run on a MacBook Air and did not cause any substantial memory pressure.

docs.title: Single-cell data I/O in bixverse¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Single-cell data I/O in bixverse. Original authors: Andrew Skelton and Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
bixverse keeps single-cell counts on disk, in compact Rust binaries for the count matrix and a DuckDB for the obs / var metadata, so that millions of cells can be analysed on a laptop. Ingestion happens once, up front, through format-specific readers that stream the data into that on-disk layout and apply the basic cell/gene QC and normalisations along the way.

This vignette walks through every reader on a small synthetic data set, so it runs end-to-end without any downloads. It covers:

  • in-memory CSR matrices plus polars tables (load_csr)
  • 10x CellRanger MTX, single and multi-sample (load_mtx, load_multi_mtx)
  • AnnData h5ad, single and multi-sample (load_h5ad, load_multi_h5ad)
  • 10x CellRanger HDF5, single and multi-sample (load_tenx_h5, load_multi_tenx_h5)
  • checkpointing to and from disk (save, load_existing)
  • archiving the counts for cold storage (archive_sc_exp)

If you have not seen the SingleCells class before, read the design choices vignette first.

docs.title: A small synthetic data set¶
docs.text: We generate a synthetic data set and treat its two halves as two "samples", so that the multi-sample readers can be demonstrated too. The counts are a cells x genes CSR matrix; obs and var are polars DataFrames.

docs.title: In-memory matrices¶
docs.text: The simplest entry point: hand the reader a cells x genes CSR matrix (a scipy csr_matrix, or anything else that carries data, indices, indptr and a shape) plus the obs and var tables directly.

docs.title: Single sample¶
docs.text:
We write one sample out in CellRanger flat-file form and point an explicit MtxIoParams at the trio (for real CellRanger output, the convenience helper bv.io.get_cell_ranger_params() auto-locates matrix.mtx / barcodes.tsv / genes.tsv).

Two MtxIoParams fields handle the common deviations from the strict CellRanger convention:

  • cells_as_rows: whether the .mtx has cells on the rows. The CellRanger default is False (genes are rows). Set to True for externally produced matrices that are transposed.
  • has_hdr: whether the barcodes/features flat files carry a header row. CellRanger itself writes headerless TSVs (has_hdr=False), but CSV/TSV exports from downstream pipelines often carry one. The example below uses has_hdr=True because write_cellranger_output() emits headers.

docs.title: Multiple samples¶
docs.text: prescan_mtx_dirs() takes one directory per sample, builds the shared gene universe across them, and load_multi_mtx() then stacks all cells into a single object with a global gene QC. The originating sample is recorded in the exp_id obs column.

docs.title: File layout variations¶
docs.text: To make the cells_as_rows and has_hdr knobs concrete, here is the same sample written with cells on the rows of the .mtx (i.e. transposed relative to CellRanger). The only thing that changes at load time is cells_as_rows=True:

docs.title: Single¶
docs.text: read_h5ad_metadata() lets you inspect the obs / var and dimensions without loading the counts; load_h5ad() ingests the matrix.

docs.title: Multiple¶
docs.text: prescan_h5ad_files() accepts a dict of paths (the keys become the sample identifiers); load_multi_h5ad() mirrors the multi-MTX workflow.

docs.title: Export¶
docs.text: save_h5ad() goes in the other direction: it writes a loaded object to .h5ad for reading with ScanPy. Only kept cells are written; assay picks raw or normalised counts for X, and any cached PCA, embeddings or sNN graph go to obsm/varm/obsp. The counts are streamed in cell batches, so the full matrix never sits in memory.

docs.title: Single sample¶
docs.text: write_tenx_h5_sc() expects the counts plus a barcode list and a features table (with at least id and name). load_tenx_h5() reads the gene-expression modality (V3 files may also carry e.g. Antibody Capture, which is filtered out via feature_type).

docs.title: Multiple samples¶
docs.text:
prescan_tenx_h5_files() takes a dict of .h5 paths (the keys become the sample identifiers), inspects each file for its CellRanger version (v2 vs v3), filters to the requested feature_type, and builds the global gene space. load_multi_tenx_h5() then mirrors the multi-MTX / multi-h5ad workflow.

gene_universe controls how the feature space is reconciled across files:

  • "intersection" keeps genes present in every input.
  • "union" keeps genes present in any input; cells from a file that lacks a given gene get zero counts for it.

Mixed v2 / v3 inputs in the same call are handled transparently, and non-gene modalities (e.g. Antibody Capture) are silently dropped when feature_type="Gene Expression".

docs.title: Checkpointing to disk¶
docs.text: Once an object is loaded, the in-memory mappings can be persisted so a fresh session can be restored without re-ingesting the counts. The on-disk binary and DuckDB already live in the store directory; save() adds the lightweight mapping cache.

docs.title: Archiving for cold storage¶
docs.text: Project done, but you want to keep the data around? The two count binaries eat disk. archive_sc_exp() compresses counts_cells.bin into a single zstd counts.bxa and, by default, deletes both binaries. The gene-based file is not archived at all, it's just a transpose of the cell-based one. Normalised values only go into the archive where they can't be recomputed from the raw counts. level (1 to 22) trades write time for size; decompression speed barely changes. Run save() first, the archive only covers the counts.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Format Single sample Multiple samples In-memory CSR bv.io.load_csr() 10x MTX bv.io.load_mtx() bv.io.prescan_mtx_dirs() + bv.io.load_multi_mtx() AnnData h5ad bv.io.load_h5ad() bv.io.prescan_h5ad_files() + bv.io.load_multi_h5ad() 10x HDF5 bv.io.load_tenx_h5() bv.io.prescan_tenx_h5_files() + bv.io.load_multi_tenx_h5()

Checkpoint with bv.io.save() and bv.io.load_existing(); archive with bv.io.archive_sc_exp(). Already loaded experiments can be stacked into a new one with bv.io.merge_sc_experiments(), and stores in the old v3 binary format are converted in place with bv.io.upgrade_sc_store(). There is no Seurat reader on the Python side.

All readers share the same MinQualityParams QC interface and write into the same on-disk SingleCells layout, so everything downstream (normalisation, HVGs, PCA, neighbours, clustering, ...) is identical regardless of how the data came in.

docs.title: Pearson residuals and scTransform¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Pearson residuals and scTransform. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
bixverse normalises once, at ingestion. Counts go in, `log1p(count / lib_size

  • target_size)` comes out, and both layers sit on disk from then on. Every downstream step reads that second layer. It's cheap, it streams, and it is why a million cells fit on a laptop.

It also has a known problem. Library-size normalisation followed by a log assumes the variance of a gene is roughly constant once you've divided the depth out. For UMI counts that isn't true. Highly expressed genes carry more variance than lowly expressed ones no matter what you divide by, so a variance-based HVG ranking partly ranks genes by how much they were expressed in the first place.

Pearson residuals fix this by asking a different question. Fit a null model of what a gene's counts should look like given only sequencing depth, then ask how far each cell deviates from it:

\[ r_{gc} = \frac{y_{gc} - \mu_{gc}}{\sqrt{\mu_{gc} + \mu_{gc}^2 / \theta_g}} \]

A gene that is nothing but depth gets residuals with variance near one. A gene with real structure gets more. As an HVG statistic that holds up well. As a PCA input it's more contested, and the caveats section goes through what the benchmarks actually say.

The catch is cost. Nothing about this is precomputable: a residual depends on the fitted model, so it has to be regenerated every time something wants it. Worse, a residual is non-zero even where the count is zero, so the matrix is dense by construction. That is exactly the trade-off the design vignette warns about, and it's why this is opt-in rather than the default.

bixverse gives you two flavours.

  • scTransform v2 (Choudhary and Satija, 2022) fits a negative binomial per gene by regression against log depth, then regularises the per-gene parameters against their expression level with a kernel smoother. Only a bounded subsample (2000 genes by 2000 cells by default) goes through the actual GLM fitting, so the expensive part doesn't scale with your data set. Everything after it streams.

  • Analytic Pearson residuals (Lause, Berens and Kobak, 2021) skip the fitting entirely. One shared dispersion for every gene, and \(\mu\) from the marginals: \(\mu_{gc} = \frac{\sum_c y_{gc} \cdot \sum_g y_{gc}}{\sum_{gc} y_{gc}}\). Closed form, no iterations, and their paper argues it ranks genes about as well as the fitted version does.

Analytic Pearson is the one to reach for first. It's a couple of orders of magnitude cheaper and you can always refit with scTransform if you need corrected counts or per-gene dispersions.

docs.title: Loading the data¶
docs.text: Two PBMC runs, so there's something to group over later.

docs.title: Fitting a model¶
docs.text: fit_residuals() fits and caches. It doesn't transform anything, and it doesn't touch the counts on disk. What lands on the object is the model, in sc.cache.residual_fit.

docs.title: Variable features¶
docs.text: find_hvg() gains a "residual" method. It ranks on the residual variance of the cached model instead of on the stored layer.

docs.title: PCA on residuals¶
docs.text: calculate_pca() takes residuals=True. Two settings have to change, and the function will tell you so rather than silently working around you:

docs.title: What it costs¶
docs.text:
The residual path has no sparse solver and no streaming solver. A residual column is dense even where the counts are not, because a zero count still has a residual of -mu / sqrt(var). So the PCA input is a real cells by genes dense matrix, and calculate_pca() warns once it gets past a few gigabytes.

Two knobs if that bites: fewer HVGs, or fewer cells. There's no third option, and sparse_svd=True errors rather than silently running the log-normalised algorithm instead.

docs.title: Multi-sample fits¶
docs.text:
Fitting one model across several samples folds their depth differences into the gene coefficients. group_column fits one model per group instead, which is what Seurat v5 does with split layers.

The fit lives on the experiment, so a second fit replaces the first. We keep going on the same object from here and refit each time.

docs.title: Covariates¶
docs.text: scTransform can take extra cell-level covariates into the design. Library size is never one of them: it enters as a fixed offset with the slope pinned, which is the change that separates v2 from v1.

docs.title: Corrected counts¶
docs.text: Residuals are a modelling device. They are not counts, they go negative, and nothing downstream that expects counts will take them. sct_corrected_counts() reverses the transform with every latent variable held at its median, which removes the depth structure while keeping the per-sample intercept.

docs.title: What the field actually thinks¶
docs.text: Residuals are not a settled win, and it would be dishonest to ship them here without saying so. Three findings are worth knowing before you build an analysis on them.

docs.title: The transform is not monotonic¶
docs.text:
This is the sharpest criticism, and it comes from Booeshaghi, Hallgrímsdóttir, Gálvez-Merchán and Pachter. A residual is a signed distance from a per-gene null, so two genes in the same cell can swap places relative to their raw counts. The transform reorders genes within a cell.

That matters more than it sounds. Marker inspection, heatmaps and anything that reads "gene A is higher than gene B in this cell" are answering a question about the transformed values, not about the counts. Their benchmark across 526 data sets found residual and scaling transformations showed exactly these within-cell rank changes, and that sctransform retained substantial depth correlation in many of them, which is awkward for a method whose stated job is removing depth.

Their proposal is PFlogPF, a shifted centred-log-ratio transform that keeps monotonicity. bixverse has it as PcaParams(clr=True) on the normal path, and it is a reasonable thing to try before reaching for residuals at all.

docs.title: The benchmarks are not one-sided¶
docs.text:
Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber compared delta-method, residual, latent-state and factor-analysis transformations in Nature Methods and found that the plain shifted logarithm followed by PCA performs as well or better than the sophisticated alternatives on simulated and real data. They did single out analytic Pearson residuals as well suited to picking variable genes and finding rare cell types, which is a narrower claim than "use residuals for everything".

That shape matches what's implemented here. Using residuals to choose genes and then running the normal pipeline is a defensible middle ground, and find_hvg(hvg_params=HvgParams(method="residual")) followed by an ordinary calculate_pca() does exactly that.

docs.title: scTransform v1 was overfitted¶
docs.text:
Lause, Berens and Kobak showed the original model is overspecified: per-gene overdispersion estimates come out strongly biased, which is why the method needs a post-hoc smoothing step to be usable at all. Their argument is that UMI data don't need gene-specific overdispersion in the first place.

v2 addresses a good chunk of this by pinning the depth coefficient rather than fitting it, and it is the version implemented here. The regularisation is still doing real work though, and bw_adjust in SctransformParams is the knob that controls how much.

docs.title: Scaling¶
docs.text:
The dense-matrix problem from "What it costs" above is the same one the Pachter paper raises: dense residual output is what makes million-cell analyses awkward, since the whole point of the on-disk sparse format is that you never materialise a matrix that size.

bixverse softens this but does not solve it. The fit and the variance sweep both stream gene by gene, so memory there is one row per worker rather than a genes-by-cells matrix, and the scTransform GLM only ever sees a bounded 2000 by 2000 subsample. Those parts scale fine. The residual PCA does not, because a dense SVD needs a dense input. At a million cells you can still fit a model and select genes on residuals; you cannot run the residual PCA, and calculate_pca() will warn you with the actual number before it tries.

docs.title: So what should you use¶
docs.text: Analytic Pearson for gene selection, then the normal log-normalised PCA, is the combination with the least to argue against it. Full residual PCA is worth trying when you suspect depth is driving your embedding, and worth checking against the default rather than trusting blindly. If you want marker-level interpretability, stay on the normalised layer or use PFlogPF.

docs.title: Where to go next¶
docs.text:
Meta cells take all of this too. Their counts are summed UMIs, so the negative binomial still applies, just at far greater depth. Prefer method="analytic_pearson" there and revisit the n_genes and n_cells defaults of SctransformParams, which are sized for raw cells and there are usually a lot more of those than there are meta cells.

Still on the list: residual-space projection of new cells onto existing components, which the Rust side can already do but has no Python entry point yet.

Everything else behaves like the parent object. The obs table is filtered to the group and held in memory, the var table is untouched, and the usual getters work.

prefix_values=True stamps the subset's group onto every value, so you get T cells_0 rather than a bare 0. Drop it if you want the raw labels. Leave cols out and everything the subset gained that the parent does not have yet gets merged, which after a pipeline run is exactly the new columns.

The join is a left join, so every cell that was not a T cell gets null. That is the behaviour you want, and the downstream methods respect it.

Results that already carry their own cell_idx skip the helper entirely. fast_cluster() returns memberships keyed in parent space, so add_obs() takes them directly.

Every lineage picked a different feature set, and the shared fraction with the global HVGs is nowhere near complete. Running one global PCA and hoping it resolves everything was never going to work.

Writing all of that back is one call. merge_subset_obs() takes the values of the dict straight from apply_pipeline_per_group(), checks that no cell shows up twice, and does a single join.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
Your first pass of clustering gives you lineages: T cells, B cells, monocytes. What it does not give you is the structure inside those lineages. The highly variable genes and the principal components were chosen to separate a monocyte from a B cell, and on that axis every T cell looks the same. If you crank up the Leiden resolution on the full object you mostly get the lineages chopped into arbitrary pieces, not naive versus memory CD4.

The fix is to throw the global feature selection away and redo it on the cells you actually care about. That is what SingleCellsSubset is for. It gives you a view onto a subset of a SingleCells object that shares the on-disk counts with the parent, but carries its own empty cache, so HVG, PCA, neighbours and clusters all get recomputed from scratch on the subset alone.

This vignette assumes you have read the design choices and the PBMC walkthrough. The standard chain is not re-explained here.

docs.title: A coarse first pass¶
docs.text: Same PBMC3k data set as the main walkthrough, run through QC, HVG, PCA, neighbours and Leiden without commentary.

docs.title: Taking a subset¶
docs.text: The constructor takes the parent, a column in obs, and the level you want.

docs.title: A note on indices¶
docs.text:
This is the one place where you can shoot yourself in the foot, so it is worth being explicit. In Python there is a single cell index space: the 0-based position in the parent's stores. cell_idx in the subset's obs, subset_to_original, cells_to_keep and every integer selection you hand to a getter live in it. Integer selections must belong to the subset, and cell ids are matched against the subset's cells only. The one exception is obs(indices=...), which takes row positions within the subset's own obs table.

cell_indices() maps ids to that space.

docs.title: Re-running the chain¶
docs.text: Same functions as on the parent. They take the subset just the same.

docs.title: Markers for the sub-clusters¶
docs.text: Differential expression on the subset is confined to it. Each sub-cluster is tested against the other T sub-clusters, not against every monocyte in the data set.

docs.title: Getting the labels back to the parent¶
docs.text: So far everything lives in the subset, in memory. To make the labels permanent, or to plot them on the parent's global UMAP, push them into the parent's DuckDB. merge_subset_obs() does the join on cell_idx for you.

docs.title: Pipelines¶
docs.text: Once you are doing this for more than one cell type, writing out HVG, PCA, neighbours and clusters by hand five times gets old. A Pipeline lets you declare the chain once. Steps chain with >>.

docs.title: One pipeline, every group¶
docs.text:
apply_pipeline_per_group() builds the subset for you and returns a dict keyed by group.

Sizing matters here. PCA with 20 components needs more than 20 cells, so a rare population that the annotation happened to call will fall over and take the whole run with it. Restrict the groups explicitly rather than hoping for the best. On this data set the coarse annotation returned five lineages. The cell below keeps groups with at least 100 cells, a safe margin over what the PCA needs, so the 24 DCs stay out.

docs.title: Source-pure meta cells¶
docs.text:
All three meta cell generators run on a subset, so you can aggregate per patient and never mix two donors into one meta cell. The catch used to be the last step: you ended up with one MetaCells object per patient and no way to run SCENIC or NMF across the lot. bv.metacells.merge_meta_cells() closes that.

step_metacells() puts the generation into the chain itself. It is the one step that changes the class of the object, so a pipeline that ends on it hands you MetaCells rather than SingleCellsSubset. Everything before it still runs per patient, which is the point when your samples are split over two plates and need correcting within a donor.

from bixverse.params import BtMetacellsParams
from bixverse.pipeline import step_harmony, step_metacells

mc_pipeline = (
    step_hvg(hvg_no=2000)
    >> step_pca(no_pcs=20)
    >> step_harmony(batch_column="plate")
    >> step_neighbours(embd_to_use="harmony")
    >> step_metacells(
        "bootstrapped", params=BtMetacellsParams(target_no_metacells=100)
    )
)

per_patient = apply_pipeline_per_group(mc_pipeline, sc, "patient_id")

meta_cells = bv.metacells.merge_meta_cells(per_patient)

A few things worth knowing:

  • bv.metacells.meta_cells_per_group() does the whole thing in one call if you do not need the per-patient objects. Same arguments, plus method and mc_params.
  • The merged obs table gains a source_id column and the meta cell ids are prefixed with it. original_cell_idx stays in the index space of its own source, so it is only meaningful alongside source_id.
  • Gene spaces are reconciled by "intersect" (the default) or "union", the latter zero-filling genes an input lacks. Both are no-ops when every input came from the same parent object.
  • Counts are carried over untouched. Normalisation is per meta cell, so row-binding leaves it valid.
  • PCA, kNN, sNN and HVG are dropped on merge. They were fitted per patient and mean nothing side by side. Recompute them on the merged object, which is the whole reason for merging.
  • validate_pipeline() checks a chain against a starting class before anything runs. apply_pipeline() and apply_pipeline_per_group() call it for you, so putting step_harmony() after step_metacells() errors immediately instead of after twenty minutes of PCA.

docs.title: Caveats and what is next¶
docs.text:
A few sharp edges to be aware of before you build on this.

Meta cell memberships come back as positions in the parent's stores, which is what makes them joinable back onto the original object. bv.de.get_pseudobulked() runs on subsets too if aggregation is all you are after.

Subsets are RNA only, so multi-modal work stays on SingleCellsMultiModal (see the multi-modal vignette).

Subsets nest conceptually but not in code: you cannot build a SingleCellsSubset from another SingleCellsSubset. If you want a third level, write the labels back to the parent and subset from there.

docs.title: A guide to single-cell plotting functions¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette A guide to single-cell plotting functions. Original author: Liesbeth François.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text: This vignette gives an overview of the different plotting functions that are available when running a single cell analysis. The plots live in bv.pl and need matplotlib (the plots extra); the extract_* functions next to them return the data behind each plot as a polars frame.

docs.title: Preparing the data¶
docs.text: We run the standard analysis using the same PBMC3k data set. For more details on the data analysis itself, please refer to the PBMC vignette. This vignette assumes familiarity with how the SingleCells class, on-disk storage and cells-to-keep logic work. To have something to group the QC by, every cell gets a random sample label.

docs.title: Joint QC plot¶
docs.text: joint_plot() compares the number of features and number of counts per cell, similar to sns.jointplot.

docs.title: Violin QC plots¶
docs.text: violin_plot() shows the distribution of each QC metric as a violin, split by sample (or any grouping variable stored in the qc object).

docs.title: Density QC plots¶
docs.text: density_plot() overlays smoothed density distributions for each group, which highlights bimodal distributions or outlier populations that violins can obscure.

docs.title: Dimensionality reduction plots¶
docs.text: After PCA, neighbour-finding, clustering and UMAP, cells can be visualised on any 2D embedding stored in the object. The scType annotation from the PBMC vignette gives us cell types to colour by.

docs.title: Other 2D embeddings¶
docs.text: UMAP is not the only game in town. All the 2D embeddings come from manifolds-rs and land in the same object, so embedding_plot() works on every one of them.

docs.title: Density-preserving embeddings¶
docs.text:
UMAP and t-SNE throw away local density. A tight, homogeneous population and a diffuse, heterogeneous one come out at roughly the same size, so reading anything into the area a cluster takes up on the plot is a mistake. densMAP and den-SNE fix this with an extra term in the loss that keeps the local radius of each cell in the embedding correlated with its radius in PCA space. Big blob now means lots of variation, small tight blob means not much. lambda_ on bv.embed.densmap_defaults() and bv.embed.densne_defaults() sets how hard that term pulls; lambda_=0 gives you plain UMAP and t-SNE back.

The t-SNE flavours come with four optimisers via approx: "barnes_hut" (classic Barnes-Hut), "qd" (the quick-and-dirty Barnes-Hut of qdtsne, tree depth capped via max_depth on the optimiser parameters, coarser by design), "fft" (FIt-SNE style interpolation) and "fft_3k" (its three-kernel variant). Here we use "fft_3k". The estimators are sklearn style, so set_params swaps the optimiser on the defaults.

docs.title: ForceAtlas2¶
docs.text:
ForceAtlas2 is a force-directed layout of the neighbour graph: edges pull, every pair of cells pushes, gravity keeps the lot together. It is what scanpy's draw_graph() does, and a common pick for data with continuous transitions (think differentiation). bv.embed.forceatlas2() lays out the kNN graph the same way scanpy does.

Not ported to Python yet: the layout of the neighbour graph the Leiden clustering ran on (R's graph = "connectivities"), the manifolds-rs wheel cannot lay out a given graph.

docs.title: Per-gene expression plots¶
docs.text: feature_plot() projects normalised expression of one or more genes onto the embedding. Here MS4A1: the high-expressing cells sit in the B cell cluster, as they should.

docs.title: Dot plots¶
docs.text:
Dot plots encode two dimensions simultaneously:

  • Dot size: fraction of cells in the group expressing the gene (at least one count)
  • Dot colour: mean (scaled) expression over all cells of the group, zeros included

docs.title: Heatmaps¶
docs.text: Dot plots summarise each group. Want to see every single cell instead? The marker heatmap puts genes on the rows and cells on the columns, with a gap between clusters. Expression is z-scored per gene and clipped at 2.5 by default, otherwise a few extreme cells eat the whole colour range.

docs.title: Stacked violin plots¶
docs.text: Stacked violins show the per-group expression distribution of several genes in a compact vertical layout.

So, what has just happened ... ? Actually quite a lot of things:

  1. The matrix is being pulled into Rust and checked against the number of min_unique_genes, the min_lib_size and in how many cells a given gene needs to be expressed to be included. Once the genes and cells have been identified that pass the minimum threshold (in that order: first gene filtering, then check the cells against that reduced feature space), the cells are written to the first binary file: counts_cells.bin. At the same time the counts are normalised: division by library size, projected against desired target size and log transformed.
  2. Rust now transposes under the hood the data that is at the moment very nice to read in from a cell-centric level, less so from a gene-centric level. That is why we also have counts_genes.bin.
  3. Lastly, the observation and variable data is being reduced based on step 1 and written to the sc_duckdb.db and stored there.

What is cells to keep? Well, these are the (0-based) indices of cells that shall be included in the analysis, think HVG selection, PCA, kNN generation, etc. This used to be THE foot gun of this package, and it is still the thing to keep in your head. The cells_to_keep indices will be the ones loaded in by Rust. The other cells are not lost, they are still on disk (a massive difference between filtering in memory and on-disk work!). Also the DuckDB state will get updated, but let's get to this later.

Every index you hand to or get back from the package is a 0-based position in the binary store: cells_to_keep, the cell_idx column of obs, the gene_idx column of var and the cells / genes arguments of the count getter. There are also getters for the identifiers.

The print changed now! We have now told the experiment that only a subset of 682 cells shall be used in any downstream analyses. Understanding this is very important. Most functions will only return and work on the filtered cells, and you have to carefully think and remember what you did when. set_cells_to_keep takes 0-based indices or cell ids, as a numpy array or a list; hand it a polars Series and it complains, hence the .to_numpy().

Here is the Python-specific foot gun: sc.obs() returns all cells in the store, kept or not. The to_keep column tells you which is which, and filtered=True gives you only the kept ones.

The parents column is what makes this more than a cell counter. The kNN records the id of the PCA it was built on, and the neighbour graph (connectivities, the sNN by default) records the kNN. So watch what happens if we re-run the PCA on the same cells, just with fewer components, and don't touch the neighbours:

In [20]: Copied! 
bv.pp.calculate_pca(sc, 5)

sc.cache_status().select("artefact", "stale", "reason")

The PCA is fine. The kNN is stale because the PCA it points at no longer exists, and the neighbour graph is stale through the kNN, even though its own cell set never moved. A row-count check would have waved both of those through. The print says so too:

In [21]: Copied! 
sc
sc Out[21]:

In [22]: Copied!

Cached `connectivities` is stale: its upstream `knn` is stale. Re-run the step that produces it, or drop it, before using it.

Functions that only read a cached artefact for a metric warn on a stale one. Anything that hands cached indices to Rust or writes a result back onto the experiment, find_neighbours, find_clusters, the meta cell generators, errors outright rather than computing nonsense:

In [23]: Copied!

    bv.graph.find_clusters(sc)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"ValueError: {e}")

ValueError: Cached `connectivities` is stale: its upstream `knn` is stale. Re-run the step that produces it, or drop it, before using it.

Regenerating the neighbours puts the chain back together:

In [24]: Copied!

sc.cache_status().select("artefact", "stale", "reason")

set_cells_to_keep() warns about exactly the same thing, listing what it just invalidated. There is no global switch to turn the checks off or into errors.

Two things it deliberately does not do. Artefacts that carry no stamp (say, you assigned sc.cache.pca_factors yourself, which drops the stamp) report as unstamped and pass, because nothing is known about them either way. And the stamp tracks provenance, not parameters: a kNN built on the first 5 PCs and one built on all 10 of the same PCA look identical to it. Neither of those can produce an index mismatch, which is what this is here to stop.

If you want to go back to a clean slate, reset_cells_to_keep() restores every cell in the binary file and wipes the cache and the HVG selection. A PCA that took forty minutes is not the package's to bin, so with anything in the cache it raises unless you pass force=True:

sc.reset_cells_to_keep(force=True)

Filtering never deleted anything, it only ever flipped a to_keep flag in the DuckDB, so nothing is lost by resetting. The cache has to go though: a PCA computed on 682 cells does not describe 929 of them.

If you understand the concept shown above, you are good to go to analyse millions of cells on small compute without having 100's of GB of memory available. Let's just talk also about the 2nd big foot gun: the counts.

In [25]: Copied! 
raw_counts = bv.get_counts(sc, cells=range(50))

print(raw_counts.matrix.shape)

csr = raw_counts.scipy_csr()

print(type(csr))
raw_counts = bv.get_counts(sc, cells=range(50)) print(raw_counts.matrix.shape) csr = raw_counts.scipy_csr() print(type(csr)) 
(36, 81)

<class 'scipy.sparse._csr.csr_matrix'>

Fewer than 50 rows? get_counts respects the cells to keep by default, so of the first 50 store cells you only get the kept ones back (more on that below). This is the smart way: rows are cells, so Rust ONLY loads the cells that are needed. The stupid way is to pull everything and slice afterwards. Timing both on this toy data set:

In [26]: Copied! 
n_rep = 10

the_correct_way = timeit.timeit(
    lambda: bv.get_counts(sc, cells=range(50)).scipy_csr(), number=n_rep
)
the_incorrect_way = timeit.timeit(
    lambda: bv.get_counts(sc).scipy_csr()[:50], number=n_rep
)

print(f"the_correct_way: {the_correct_way / n_rep * 1e3:.2f} ms")
print(f"the_incorrect_way: {the_incorrect_way / n_rep * 1e3:.2f} ms")
n_rep = 10 the_correct_way = timeit.timeit( lambda: bv.get_counts(sc, cells=range(50)).scipy_csr(), number=n_rep ) the_incorrect_way = timeit.timeit( lambda: bv.get_counts(sc).scipy_csr()[:50], number=n_rep ) print(f"the_correct_way: {the_correct_way / n_rep * 1e3:.2f} ms") print(f"the_incorrect_way: {the_incorrect_way / n_rep * 1e3:.2f} ms") 
the_correct_way: 0.26 ms
the_incorrect_way: 0.32 ms

The difference seems marginal here, but it WILL bite you if you do this on large data sets. Also, the memory advantages this approach gives you will disappear if you load everything to throw most of it away. Also, another thing to REALLY consider... The indices you supply should match what the binary files have (0-based!) and again you need to THINK about the cells to keep. A nasty example here:

In [27]: Copied! 
counts_filtered = bv.get_counts(
    sc,
    # cells 0 to 9 as they were written to disk
    cells=range(10),
    # genes 0 to 9 as they were written to disk
    genes=range(10),
    use_cells_to_keep=True,
)

counts_unfiltered = bv.get_counts(
    sc,
    cells=range(10),
    genes=range(10),
    use_cells_to_keep=False,
)

for label, counts in (("filtered", counts_filtered), ("unfiltered", counts_unfiltered)):
    n_cells, n_genes = counts.matrix.shape
    print(f"Number of cells: {n_cells} | Number of genes: {n_genes} ({label} version)")

print(f"cells returned with use_cells_to_keep=True: {counts_filtered.cells}")
counts_filtered = bv.get_counts( sc, # cells 0 to 9 as they were written to disk cells=range(10), # genes 0 to 9 as they were written to disk genes=range(10), use_cells_to_keep=True, ) counts_unfiltered = bv.get_counts( sc, cells=range(10), genes=range(10), use_cells_to_keep=False, ) for label, counts in (("filtered", counts_filtered), ("unfiltered", counts_unfiltered)): n_cells, n_genes = counts.matrix.shape print(f"Number of cells: {n_cells} | Number of genes: {n_genes} ({label} version)") print(f"cells returned with use_cells_to_keep=True: {counts_filtered.cells}") 
Number of cells: 8 | Number of genes: 10 (filtered version)
Number of cells: 10 | Number of genes: 10 (unfiltered version)
cells returned with use_cells_to_keep=True: [0 1 2 3 4 6 7 9]

Wait, what happened here ... ? Because we set the cells to keep in the step with the pseudo mitochondrial counts, some of these indices are now "bad cells". They are not filtered, they are just not returned. The cells attribute of the result tells you which store cells you actually got.

If you want to avoid thinking about indices altogether (which is recommended), just use the identifiers:

In [28]: Copied! 
counts_by_id = bv.get_counts(
    sc,
    cells=["cell_0001", "cell_0003", "cell_0100", "cell_0117"],
    genes=["gene_001", "gene_002", "gene_003", "gene_081"],
)

print(f"cells: {sc.cell_ids(counts_by_id.cells)}")
print(f"genes: {sc.gene_ids(counts_by_id.genes)}")

counts_by_id.scipy_csr().toarray()
counts_by_id = bv.get_counts( sc, cells=["cell_0001", "cell_0003", "cell_0100", "cell_0117"], genes=["gene_001", "gene_002", "gene_003", "gene_081"], ) print(f"cells: {sc.cell_ids(counts_by_id.cells)}") print(f"genes: {sc.gene_ids(counts_by_id.genes)}") counts_by_id.scipy_csr().toarray()

And that's it. If you understand this vignette and the design choices, we have answered the why, the how and can move on to the what in the other vignettes with some example analyses and how to actually use the package to analyse single cell experiments.

docs.title: Thinking about single cells the bixverse way¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Thinking about single cells the bixverse way. Original authors: Gregor Lueg and Grant Neilson.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text: Before diving into this vignette, it would be really recommended to read the design choices to understand why single cell has been implemented the way it is in this package. This will make understanding the downstream text much easier. The aim of this vignette is to take some small synthetic data and point out some quirks due to design choices made.

docs.title: Synthetic data¶
docs.text: Let's start with some synthetic data that is powering all the tests in the package. It's very simple data with 1,000 cells, 100 genes and three very clearly defined cell groups. Genes 1 to 10 define cell_type 1, genes 11 to 20 the next cell type and 21 to 30 the last cell type. The remaining genes are noise genes.

docs.title: Loading in data¶
docs.text: An experiment is a directory. If you read the design docs, you know why you have to provide a path here. If you do not know why, go back to the docs. We point it at a temporary directory that is still empty:

docs.title: Interacting with the data¶
docs.text: Let's now look into how we interact with the data... We will actually apply some filters here (the synthetic data is weird, but does the job of assumption testing).

docs.title: Understanding mapping and filtering¶
docs.text: As data is stored on disk, we need to carefully synchronise state here between the DuckDB, the binary files and tell the Rust kernel which cells to use and what to do... There is a bunch of helpers for this. You might have spotted the kept count in the print. This is very important! Let's check this out:

docs.title: The cache knows when you've moved the goalposts¶
docs.text:
Here is where the foot gun used to go off. Anything cached on the experiment, the PCA, the embeddings, the kNN, the neighbour graph, was computed against a particular set of cells. Change the cell set and those artefacts describe a world that no longer exists. Re-run the PCA, forget the kNN, and you'd end up with a PCA over 682 cells sitting next to a kNN over 929. Nothing complained. It either crashed somewhere deep in Rust or, worse, quietly gave you mis-aligned biology.

The cache lives in memory on sc.cache; bv.io.save(sc) writes it next to the stores so load_existing brings it back. Every cached artefact carries a provenance stamp: a hash of the cell set it was computed on, plus pointers to whatever it was derived from. Let's build a small cache and look at it. Note that none of these return anything; they write into sc.

docs.title: Understanding count retrieval¶
docs.text: You have actually two files on disk... If you read the design doc you know why (if you don't, please read it!). The gene-major file serves the gene-centric work under the hood (HVG selection, for example). When you pull counts yourself, bv.get_counts() reads the cell-major file and hands back a Counts: the CSR matrix plus the 0-based store indices of its rows and columns. Let's say you are interested in the first 50 cells.

That is the picture people know from the paper, and it is worth being clear about what produced it. Neighbourhoods overlap, so smoothing over them makes nearby cells resemble each other in every gene at once. Gene-gene correlation after imputation is inflated, badly, and the inflation is a property of the graph rather than of the biology. Do not feed these values into Hotspot, SCENIC, differential correlation or CoReMo: those methods measure exactly the quantity MAGIC manufactures, and they will report the graph back to you as a finding. extract_dot_plot_data() has no layer argument for the same reason.

The layer is tracked like every other cached artefact, so it goes stale when the graph under it moves.

knn=30 is the neighbour count for the geodesic graph Palantir builds on the multiscale space, a different knob from the k of the input kNN graph. num_waypoints stays at its 1200 default; the reference notebook drops it to 500.

Two things do not mirror the reference, and both change what you get.

use_early_cell_as_start is True, so the early cell you name is the one that gets used. The reference snaps it to the nearest boundary cell of the diffusion map instead, and that candidate set is small, at most two cells per multiscale component. On a branching manifold the snap will cheerfully move a root cell onto a branch tip and run the whole trajectory backwards.

n_eigs is pinned at 10, leaving nine multiscale components. Left at None the count comes from the largest eigengap, and nothing stops that from landing on 3, i.e. two components. Two components cannot resolve a three-way branch: the erythroid arm separates fine but the monocyte and dendritic fate probabilities end up correlated, their branch masks collapse onto each other, and the gene trends for those two lineages come out nearly identical. There is a section on that below.

docs.title: Trajectory inference with Palantir and PAGA¶
docs.text: Python port of the R vignette Trajectory inference with Palantir and PAGA. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

docs.title: Intro¶
docs.text:
Two trajectory methods live in bixverse, both operating on the kNN graph you already built with bv.graph.find_neighbours().

Palantir (Setty et al., 2019) models differentiation as a Markov chain over a multiscale diffusion map of the cells. Out come a pseudotime per cell, the probability of each cell reaching each terminal state, and the differentiation entropy derived from those probabilities. It needs a start cell and, optionally, the terminal states.

PAGA (Wolf et al., 2019) abstracts the cell-level graph into a cluster-level one, where the edge weight between two clusters measures how much more connected they are than a random null model expects. Its maximum spanning forest is the backbone people usually draw. PAGA needs a clustering and nothing else.

The data set is the one from the Palantir sample notebook: 4142 human CD34+ bone marrow cells across 16106 genes, already filtered. Three lineages come out of it, erythroid, monocyte and dendritic cell, all seeded from a haematopoietic stem cell pool.

The two supporting pieces from that notebook are here too. MAGIC (van Dijk et al., 2018) smooths counts over the same kNN graph, which is what makes the marker plots readable. Gene trends fit a landmark Gaussian process per branch, the Mellon-based estimator the reference uses rather than the legacy GAM. Both are restricted to a gene subset in bixverse, for reasons spelled out where they come up.

docs.title: Feature selection, PCA and neighbours¶
docs.text:
Standard pipeline. The one choice worth spelling out is k = 30 on the kNN graph: Palantir builds its diffusion kernel from whatever graph is stored on the object, and 30 neighbours is what the reference uses. The distance metric has to be euclidean, since the diffusion kernel is a Gaussian over a metric distance and cosine is not one.

pruning does not have to move with k. A Jaccard threshold p asks two cells to share a fraction 2p / (1 + p) of their neighbourhoods, whatever k is, so the default 1/16 keeps the same ~12% at k = 30 as at k = 15.

docs.title: MAGIC imputation¶
docs.text:
MAGIC builds a row-stochastic operator over the kNN graph and applies it three times, so every cell becomes a weighted average of its neighbourhood. It is the same adaptive-bandwidth kernel Palantir uses for its diffusion map, so the two agree on what a neighbourhood is.

bv.pp.run_magic() writes the result onto the object as a cached layer, sc.cache.magic. It takes a gene list rather than doing everything, and that is deliberate: the output is dense, and the whole point of the on-disk store is not holding a dense cells-by-genes matrix. Pick the genes you want to look at.

docs.title: PAGA¶
docs.text: PAGA is the cheap one, so start there. It reads the kNN indices and a clustering, ignores the distances entirely, and gives back a clusters-by-clusters graph.

docs.title: Palantir¶
docs.text: The start cell and the three terminal states come straight from the reference notebook. The start cell was picked there for high CD34 expression; the terminal states are one cell each in the dendritic, monocyte and erythroid tips.

docs.title: Results back onto the object¶
docs.text: PalantirRes is keyed by cell id, not position, so join it onto obs on cell_id rather than assuming the two are in the same order.

docs.title: Letting Palantir find the terminal states¶
docs.text: Drop terminal_states and they get detected from the waypoint Markov chain instead. Handy when you have no prior, but treat the result as a starting point rather than an answer: the detection reads extremes of the multiscale space, and on data sets this size those are not always well determined.

docs.title: Gene trends¶
docs.text: bv.traj.run_gene_trends() does two things. First it assigns cells to branches: for each fate, the probability threshold is an expanding quantile over the pseudotime-sorted cells, made monotone with a cumulative maximum, so a fate's bar can only rise as differentiation proceeds. Then it fits a landmark Gaussian process with a Matern-5/2 kernel per branch, on a 500 point pseudotime grid.

docs.title: Where this can go wrong¶
docs.text:
Palantir has more moving parts than most methods in this package, and several of them fail quietly rather than loudly. In rough order of how often they bite:

  • Pruning too hard. Upstream of Palantir entirely. It costs you clusters, not pseudotime, but a one-cell cluster then walks into PAGA and comes back out as a fat edge into a dot, because the null model has almost no possible edges to normalise against. rescue=True (the default) reconnects the small components pruning cuts off, so this mainly bites with it switched off.
  • The start cell. Covered above. Set use_early_cell_as_start=False to get the reference behaviour and it can move your root onto a branch tip. If pseudotime comes back anti-correlated with what you expect, check start_cell on the result object first. Note that pseudotime is not pinned to zero at the start cell either: the refinement can put the minimum on a neighbour, and a start cell far from zero means it disagreed with your anchor.
  • eigen_converged is False. The diffusion eigensolve ran out of restarts, so the multiscale embedding is under-resolved. Everything downstream converges happily on noise, which is exactly why this is reported in run_info. Raise lanczos_max_restarts.
  • repair_edges > 0. The kNN graph was disconnected and Palantir bridged it to carry on. Raise k on find_neighbours() rather than living with the bridges.
  • stranded_waypoints > 0. Waypoints from which no terminal state is reachable. Their cells lose fate probability mass, so rows sum below one. A large count means the pseudotime-directed pruning cut too hard.
  • n_eigs. The one that bites hardest, and it is silent. Left at None the eigenvector count comes from the largest eigengap, and if that lands on 3 it leaves two multiscale components for a three-way branch. Nothing errors. What happens instead is that two of the three fates stop separating: their probabilities correlate, the branch selection hands the two branches almost the same cells, and their gene trends come out on top of each other. If two lineages give you the same curve, count the components before you blame the estimator. The check is below.
  • Branch masks are permissive by design. Even at a sensible n_eigs, a cell belongs to a branch when its fate probability is near the top of what has been seen up to its pseudotime, so the uncommitted trunk sits in every branch at once. That is the reference's logic and it is the right one, but it means two branches only diverge where their late cells differ. Check branch_cells overlap before reading much into two curves that hug.
  • The gene trend defaults are prior-dominated. Pseudotime is min-max scaled to [0, 1], so the reference's length_scale = 1 spans the entire domain and its sigma = 1 sits at roughly the signal scale of log-normalised expression. Almost any gene resolves into a smooth monotone or single-peaked curve. That is a presentation choice, not inference. Shorten length_scale in GeneTrendsParams before believing a bump.
  • Double smoothing. MAGIC averages over the graph and the GP averages over pseudotime. Running both is defensible for a figure and rarely necessary for the trend itself. If a feature only shows up with use_magic=True, that is worth knowing about.
  • A stale imputed layer. The layer is stamped against the kNN graph it came from, so sc.cache_status() flags it once the graph or the cell filter moves. run_gene_trends(use_magic=True) refuses to fit a stale one.

Counting the components: the multiscale frame has one column per component. The run below leaves n_eigs at the eigengap default and compares the monocyte and dendritic branch masks against the pinned run.
